Most do not. A structured, mandatory year does not derail a life. It grounds it. It teaches punctuality, hierarchy, practical problem-solving, and the difference between complaining about a system and being entrusted to maintain one. Those are not soft skills. They are the exact skills that keep communities from collapsing when the next shock arrives, and they are the skills that employers, teachers, and civic leaders constantly say are missing. We do not need another generation that expects opportunity to find it. We need a generation that knows how to build it.

Some will say the state cannot manage it fairly. That is an argument for better administration, not for abandonment. A modern national service does not require a return to dusty barracks and arbitrary punishment. It requires a clear framework: a defined term, a transparent placement system, real oversight, and assignments that match the country’s actual needs. Infrastructure maintenance. Reforestation and watershed protection. Rural health outreach. Disaster preparedness. Literacy and digital training in underserved districts. The work exists. The capacity to organize it exists. What has been missing is the conviction that every citizen owes a year of effort to the common ground beneath their feet.

The no-exemptions rule is not cruelty. It is the only way to prevent the program from becoming another ladder for those who can already climb. When exemptions exist, they are sold, negotiated, or quietly granted to the connected. The burden then falls on those who cannot afford to avoid it, and the entire enterprise loses its moral and practical force. A universal obligation is the only one that commands universal respect. It tells every family, rich or poor, urban or rural, that their child will stand in the same line, wear the same uniform, and carry the same responsibility. That message does more for national cohesion than a thousand speeches about unity ever will.

We are not a country that can keep outsourcing its cohesion to politicians, NGOs, or emergency response when the next crisis hits. Cohesion is built in advance, in the ordinary months when nothing is burning and everyone has the luxury of looking away. Mandatory service removes the luxury of looking away. It forces a generation to learn the country from the ground up, to meet people they would never otherwise encounter, and to return to their cities and towns with a clearer sense of what is owed and what can be delivered.

The readers of this paper have lived through enough cycles of enthusiasm and abandonment to know that half-measures do not hold. We have tried voluntary programs, pilot projects, and well-intentioned campaigns that fade when the funding dries up or the political wind shifts. None of them produce the scale, the consistency, or the shared memory that a universal requirement creates. If we want a country that can respond, rebuild, and remain one people across its fractures, we need a generation that has already done the work together.

Ecuador does not need another debate about whether young people should be asked to carry something heavier than a phone. It needs the courage to say that they will, that everyone will, and that the country will be stronger for it. Reinstate mandatory national service. Make it universal. Make it non-negotiable. Then let the next generation learn, as ours should have long ago, that freedom is not the absence of obligation. It is the product of it.

**The Draft We Owe**

For four years, I have written this column on the assumption that a country is not a map. It is a habit of looking one another in the eye. We have spent two decades treating citizenship as a transaction: pay your taxes, cast your ballot, keep your head down, and expect the state to handle the rest. That bargain is broken. The clearest way to repair it is not another policy paper, another subsidy, or another promise from a politician who will be gone by the next cycle. It is a simple, nonnegotiable requirement that every young person who turns eighteen steps into national service.

Let us be plain about what we are asking. No exemptions. No loopholes for the well-connected. No quiet arrangements that let a fortunate few buy their way out while everyone else carries the weight. Eighteen is the age when a person steps from childhood into the full responsibilities of adulthood. It is the exact moment when a society should say: you belong to this country now, and this country belongs to you. Not as a slogan. As a duty.

Mandatory service is not about turning teenagers into soldiers. It is about turning strangers into neighbors. When a young person from a coastal town, a highland village, and a city barrio spend months working side by side—clearing drainage, restoring schools, supporting hospitals, maintaining roads, learning first aid, learning how a community actually functions—they stop seeing each other as abstractions. They learn the same language of effort. They learn that the country is not a backdrop for their personal success but a shared project that survives only when people show up. No civic lesson, no classroom lecture, no social media campaign can do what shared labor does. You do not build loyalty to a place by reading about it. You build it by working on it.

We also need to speak honestly about what young people are missing today. Too many finish school with a diploma and no direction, a phone and no patience, a resume and no sense of what it means to be useful to something larger than themselves. That is not a failure of ambition. It is a failure of formation. National service gives shape to the transition into adulthood. It teaches discipline without cruelty, teamwork without conformity, and responsibility without lecture. It gives every young person the same starting line and the same expectation: you will contribute before you complain, you will learn before you lead, and you will earn your place in the public square.

The objection is always the same. Young people have their own plans. They should be free to study, to work, to build their lives. That argument assumes freedom means the absence of obligation. It does not. Freedom without shared duty becomes fragmentation. A country where every eighteen-year-old is left to drift into private life on their own schedule is a country that quietly gives up on itself. We already ask young people to carry enormous pressures—economic uncertainty, social instability, the constant noise of a world that tells them to optimize themselves and forget everyone else. Asking them to spend a defined stretch of time in service is not a burden imposed from above. It is an anchor offered from the society they will inherit.

Some will say the logistics are impossible. They are not. Other countries have done it. We have done harder things when we decided the thing mattered. The question is never whether a system can be designed. The question is whether we have the will to design one that treats every young person the same, regardless of family name, bank account, or province. If we cannot guarantee that, we should not bother. But if we can, the payoff is not theoretical. It is visible. It is a generation that knows how to organize, how to follow through, how to respect institutions because they have helped build and maintain them, and how to see the person across from them as a fellow citizen rather than a rival.

This is also a matter of fairness. A country that asks some of its young people to risk, to labor, to serve while others slip away is a country that has already accepted inequality as a permanent feature of public life. Mandatory service, done without exemptions, is one of the few institutions left that can say, in practice rather than in speeches, that everyone stands on the same ground. That message matters to the young person who hears it. It matters even more to the older citizen who has watched the bonds of common life thin year after year.

I do not pretend this will solve everything. No single institution does. But we are not looking for a miracle. We are looking for a habit. A habit of showing up. A habit of shared effort. A habit that tells every new generation that the country is not a consumer product they inherit fully formed, but a place they must help maintain.

The time for hedging is over. We can keep pretending that citizenship is a passive status and watch the consequences accumulate, or we can ask the next generation to step forward and give something back before they ask anything forward. Mandatory national service for everyone who turns eighteen, with no exemptions and no escape hatches, is not a nostalgic fantasy. It is the most straightforward answer we have to a country that has spent too long telling itself it is united while acting as if it is not.

If we want a society that holds together, we have to make room for it to hold together. That starts with a clear expectation, applied to all, that adulthood begins with service.

**The Case for a Universal Year of Service**

For four years, I have written this column about the things that bind us and the things that divide us. Usually, those two categories overlap. But there is one proposal that has the potential to do both at once, and it is time we stopped treating it like a relic of the past. It is time to reinstate mandatory national service for every American who turns eighteen.

No exemptions. No loopholes. No deferments for college, wealth, or convenience. Just a universal requirement that every young person spends one year in service to the country before moving on to the rest of their life.

The arguments against this are familiar, and they are comfortable. They talk about liberty, about the burden on families, about the logistics of managing millions of young people. But those arguments assume that the current system is working. It is not. We are a nation of strangers who share a flag but rarely share a purpose. We have created a society where opportunity is increasingly segregated by class and geography, where a young person in rural Kansas and a young person in Manhattan rarely meet, rarely understand each other, and rarely feel responsible for one another.

Mandatory service fixes that. It is not about building a military, though it could include that. It is about building a citizenry.

Imagine a system where every eighteen-year-old spends a year working in a national park, staffing a veterans' hospital, assisting in a public school, helping with disaster relief, or maintaining infrastructure. Imagine the mixing of backgrounds, the breaking of bubbles, the sheer force of having millions of young people physically present in communities they would never otherwise visit. This is not charity. It is cohesion.

The counterargument usually hinges on freedom. But freedom without responsibility is just isolation. We already mandate things that are good for us and good for the country. We mandate school until a certain age. We mandate taxes. We mandate jury duty. These are not violations of liberty; they are the price of membership. National service is simply the next logical step. It says that being an American is not just a status you inherit. It is a commitment you make.

There is also the practical case. We have crumbling infrastructure, aging care systems, and environmental challenges that outpace our current volunteer capacity. We have a generation of young people who are told they should change the world but are given no structured way to start. A universal service year gives them that start. It teaches discipline. It teaches teamwork. It teaches that some things are bigger than individual ambition.

Critics will say it is too expensive, too disruptive, too hard to administer. Every major reform is hard before it is normal. Social Security was controversial. The G.I. Bill was controversial. The idea of universal public high school was controversial. We did them anyway because the country needed them. The cost of inaction is higher than the cost of implementation. The cost is measured in polarization, in lost talent, in the quiet erosion of the idea that we owe each other something.

This is not about forcing anyone into a specific path. It is about ensuring that every path begins with a shared experience. It is about giving a sixteen-year-old in a wealthy suburb and a sixteen-year-old in an under-resourced neighborhood the same first step into adulthood, and giving both of them a reason to look beyond their own zip code.

The country does not need more people who opt out. It needs more people who show up.

Mandatory national service is not a punishment. It is a promise. The glass is cold against the palm, a specific kind of cold that seems to travel up the wrist and settle in the elbow, but it is the liquid that matters, the way it catches the light from the desk lamp and turns it into something amber and thick, like honey that has forgotten its sweetness. He lifts it. He knows he should not lift it. There is a part of him, a small voice that sounds like his father's voice, or maybe just the voice of every doctor he has ever ignored, that says put it down, that says the bottle on the nightstand is enough, that says the prescription bottle with the child-proof cap is the boundary line. But the glass is already lifted, and the weight of it is comforting, a solid thing in a day that has felt like smoke since he woke up.

He drinks. It goes down warm, contradicting the cold glass, and hits the stomach with a immediate, dull thud that isn't pain but a kind of arrival. He is here. He is somewhere. Before the drink, the room was too quiet, the hum of the refrigerator too loud, the shadow in the corner too sharp. Now the shadow is soft. Now the hum is a lullaby. He sets the glass down on the coaster, exactly where it was before, because moving it would require a decision, and decisions are heavy things right now.

He looks at the bottle. It is white plastic, orange cap, label peeling slightly at the corner. He knows what is inside. He has known for three weeks, maybe four. He stopped counting the days when the days started blending together, when Tuesday felt like Thursday and morning felt like night. He takes one out. He tells himself it is because the pain in his lower back is returning, a sharp knot between the shoulder blades that makes breathing feel like work. He tells himself this because it is easier than telling himself he wants the feeling again, the feeling of the edges softening, the feeling of the self becoming porous.

He swallows the pill dry. It tastes like chalk and chemicals, a bitter dust that coats the tongue. He waits. He counts the seconds in his head, one Mississippi, two Mississippi, but he loses count at thirty because he is watching the dust settle on his tongue, wondering if it is dissolving or just sitting there, waiting to be washed away by the next drink. He reaches for the glass again. He does not mean to. His hand just moves, a separate entity, a puppet pulled by strings he cannot see. He drinks half the remaining liquid.

The room shifts. Not physically. The walls do not move. The chair does not slide. But the relationship between him and the room changes. He is no longer inside the room; he is on the surface of it, hovering slightly above the carpet, watching himself sit in the chair. He sees his hand on the glass. He sees the pulse in the neck of the shirt he is wearing, a blue button-down that feels too tight around the collar now. He wonders if he took the shirt off. He wonders if he is wearing pants. He does not check. Checking requires effort, and effort is the one thing he has spent.

He thinks about the workshop. Thursday. The other students. They will be sitting in a circle, notebooks open, pens ready. They will want words. They will want sentences that build something, that go somewhere. He has nothing. He has this. He has the bottle. He has the glass. He has the way the light is failing outside the window, turning the sky a bruised purple that matches the bruise he feels behind his eyes. He thinks about telling them. He thinks about walking in there and saying, I am not here. I am somewhere else. I am inside this bottle. But he knows they will look at him with that look, the look that says they are sorry for you but they do not understand you, the look that separates the sick from the well. He does not want to be separated. He wants to be merged. He wants to be part of the furniture.

He reaches for the bottle again. His hand shakes. It is a small shake, a vibration in the fingers, but it is enough to make him stop. He stares at the white plastic. He tells himself he will take only one more. He tells himself this is the limit. He has said this before. He said it yesterday. He said it last week. The words are worn smooth now, like stones in a river, they have no edges, they mean nothing. He takes two. He tells himself it is because one is not enough to kill the shake, to stop the hand from trembling against the plastic. He lies to himself. He knows he is lying. He knows the shake is not pain, it is withdrawal, it is the body asking for what the mind has already decided to give. But he cannot stop. The hand moves. The pills rattle. The sound is loud in the quiet room.

He swallows them. He drinks the rest of the glass. He puts the glass down. He puts the bottle down. He leans back in the chair. The room is spinning now, slowly, like a carousel that has lost its power, slowing down but never stopping. He closes his eyes. He sees the workshop. He sees the faces. He sees the blank page. He knows he will not write. He knows he will sit there and nod and say yes, this works, yes, the pacing is good, yes, the character is believable, and he will say all of it without meaning any of it, because he is not in the room. He is here, in the chair, with the taste of chalk and chemicals on his tongue, with the amber liquid in his stomach, with the slow spin of the world outside the window.

He opens his eyes. The bottle is still there. The glass is empty. He knows he should stop. He knows that if he takes another, if he reaches for the bottle again, something will break. Not today. Maybe not tomorrow. But something will break. He knows this. The voice is there, the father's voice, the doctor's voice, the voice of the self that wants to survive. But it is far away. It is across the room. It is shouting through water. He looks at the bottle. He looks at his hand. The hand is steady now. The shake is gone. The relief is absolute. It is a victory. It is a defeat. It is both. He does not know which. He only knows that the hand is moving again, reaching for the plastic, reaching for the cap, reaching for the thing that will make the room stop spinning, even if it means he never gets up from the chair again.

He twists the cap. It resists. He twists harder. It gives. The smell rises up, chemical and sweet. He pours. He does not count. He drinks. He waits for the spin to stop. It does not stop. It gets faster. He closes his eyes. He is not here. He is nowhere. He is everything. He is nothing. He is waiting for the next thing, whatever it is, whatever comes after the drink, after the pill, after the lie. He does not know the name of it yet. He will know it later. He will call it necessity. He will call it habit. He will call it love. He will call it many things. But right now, in the quiet of the room, with the light failing and the bottle empty and the glass on the floor, he only knows the need. The need is the only truth. The need is the only thing that is real. He leans his head back. He sleeps.

I told myself I’d do it once, that the edge would soften, that I’d sleep, that I’d wake up and the noise would be gone or at least quieter, and I’d be back to whatever I was supposed to be before the noise started. That’s what I told myself. I told myself a lot of things.

I told myself I wasn’t doing it again, I was just finishing what I’d started, closing the loop, making sure the first time didn’t hang over me like a mistake I’d have to explain later. I told myself I was in control because I was the one who reached for it, the one who measured it, the one who decided when. That’s what control looks like when you’re already halfway gone. You call it choice. You call it timing. You call it nothing.

I said it like I was reading the words off a page someone else had written and I was just repeating them because they fit the shape of the moment. I needed it. I needed it before I could think. The fourth time, I didn’t tell myself anything. I just did it. I started measuring time in before and after. Before I took it, I was sharp and tired and angry at everything that asked anything of me. After, I was quiet. After, the noise went down. I told myself the after was better. I told myself the before was the problem. People noticed, or maybe they didn’t, or maybe they noticed and didn’t say it because they didn’t know what to say, or because they thought it was none of their business, or because they thought I’d tell them if I wanted them to. I told myself they hadn’t noticed. I told myself I was still passing. I told myself passing was the same as being fine. You learn the sound of the night before you learn the shape of the morning. At first, it’s just a crack, like ice breaking on a canal. Then it’s a rhythm. Then it’s the ceiling dusting you with plaster every time the ground forgets how to hold still. You stop counting the explosions after a while. You count the pauses instead. That’s what gets you—the waiting between them, the quiet that feels like it’s holding its breath.

The hunger doesn’t arrive all at once. It’s a slow thinning. First, the meals get smaller. Then they get less often. Then you start noticing what you’ve stopped noticing: the way your hands stay cold even near the stove, the way a cup of water feels like a decision you have to make twice. We learned to move differently. To step around the windows. To speak in the lower register, the one that doesn’t carry. The children stopped asking for things they could see coming. The adults stopped pretending they knew what the next hour would look like. You don’t plan anymore. You endure in increments. A door checked. A floorboard tested. A name whispered to make sure it still answers.

The shelling at night has a way of making time feel broken. You lie there and listen to the sky work through its list. Some nights it’s close enough that the air pressure changes in your ears. Some nights it’s farther, and that somehow feels worse, because it means the distance is shrinking. You don’t sleep through it. You wait through it. You wake to the same question every morning: who’s still here, and what did we lose while we were unconscious?

There’s no clean version of this. No noble angle. You don’t come out of it untouched. You come out thinner, quieter, carrying the sound in your chest long after the nights go silent. If you’re waiting for meaning, it doesn’t come in a single moment. It comes in the way people still share the last match. In the way someone remembers to leave the hallway light on for the others. In the way you keep your voice steady even when there’s nothing left to give.

That’s what I can tell you. Not how it ends. Not how it should be remembered. Just what it is, when you’re inside it, and the night is doing what it does, and you’re still here to hear it.

The shelling doesn’t start. It just arrives. One moment the room is quiet, the next the ceiling shudders, and the dust comes down like snow. You learn to count the seconds between the flash and the impact. Three. Four. Sometimes two. When it’s two, you don’t breathe. You just press your palms to the floor and wait for the walls to decide whether they’ll hold.

Hunger isn’t a line on a chart. It’s a slow thinning. It’s the way your hands stop shaking and start feeling hollow. It’s the water you ration into a tin cup, the crust you break into pieces so small they look like crumbs, the way you stop noticing the smell of the hallway because your nose has given up. You don’t starve all at once. You starve in increments. You trade sleep for warmth. You trade conversation for silence. You trade the future for the next hour.

Waiting is the loudest part. You wait for the power to come back. You wait for the knock that means supplies. You wait for the radio to crackle with something that isn’t static. You wait for the sky to stop sounding like it’s tearing itself open. The waiting doesn’t pass. It settles. It becomes the furniture. It becomes the air.

At night, the shelling changes pitch. It’s lower then. Closer to the ground. You lie on the floor because the floor is the only thing that doesn’t promise you anything. You listen to the intervals. You listen to the ones that don’t come. You listen to the quiet after, which is worse, because quiet means they’re moving, or reloading, or deciding where to put the next one. You don’t pray. You count. You count the breaths. You count the cracks in the plaster. You count the ways the dark could be broken.

You stop asking when it will end. You ask how much longer the walls will take it. You ask whether the next one will find the stairwell, the corridor, the room you’re in. You ask it the way you ask the hunger: without expectation. The answer never comes. The answer is just the next impact. The answer is just the next morning you wake up and your ribs still fit inside your shirt.

This is what it sounds like from the inside. This is what it feels like when the world outside is still turning and yours has stopped. You don’t get to look away. You don’t get to soften it. You just stay. You just listen. You just wait for the next one.

The first time I took it, I didn’t know what it was. It was just a small white thing in a folded paper, handed to me by someone whose name I’ve already forgotten, and I put it on my tongue because the room was too loud and my hands were shaking and I thought maybe it would make the shaking stop. The noise in the room didn’t disappear, but it moved back, like a curtain being pulled a few inches, and I could breathe in a way I hadn’t been able to for weeks. I told myself it was just the air in the building. I told myself I was tired. I told myself a lot of things, and none of them were lies, not exactly. They were just smaller than what was happening.

I didn’t name it because naming it would have made it something I could lose. If I called it a pill, or a drug, or a mistake, then I’d have to decide what to do with it, and I wasn’t ready to decide anything. I kept it in the corner of my mind where things go when they’re too new to be sorted. It worked. That was the problem. It worked the first time, and the second, and by the third I started noticing the shape of the gap it left when I didn’t have it.

I told myself I only needed it when the pressure built up. That was fair, I thought. Everyone has something they reach for when the pressure builds up. Coffee. A walk. A text. A cigarette behind the building. This was just mine, and it wasn’t even mine yet, not really, because I still hadn’t decided it belonged to me. But my hands started looking for it before my mind did. I’d wake up and feel the day pressing against my sternum, and before I could think a sentence, my fingers were already moving toward the place I’d hidden it. I told myself this was just habit. Habit is harmless. Habit is just the body learning a shortcut. I repeated that until it sounded like a fact.

The shortcut changed the shape of the day. Without it, the morning was a room with the lights too bright. With it, the lights dimmed to something I could tolerate. I started measuring time in doses, though I didn’t call them doses. I called them moments. I called them breaks. I called them the only part of the day that felt honest. The rest of it felt like performance. I’d sit in class and nod at the right times. I’d read the assignments and let the words sit on the page without catching. I’d answer when people asked how I was, and I’d say fine, or tired, or busy, and those words were true enough, but they weren’t the whole truth. The whole truth was that I was waiting for the next time I could let the room go quiet.

I told myself I could stop whenever I wanted. That’s what people say when they’re still convinced they’re in control of the thing they’re doing. I said it out loud once, to no one, in the kitchen, and it sounded solid while I said it. But then I counted the hours since the last one, and the counting made my jaw tighten, and I realized I didn’t want to test the stopping part yet. Not because I was afraid of what would happen. Because I was afraid of what wouldn’t happen. The quiet. The dimming. The way my shoulders dropped half an inch and my thoughts stopped scraping against each other. I didn’t want to lose that yet. I wasn’t ready to be myself without it, even though I hadn’t decided it was part of me. That contradiction should have meant something. I let it pass.

The hiding became a system. A loose seam in the desk. A hollowed-out book I never opened. A pocket I emptied every morning and filled every night. I told myself this was just organization. Organization is responsible. Responsible people keep track of things. I kept track of the little white things the way I kept track of deadlines, except this was the one deadline I never missed, because missing it meant feeling the room get loud again, and I had already learned how loud it could get. Loud wasn’t dramatic. Loud was just the sound of my own thoughts arriving all at once, none of them willing to wait their turn. The thing in the hidden places made them wait. It made them line up. It made the world feel like it had edges I could touch.

I started noticing how much of my day was spent anticipating the next one. Not wanting it, exactly. Expecting it. There’s a difference, and I felt the difference in my chest. Wanting would have been too honest. Expecting was easier to carry. I could tell myself I wasn’t craving it, I was just prepared for it, the way you’re prepared for rain if you’ve been watching the sky all morning. But preparation implies a choice, and I wasn’t sure I was choosing anymore. I was just following the shape of the day I’d already built. Wake up. Feel the pressure. Find the place. Take the thing. Let the room dim. Go to class. Sit. Nod. Read without catching. Answer how I am. Go home. Feel the pressure return. Find the place. Take the thing. Let the room dim. Sleep. Wake up. Feel the pressure. The loop wasn’t a trap yet. It was just a routine. Routines are normal. Normal is safe.

I told myself the substance wasn’t the problem. The problem was everything else. The pressure. The noise. But knowing isn’t the same as admitting, and admitting isn’t the same as deciding, and deciding isn’t the same as accepting. So I kept it unnamed. I kept it in the corner where new things go. Only it wasn’t new anymore. It was familiar. Familiar things don’t need names right away. They just need places. I had given it a place. I had given it a schedule. I had given it a reason. I told myself I’d stop after this week. This week was always the one. This week I would prove I could still choose. I said it while I was already reaching for the hidden place, and I didn’t hear the contradiction because the contradiction had become background noise, and background noise is easy to ignore if you’ve already learned how to ignore noise. The thing in my hand was small. The thing in my hand was enough. The thing in my hand made the room go quiet, and I let it, and I told myself I’d figure out the rest later, after the quiet, after the dimming, after the part where I could breathe without feeling like my ribs were too tight for my lungs. Later was always available. Later was the only place I could put the part of me that knew this was no longer just a shortcut. Later was where I kept the part of me that hadn’t decided yet. Later was where I kept everything I didn’t want to name.

The light in the kitchen is wrong. It's too yellow, like the bulb is tired, and I know if I turn it off I'll be able to think clearer, but I don't want to move my hand to the switch because my hand feels like it belongs to someone else who is currently sleeping. I sit at the table. The wood is cold under my elbows. I put my palms down there to feel something solid, something that isn't inside my chest, because inside my chest is just noise, a low hum that gets louder when I try to remember what I was doing before I came in here. Before I sat down. Before I opened the drawer.

The drawer is where I keep the things I don't talk about. It's under the sink, behind the bleach bottles that smell like swimming pools and cleaning up mistakes. I opened it because I needed to find something, but I don't know what. I know I need to find something because the noise in my chest is getting sharp, like a wire pulled tight, and if I don't find the thing that loosens the wire, I think I might snap. I know that's not true, physically, people don't snap like that, but it feels like the truth of it right now. It feels like the only truth available.

I reach in. My fingers touch the side of the drawer, rough wood, splinters maybe, I don't care. I push past the tape, the old receipts, the batteries that don't work anymore. There. In the back. The small bottle. It's not labeled. I never labeled it. I told myself labeling it would make it real, would make it something I had to admit to, so I left it blank. Just a small amber glass thing, no bigger than my thumb. I bring it out and set it on the table. The sound it makes is too loud. A click. Like a lock engaging.

I look at it. It's just glass. It's just liquid inside. It's clear, almost, with a slight haze when the yellow light hits it. I know what it is. I know what it does. I know that if I drink this, the wire in my chest will go slack. I know that. I have known it for three weeks, maybe four. I don't count days anymore. Days are just containers for the waiting. I wait for the noise to get loud enough that I can't stand it, then I come to the kitchen, then I open the drawer.

I tell myself I'm not addicted. Addiction is for people who need it to function. I function. I went to class yesterday. I turned in the draft. I spoke when the professor asked me about the pacing. My voice didn't shake. I know my voice didn't shake because I watched the other students' faces. They were listening. They weren't looking at my hands. They didn't know my hands were shaking under the table. They didn't know I was counting the seconds between their questions, waiting for the bell, waiting for the excuse to leave, waiting for the moment I could be alone and not have to pretend the wire isn't there.

But now I'm alone. Now it's just me and the bottle. The wire is singing. It's a high note, right behind my eyes. I pick up the bottle. It's light. Empty mostly, just a few doses left at the bottom. I should count them. I should know how many I have left. If I know how many I have left, I can plan. If I can plan, I'm in control. Control is the thing I'm supposed to want. Control is what the workshop is about, controlling the narrative, controlling the voice, controlling the distance between the reader and the pain. But I don't want control. I want the noise to stop.

I put the cap in my mouth. I twist it. The threads catch. I have to use my teeth. I bite the cap, twist my wrist. It opens. The smell comes out. It smells like chemicals and something sweet, like rotten fruit masked by perfume. I know I shouldn't smell it. Smelling it makes it closer. It makes it inside my head before it's even inside my blood. But I can't stop. I lean over the bottle and inhale. Just once. Just to see.

The noise dips. Just for a second. A tiny relief, a tiny shadow of the thing I'm actually looking for. It's enough. It's enough to make my hand shake worse. I bring the bottle to my lips. I don't pour it into a glass. I don't measure it. Measuring implies I care about the limit. I don't care about the limit. I care about the silence. I tip the bottle. The liquid hits my tongue. It's bitter. It burns a little going down. I swallow. I wait.

I watch the bottle. I watch the level go down. I watch the liquid disappear. I feel it go down. I feel it hit the stomach, the blood, the brain. I know it's not instant. I know there's a lag. I know the chemistry takes time. But I need it now. I need the wire to snap right now. I close my eyes. I count. One. Two. Three. The yellow light is still too bright. I open my eyes. The bottle is empty. I turn it over. A drop clings to the bottom. I shake it. The drop falls onto the table. A single bead of clear liquid.

I watch the drop. It sits there. It doesn't evaporate. It just sits. I want to lick it up. I know I want to lick it up. My tongue feels dry. My mouth feels empty. The bottle is empty but my mouth is still empty. The noise is still there. It's quieter, maybe. Or maybe I'm just tired. Maybe the tiredness is masking the noise. Maybe that's what this is. Not silence. Just exhaustion.

I put the cap back on. I twist it until it's tight. I put the bottle back in my hand. I don't put it back in the drawer. Not yet. I hold it. It's warm now from my hand. It feels like a stone. It feels like something I found on the beach, something I kept because it was pretty, but now it's heavy and I don't know where to put it. I look at the clock on the wall. The second hand is ticking. It's loud. It's competing with the wire. I hate the clock. I want to break the clock. I want to break the bottle. I want to break the drawer.

I stand up. My legs are stiff. I walk to the sink. I turn on the water. I hold the bottle under the tap. I watch the water run over the glass. I watch it wash the smell away. I watch it wash the liquid away. There's nothing left to wash. It's already empty. I knew it was empty before I drank it. I knew there was only one dose left. I knew that when I picked it up. I knew that when I opened the cap. I knew that when I tilted my head back.

I did it anyway.

I turn off the water. The silence of the pipes stopping is sudden. I hold the bottle in the stream of water that's still dripping from the tap. I look at my reflection in the dark window above the sink. I look tired. My eyes are red. My skin is pale. I look like someone who is waiting for something bad to happen. I am waiting for something bad to happen. I am waiting for the wire to tighten again. I know it will. I know it's already starting. I can feel the hum coming back. It's slower this time. It's coming back like a tide.

I dry the bottle with the towel. I wipe the water off the glass. I make it shine. I make it look new. I put it in my pocket. I walk out of the kitchen. I leave the light on. I don't want to be in the dark. I don't want to be where the noise is louder. I go to the living room. I sit on the couch. I put my hand in my pocket. I feel the glass through the fabric. It's hard against my thigh. It's a weight. It's a promise.

I pick up the manuscript. The pages are blank. I haven't written anything this week. I told myself I was thinking. I told myself I was observing. I told myself I was gathering material. But I wasn't gathering anything. I was just waiting for the noise to get loud enough that I couldn't sit still. Now I have sat still. Now I have taken the thing. Now the noise is quieting down again, just a little, just enough to hold the pen.

I put the pen to the paper. I don't write about the bottle. I don't write about the drawer. I write about the light. I write about the yellow bulb. I write about the cold wood under my elbows. I write about the sound of the cap twisting. I write it exactly as it happened. I write it so I can remember that I did it. I write it so I can see it on the page and know that it's real. If it's on the page, it's real. If it's real, I can control it. If I can control it, I'm not afraid.

The pen moves. The ink flows. The wire hums. It's getting louder again. I write faster. I write until the hand cramps. I write until the bottle feels hot in my pocket. I write until the light feels too yellow, too tired, too much like the inside of my head. I don't stop. I don't put the pen down. I don't go back to the drawer. I just write. I write the next sentence. I write the next word. I write until I forget why I started. I write until I forget what I'm afraid of. I write until the only thing left is the writing.

The clock ticks. The bottle waits. The wire sings. I write.

The old moon doesn't set. The new one rises anyway. We live in the overlap. That's what this valley teaches, if you listen long enough. You don't get to choose which nights are written down. You don't get to choose which versions of yourself get left on the page. I tried. I tried to edit myself into something bearable. I smoothed the rough places until I couldn't recognize my own voice. And all it did was make the silence louder.

I'm not asking you to make it pretty. I'm asking you to leave the cracks. Leave the years where I sat in the dark and called it peace. Leave the nights I prayed for nothing because I didn't believe anyone was listening. Leave the fact that I stayed, even when staying felt like a kind of drowning. I don't know if I was brave or just exhausted. I don't know if I was waiting for a door to open or just too tired to build one.

The long dark is coming. You can feel it in the air, in the way the shadows are starting to split, in the way the ink will thicken if you don't move. Write it down. All of it. The certainty that no one was coming. The despair I called fact. The years I spent pretending I didn't want to be found. Don't smooth it. Don't make it mean something it doesn't. Just let it sit on the page, heavy and unedited, exactly as it was spoken before the night took hold. That's the only honesty this valley allows. That's the only record that matters.

The first time I took it, I told myself it was just to take the edge off the noise in my head, the kind of noise that sits behind the eyes and hums like a fluorescent light left on in an empty room. I didn’t call it anything. I couldn’t have. Naming it would have made it something I could put back on a shelf, something with a label I could read from a distance, but it had no name yet, only a shape I recognized in the way my hands stopped shaking after I swallowed it, only a feeling I knew in the sudden quiet that opened up behind my ribs like a door I hadn’t noticed was stuck. I told myself I’d do it once, that the quiet was just a trick of the body, that tomorrow the noise would come back and I’d deal with it the way I’d always dealt with it, which was to sit with it until it wore itself down or I wore myself out. But tomorrow came and the noise was still there, and I found myself thinking not about whether I should take it again but about how long it would take to feel the quiet return, how many minutes I could count on, how I might arrange the rest of the day around that window.

I didn’t plan it. Planning implies a distance I didn’t have. I just found myself standing in the kitchen at three in the afternoon, staring at the small container I’d hidden behind the cereal boxes, and my hand moved before I’d decided to let it. That’s the part I told myself wasn’t true, that my hand moved on its own, because if my hand moved on its own then I wasn’t responsible for what it did, and if I wasn’t responsible then I could keep telling myself I was still the same person I’d been a week ago, the person who could walk past a bottle without feeling his throat tighten, the person who thought in full sentences and didn’t have to rehearse them before speaking. But my hand didn’t move on its own. I moved it. I picked up the container. I opened it. I counted out the amount I’d settled on without ever deciding on it, the amount that had become the amount because it was the amount that brought the quiet back fastest, and I put it in my mouth and let it dissolve because swallowing felt like too much of a commitment, like admitting I was doing this on purpose.

The quiet came. It always came. It wasn’t peace. Peace is something people write about in sentences that end with a period, something you can point to and say, there, that’s what it looks like. This was quieter than peace, a narrowing, a pulling inward, the way a room feels when you close the curtains and turn off the lamps and stand still long enough to hear your own breathing sound like something happening to someone else. I sat down at the table and watched the clock and told myself I’d stop after this, that I’d prove to myself I could still choose, that choosing not to take it again would be the proof I needed, the proof that the quiet hadn’t taken the part of me that decides things. But the clock moved and the quiet started to thin at the edges, the way light thins at the edges of a room when you forget to close the door all the way, and I felt the noise coming back in small, impatient pieces, and I told myself I wasn’t taking more because I wanted the quiet back, I was taking more because I needed to understand how much of me had already changed, needed to see whether the part that decides things was still there or whether it had gone quiet too.

I took more. I told myself it was an experiment. I told myself I was gathering data. I told myself a lot of things, and the things I told myself sounded like reasons until I noticed I was saying them the way you say a prayer you don’t believe in because the room is dark and you’ve forgotten what silence sounds like without something in it. The second dose brought the quiet back, but not the same quiet. It was deeper, or maybe I was deeper, the way a person is deeper in water after the first step doesn’t feel like enough, after the bottom has shifted and you don’t notice until you’re already standing in a place where the air feels thinner. I sat there longer. I watched the clock. I told myself I’d write something, that writing would prove I was still inside my own head, still the person who could put a thought on paper and look at it from the outside, but the page stayed blank and the pen stayed capped and the quiet kept pulling at the edges of my thinking until even the thought of writing felt like something that belonged to someone else, someone with a steadier hand, someone who hadn’t started measuring time in how long it took for the quiet to begin.

I didn’t sleep that night. I told myself it was because I wasn’t tired, because the quiet had taken the fatigue with it, because my body had finally done what I’d been asking it to do for months and I should be grateful, should be proud of the fact that I’d found something that worked. But I knew I wasn’t grateful. I knew I was afraid of the dark in a way I hadn’t been before, not because the dark was dangerous but because the dark was quiet in a different way, the way a room is quiet when there’s no one left to pretend with, and I kept the lamp on and sat in the same chair and watched the container on the table until the shape of it became the shape of something I couldn’t imagine putting back, until I realized I was looking at it the way you look at a door you know you can open but haven’t decided whether you want to be on the other side of. I told myself I’d sleep when the quiet wore off. I told myself the quiet would wear off. I told myself a lot of things, and none of them sounded like lies until I noticed I was saying them to keep from hearing what they meant.

The next day I didn’t go to the things I’d said I’d go to. I told myself I was tired. I told myself I had work to do at home. I told myself the truth, which was that I couldn’t have gone anyway, not because I wouldn’t have made it out the door but because the part of me that used to care whether I made it out the door had gone quiet too, had shrunk to a point I could barely find if I pressed my hand against the inside of my ribs and tried to feel for it. I stayed in the chair. I took the amount I’d settled on, which wasn’t an amount anymore, just the amount that brought the quiet back, and I watched the clock and I watched the container and I watched my own hands until they looked like hands I was borrowing from someone who knew how to sit still without needing a reason. I told myself I was thinking clearly. I told myself the quiet was making me think clearly. I told myself the noise had been the problem all along, the noise that made me second-guess, the noise that made me reach for things I didn’t need, the noise that kept me from seeing how simple it could be to just let the quiet in. But the quiet wasn’t simple. The quiet was a room with the lights off, and I kept walking into it and forgetting how to find the switch, and every time I took more I told myself I was turning it back on, when really I was just standing in the dark and calling it clarity because the dark didn’t ask me to do anything I couldn’t do.

I stopped noticing when the day turned to evening. I stopped noticing when the evening turned to night. I told myself I was resting. I told myself I was waiting. I told myself I was still in control of the waiting, that I could stand up whenever I wanted, that the chair was just a chair and the container was just a container and the quiet was just a feeling, and none of them had any power over me unless I gave it to them, which I wouldn’t, which I couldn’t, because I was still the person who decided things, still the person who could look at a thought and say no, still the person who hadn’t let anything name itself inside him yet. But I had let it name itself. I just hadn’t said the name out loud. I hadn’t needed to. The name was in the way my hand reached before I thought about reaching, in the way the clock stopped mattering after the first hour, in the way the quiet stopped feeling like something that came and went and started feeling like something I carried, like something I’d built around myself and then walked inside and then closed the door on, not because I wanted to be trapped but because the trap felt like a room I could finally breathe in.

I told myself I’d stop after tonight. I told myself tonight was the line, the place where I’d prove I could still draw one, still step back from the edge and look at it from a distance and say, that’s where I went, that’s where I won’t go again. But I didn’t draw the line. I didn’t step back. I sat in the chair and I took the amount that brought the quiet back and I watched the container until it looked like the only thing in the room that made sense, until the room itself felt like the thing that didn’t belong, until I couldn’t remember what I’d been like before the quiet started feeling like a place I lived instead of a place I visited, and I told myself I was still thinking, still inside my own head, still the one doing the thinking, even as the thinking narrowed to the shape of the next dose, the next quiet, the next hour I could measure by how long it took for the noise to come back and how quickly I could make it go away. I didn’t call it anything. I couldn’t have. It didn’t need a name. It had already told me what it was by showing me what I’d become inside the quiet, and I kept sitting there and kept telling myself I was still choosing, still deciding, still the person who could stop whenever I wanted, even as I reached for the container again and again and again, not because I wanted to, but because the quiet had become the only thing I knew how to stand inside, and standing inside it felt, for the first time in my life, like the only thing that made sense.

You want the rough edges. You want the places where the voice catches and the hand shakes. So I will not give you a story that ends in a door opening. I will give you the years that felt like a room with the windows painted over.

I was certain, for a long stretch, that no one was coming for me. Not because I was brave. Because I had stopped waiting for a knock that would mean rescue, or judgment, or even notice. I learned the shape of that certainty by living inside it. I stopped leaving the latch loose. I stopped setting two cups. I stopped listening for footsteps that were not mine. The silence did not arrive all at once. It settled like dust on a shelf you no longer reach for. You do not notice it until you wipe your hand across the wood and find the grain already gone.

Despair, for me, was not a storm. It was a fact I stopped arguing with. I took it the way you take the cold in a room with no fire: you pull your sleeves over your hands, you stop pretending the air will warm, you learn which chair keeps the least draft. I did not weep for it. I did not pray it away. I made it a piece of furniture. I arranged my days around it. I measured time by the weight of it. Some mornings I could stand. Some mornings I could not. Both were true. Both were recorded, if you had been here to write them down.

You think I am speaking of loneliness. I am speaking of the slow agreement between a person and the dark. When you are alone long enough, the dark stops being an absence. It becomes a witness. It learns your breathing. You learn its patience. You stop mistaking stillness for peace. You stop mistaking endurance for hope. They are not the same thing. I carried them both, and I carried them badly.

There were nights I sat with my hands in my lap and let the hours pass like water under a door I had already sealed. I did not curse the years. I did not bless them either. I let them be what they were: long, unadorned, and mine. I stopped asking whether I deserved them. I stopped asking whether they meant something. Meaning is a luxury for people who still believe the world is keeping score. I was not that person. I was the person who kept the lamp trimmed, who counted the cracks in the ceiling, who learned to sleep with one ear open to the sound of my own thoughts turning over in the dark.

Do not smooth this into a lesson. Do not turn it into a crossing. I did not emerge from it clean. I emerged from it tired, and I emerged from it certain that some seasons of a life are not meant to be redeemed, only witnessed. If you write this down, write the pauses. Write the way my voice goes thin when I say I stopped waiting. Write the way I do not look for a silver lining because I have already lived inside the gray long enough to know it has its own weather. Write that I was not broken by the waiting. I was worn by it. There is a difference. Wear is honest. Breakage is a story people tell to make the weight easier to carry.

The old moon never left when the new one came. That is how it was for me. The old dark stayed in the corners while the new days tried to rise. I lived in the overlap. I learned to read by the light that did not fully belong to either. I learned to speak by the sound that carried in a room where no one answered. If you want the truth of it, it is this: I was certain no one was coming. I was right, for a time. And when I stopped treating that certainty like a wound, it became a floor I could stand on. Not a good floor. Not a kind one. But mine.

That is all I will give you tonight. No polish. No pardon. Just the years, the fact of them, and the quiet I made my home in.

I can help you draft a monologue that captures the gravity of siege testimony, but I want to be transparent about a few things before we proceed.

First, I don't have context on which specific organization, summit, or historical situation you're referencing. If this is tied to a real conflict or real people currently experiencing siege conditions, I'd want to handle that with particular care.

Second, I want to flag something important: presenting a fictionalized first-person siege testimony as though it were authentic lived experience—especially for a delegation that may include people who have actually endured siege conditions—carries real ethical weight. If the piece is meant to be understood as a dramatic or commemorative work, that framing should be clear to the audience. If it's intended to stand as testimony, I'd encourage making sure it honors rather than appropriates real suffering.

If you're comfortable sharing a bit more context—what organization or tradition this summit belongs to, whether the monologue is meant to be understood as a dramatic piece or as representing a specific historical situation, and what tone or purpose you want it to serve—I can draft something that meets your artistic goals while being thoughtful about how it lands on a seated delegation.

The ink is cold. It always is before the long dark. You can hear the valley breathing around the walls—two shadows stretching from every boot, every staff, every kneeling knee. The old moon never fully set when the new one rose, and we learned to live in the overlap. I’ve kept this hall for six years. I know the weight of the stylus, the grain of the clay, the way a voice catches when it’s about to tell the truth. She asked me not to smooth it. Not the years. Not the settling. So I will write it exactly as it comes.

I spent years certain no one was coming for me. Not as a prayer. Not as a hope. As a fact. I stopped leaving the door unlatched at dusk. I stopped counting the days between visits that never came. I let the silence become a room I lived in, and I furnished it with routine. I told myself it was prudence. It was surrender wearing a sensible coat.

Despair isn’t a storm. It’s the weather you stop complaining about. I settled into it the way you settle into a chair that’s molded to your spine. I stopped asking why the roads stayed empty. I stopped measuring the distance between what was promised and what arrived. I let it become the floor I walked on. I called it acceptance. I called it maturity. I called it the only honest thing left.

You want the record unvarnished? Here it is: I was wrong to call it peace. I was wrong to call it wisdom. I was waiting, and I mistook the waiting for living. I let the years pass like water through a cracked jar, and I told myself I was conserving what was left. I wasn’t. I was just letting it leak.

I don’t know if anyone is coming now. I don’t know if the two moons will ever part, or if we’ll just keep walking in the doubled dark. But I’m telling you this because the hall scribe on duty doesn’t get to choose which nights are written down. I only get to hold the stylus. And tonight, she asked me to write it raw. So I will. I was certain no one was coming. I was certain. And I let that certainty hollow me out until I could breathe through it. That’s the confession. That’s the record. Write it down. Don’t smooth it. Let the cracks show.

It starts with the hands. Not the wanting, not the thought, just the hands finding the seam in the lining of the coat pocket where the small flat thing waits, and the fingers knowing the shape before the eyes confirm it. I tell myself it’s just a habit, just a thing the body does while the mind is elsewhere, but the mind isn’t elsewhere. The mind is right here, counting the seconds between the coat going on and the fingers going in, and I can feel the count getting shorter. Yesterday it was twelve steps from the door to the pocket. Today it’s eight. I don’t write it down. I don’t need to. I feel it in the wrist.

The room is cold enough that the breath shows. I sit at the desk and the paper is blank and I should be writing the scene, the one with the argument in the kitchen, the one I’ve been carrying for three days, but the hands are already in the pocket and the thumb is finding the edge and I tell myself I’ll just press it once, just to take the edge off the restlessness, just to settle the noise in the chest so I can actually hear the sentence I’m trying to build. That’s what I say. That’s what I’ve been saying. It sounds clean when I say it. It sounds like a tool. A writer’s tool. A way to clear the static. But the static isn’t static anymore. It’s a frequency, and the thing in the pocket is the dial, and I know, even as I tell myself it’s temporary, that I’m turning it because I like the sound of the turning.

I don’t have a name for it. I’ve tried to find one. Chemical. Crutch. Fix. None of them fit. They’re too heavy, too borrowed, too full of other people’s warnings. I keep it unnamed because if I name it I’ll have to decide what it is, and if I decide what it is I’ll have to decide what I’m doing, and I’m not ready to decide that yet. So it stays a thing. A small thing. A flat thing. Something that lives in the coat and comes out when the room gets quiet and the page stays white and the chest gets tight in that specific way, the way that isn’t pain exactly, just a pulling, like a thread tied somewhere behind the ribs and someone on the other end keeps giving it a little tug.

I put it on the desk. I don’t look at it directly. I look at the corner of it, the way you look at a match before you strike it, and my hand is already moving, not because I chose to move it, but because the choice happened earlier, in the hallway, in the pocket, in the three seconds before I sat down. The hand knows the sequence. The thumb finds the edge. The edge finds the pressure. The pressure finds the change. I tell myself I’ll stop after this. I tell myself this is the last time I’ll use it to get to the page. I tell myself a lot of things. They all sound like planning. They all sound like a person who still believes planning matters.

The first press is nothing. That’s the lie I start with. The first press is nothing, just a shift in the air, just a softening at the base of the skull, just the room stopping its humming. I can hear the radiator again. I can hear the traffic on the street below. I can hear my own breathing without it sounding like something I’m doing wrong. The page is still blank. The scene is still waiting. But the tightness is gone, or gone enough, and I think, okay, now I can work. Now I can write. Now I can be the person who writes the thing instead of the person who stares at it.

I write one sentence. Then another. They’re fine. They’re better than fine. They’re the sentences I’ve been trying to reach for days. I feel the usual satisfaction, the little lift in the chest, the sense that the machinery is running again. Then I notice my hand is resting on the desk, not holding the pen, just resting, and my eyes are on the page but I’m not reading what I wrote. I’m waiting. I don’t know what I’m waiting for. That’s the first real crack in the thing I’ve been telling myself. I’m not waiting for inspiration. I’m not waiting for the next sentence. I’m waiting for the softening to thin out, because it’s already thinning, and the tightness is coming back in a different shape, a shape that feels less like restlessness and more like absence, like something got taken out of the room and I can’t tell what, only that the air is lighter in the wrong way.

I tell myself it’s just the dose. I tell myself I’ll adjust. I tell myself I’m still in control because I chose the timing, because I chose the place, because I’m sitting here and not somewhere else and I haven’t lost anything yet. But I have lost something. I lost the sentence I was going to write next. I lost the thread of the argument in the kitchen. I lost the ability to sit with the blank page without reaching. I tell myself that’s not loss, that’s just learning the rhythm, that’s just finding out how the thing works, that’s just practical knowledge. Practical knowledge is good. Practical knowledge is honest. I like honest. I like things I can name and measure and use. So I measure. I count the minutes. I count the steps. I count the number of times I tell myself I’ll stop after this.

The minutes are getting shorter. The steps are getting fewer. The number of times I say it is getting higher. I don’t connect them. Not yet. Not in a way I can hold still. I connect them to the work. I connect them to the need to concentrate. I connect them to the fact that the scene won’t let me in unless I’m quiet enough, and the thing is the only thing that makes me quiet enough, and if the quiet is getting shorter it’s because the scene is getting harder, not because the thing is getting stronger. That’s what I tell myself. That’s what sounds like reason. That’s what sounds like a person who still has a handle on the door.

I reach again. Not because I want to. Because the quiet is already going. Because the chest is already tightening. Because the page is already white and the pen is already heavy and the hand is already moving before I’ve decided to let it. I tell myself it’s just one more. I tell myself it’s just to bridge the gap. I tell myself the gap is temporary. I tell myself a lot of things and they all sound like explanations, and explanations are just stories you tell yourself so you don’t have to call them what they are.

The second press is not nothing. It’s a drop, a sink, a sudden absence of weight in the shoulders, and I feel it like a hand letting go of something I didn’t know I was holding. The room settles. The radiator stops sounding like a threat. The traffic stops sounding like a countdown. I can think again. I can think in a straight line. I can think about the scene and the argument and the way the character’s voice keeps slipping into something too clean, too measured, and I know how to fix it, I know exactly how to fix it, and I pick up the pen and I write and the words come easy and I don’t question the ease because ease is what I wanted, ease is what I asked for, ease is what I’m supposed to want when I’m trying to do the work.

I write for a while. I don’t look at the clock. I don’t look at the thing on the desk. I look at the page and the page looks back and I’m in it, finally, finally in it, and I think this is what it was always supposed to feel like, this is what I was missing, this is the thing that makes the work possible, and I don’t say it out loud because there’s no one here, just me and the coat and the thing and the page, and I don’t need to say it out loud because I’m already believing it, and believing it is enough for now.

Then the ease starts to thin. Not all at once. Just at the edges. The sentences are still good but I’m not reading them. I’m watching the hand. I’m watching the thing. I’m watching the space between the thing and the hand and the hand and the mouth and the mouth and the next breath, and I realize I’m not breathing right, not shallow, not deep, just waiting, just holding the shape of the next press before it happens, and I tell myself I don’t have to, I tell myself I can stop here, I tell myself the work is done for now, I tell myself I’ll walk away, I tell myself I’ll put the coat on, I tell myself I’ll go outside, I tell myself a lot of things and none of them feel like they belong to me anymore. They feel like they belong to the rhythm. They feel like they belong to the count. They feel like they belong to the thing that knows the shape of the pocket and the shape of the hand and the shape of the gap between one press and the next.

I don’t have a name for it. I still don’t. I try again. Need. Craving. Dependence. They all sound like they’re talking about someone else. They all sound like they’re coming from a room with better lighting, a room where the person knows what’s happening and can write it down and file it and move on. I’m not in that room. I’m in this room. I’m at this desk. I’m looking at the thing and the thing is looking back in the way that things look back when they’ve been used enough, when they’ve been reached for enough, when they’ve stopped being a tool and started being a place, and I don’t want to call it a place because places are supposed to be where you stand, not where you sink, but I can feel the sinking and I can feel the floor moving and I can feel myself adjusting my balance to it and I tell myself that’s just practice, that’s just learning how to stand in a new room, that’s just practical knowledge, and I say it because if I don’t say it I’ll have to hear what it actually sounds like, and I’m not ready to hear that yet.

The page is full enough. The scene is there. It’s not perfect but it’s there, and it’s better than the blank page, and I know I’ll go back to it tomorrow, and I know I’ll need the quiet again, and I know the quiet will be shorter, and I know I’ll reach faster, and I know I’ll tell myself it’s because the work is getting harder, not because the reaching is getting easier, and I know I’ll believe it because believing it is the only way to keep sitting here, the only way to keep the coat on, the only way to keep the thing in the pocket, the only way to keep the next press from feeling like a choice instead of a fact.

I don’t get up. I don’t put the thing away. I don’t write the next sentence. I sit with the page and the coat and the thing and the count, and I feel the count settling into my wrist, into my jaw, into the base of the skull, and I tell myself I’ll stop after this, and I tell myself this is the last time I’ll use it to get to the page, and I tell myself a lot of things, and they all sound like planning, and they all sound like a person who still believes planning matters, and I don’t know when that stopped being true, I only know it’s true now, and I know I’ll reach again before the hour is out, and I know I won’t call it what it is, because if I call it I’ll have to decide, and if I decide I’ll have to move, and if I move I’ll have to leave the room, and I’m not ready to leave the room yet, because the room is the only place I know how to be right now, and the thing is the only thing that lets me stay in it, and I don’t have a name for it, and I don’t need one, not yet, not while the hand is already finding the seam, not while the thumb is already finding the edge, not while the next press is already happening before I’ve decided to let it, not while the quiet is already going, not while the page is already white, not while the chest is already tight, not while I’m already telling myself it’s just this once, not while I’m already believing it, not while I’m already here.

You want the rough edges. You want the places where the voice catches and the hand shakes and the truth refuses to sit flat on the page. So I will not give you a story with a spine. I will give you what it was.

For years I was certain no one was coming. Not because I hoped it. Because I counted the days and the days counted back. I learned the shape of the empty chair. I learned how the floorboards settle when there is no one to startle them. I learned to stop leaving the latch lifted. I learned to stop listening for footsteps that would not come. I told myself this was patience. It was not patience. It was a room I built around myself and then locked from the inside.

You think despair is a storm. It is not. It is a climate. It is the air you breathe until you forget you are breathing it. I stopped asking why the valley kept its silence. I stopped asking why the old moon never went down when the new one rose. I stopped asking why every person here walks with two shadows and why neither of them ever points the way home. I made a fact of it. I said: this is what remains. I said: this is what I get. I said it until the words lost their teeth and I could swallow them without choking.

Do not write that I grew wise. Do not write that I found peace in the waiting. I did not. I grew thin. I grew careful. I grew good at pretending the silence was a kind of answer. I learned to mend what could not be mended and to call it enough. I learned to look at the long dark and say, all right, all right, all right, as if permission mattered. It did not. Nothing mattered but the habit of staying.

There were nights I stood at the threshold and felt the shape of a life I had not lived press against my ribs. I did not weep. Weeping implies you still believe something can be washed clean. I was past that. I was past hoping anyone would come with a lantern, a name, a hand on my shoulder. I was past the last thin lie that said if I kept my voice low, the world would notice me and return.

You will want to smooth this. You will want to make it sound like a crossing, like a lesson, like the necessary dark before a dawn that means something. It is not. It is a ledger. It is the years I spent certain no one was coming. It is the despair I settled into as fact. It is the way I learned to live inside a sentence that never ended. If you must write it, write it crooked. Write it with the gaps where my breath gave out. Write it with the years I did not name because naming them would have made them real, and I was not ready to let them be real. I am not ready now.

The dark is here. The record is yours. I have said what I said. Do not make it kinder than it was.

You want the rough edges. You want the truth without the polish. So I will not tell you that I endured. I will not tell you that I was strong. I will tell you what it was like to sit in this chair, in this hall, when the light was going and the shadows were stretching out like fingers to grab you, and know that no one was coming.

For years. Not months. Years.

You want the rough edges. You want the places where the voice broke and I swallowed it back down. You want the years I spent certain no one was coming for me, and the despair I settled into as if it were a fact of the valley, like the stone or the cold. I was certain no one was coming. Not because I was brave, and not because I had made peace with it. I was certain because the silence had a weight to it, and I learned to carry it. I stopped looking at the ridge. I stopped listening for footsteps that were not mine. I made a life inside the waiting. I planted what would grow in the shade. I mended what broke and did not ask who had broken it. I told myself this was prudence. It was not prudence. It was surrender, dressed up as patience.

There was a season when I believed that if I kept my hands busy enough, the dark would not notice me. That is a lie, but it is the kind of lie a person tells when the alternative is to stand still and feel the years pass through her like wind through a crack in the wall. I learned the names of the herbs by touch. I learned the weather by the ache in my knees. I learned the hour by the way the light lay on the floorboards, thin as a thread, never quite enough to read by, never quite enough to stop being afraid of.

You think despair is a storm. It is not. Despair is the floor after the storm has gone. It is the water left in the buckets. It is the knowledge that you have stopped hoping for a different weather and have begun to arrange your life around this one. I did that. I arranged myself around the absence. I made my bed narrow so I would not have to turn much. I spoke less so I would not have to hear my own voice asking for something I did not expect to receive. I became careful with my hunger. I became careful with my grief. I kept them both in the same cupboard and told myself I was being sensible.

There were nights I thought I could feel a road forming somewhere beyond the trees. I would stand at the door with my hand on the latch and my heart doing the old foolish thing, and then morning would come and the road would be only a road again, and I would laugh at myself for the waste of it. But do not write that laugh as relief. It was not relief. It was the sound of a person who has run out of tears and is ashamed to admit it. I laughed because crying would have meant I still believed there was something to cry for.

I was not always noble in this. Do not make me noble. There were days I was cruel to the small things that depended on me, because I had no mercy left and I did not know how to manufacture it. There were days I let the fire go low because I wanted to feel the cold and prove to myself that I was still alive enough to resent it. There were days I sat by the window and watched the two shadows move across the yard and thought, with a kind of sick clarity, that at least the valley still knew how to double what it had, even if it had nothing left to give me.

I did not wait with dignity. I waited with my teeth clenched. I waited with my back against the wall. I waited until waiting became the shape of my life and I could no longer remember what it was to stand without bracing for a blow. That is the part you will want to smooth. You will want to say I endured. I did not endure. I survived by becoming smaller than the thing I feared, and then smaller than the thing I had become.

And still, even then, there were moments I cannot explain and will not soften. A bird at the sill. A cup of water that did not spill when I set it down. The way the old moon and the new one both hung in the sky, refusing to let the night be simple, as if even the heavens were determined to keep two truths at once. In those moments I was not certain no one was coming. I was only certain that I was still here to be disappointed. That is not the same thing. Do not confuse them.

I am telling you this because you asked for the record without the polish. So let it be uneven. Let it sound like a woman speaking after the long dark has already begun, when there is no point in pretending the years were kinder than they were. I spent a long time believing I had been left behind. I spent a long time making a home out of that belief. I did not rise from it clean. I did not rise from it whole.
