Colleagues, students, and guests: welcome to the graduate seminar. For the next hour, we are not here to weigh two reasonable positions and meet in the middle. We are here to test a proposition that the university has spent a century romanticizing and a generation refusing to examine. The motion is simple: tenure should be abolished across this university. And the side I am asking you to inhabit does not concede that the current system has redeeming structural merits. It argues that tenure, as it operates today, is a liability masquerading as a safeguard, a mechanism that has outlived its justification and now actively degrades the academic mission it claims to protect.

Let’s begin with what tenure actually does, stripped of its ceremonial language. It converts a probationary professional relationship into a permanent one after a single, high-stakes evaluation window. That window is supposed to guarantee intellectual freedom. In practice, it guarantees insulation. Once the clock runs out, the primary accountability mechanism in any professional enterprise disappears. You are no longer evaluated on whether your work remains rigorous, whether your teaching meets the standards the department expects, whether your scholarship continues to engage the field, or whether your presence serves the institution’s educational mission. You are evaluated, if at all, by processes that are slow, politically constrained, and easily gamed. The result is not a sanctuary for independent thought. It is a structural exemption from the ordinary standards of professional performance that govern every other knowledge-intensive field.

Second, tenure does not protect dissent. It protects comfort. The argument that tenure shields unpopular or risky scholarship assumes that the greatest threat to intellectual freedom comes from outside the university or from administrative whim. That assumption is outdated. The real pressure inside a university today is not censorship. It is conformity, risk-aversion, and the quiet gravitational pull of career management. Tenure does not stop that. It often accelerates it. When a scholar knows that a single irreversible decision will lock in their position for decades, the incentive is not to pursue the most demanding questions. It is to secure the safest path to the guarantee. The system rewards those who navigate the review process skillfully, not those who take the kinds of intellectual risks that actually move a field forward. What we call protection often functions as a ceiling on ambition.

Third, tenure distorts the labor structure of the university. It creates a two-tier system in which a small, permanent core enjoys job security while a large, expanding periphery of contingent faculty carries the teaching load, often without the resources, support, or institutional standing to do that work well. This is not an accidental byproduct. It is a structural outcome. When a department can grant permanent status to a limited number of people and then rely on contract labor for the rest, it internalizes a hierarchy that is difficult to justify on educational grounds. The students in this room know this. They see it in the turnover, in the fragmented attention, in the way course offerings and advising structures shift with staffing cycles rather than curricular coherence. Abolishing tenure would not, by itself, solve that problem, but it would remove the institutional logic that treats permanent security as a prize to be rationed rather than a condition to be earned and maintained through continuous contribution.

Fourth, tenure is frequently defended as a bulwark against administrative overreach. That defense ignores how universities actually operate now. Administrative expansion, budget pressure, enrollment volatility, and the demand for measurable outputs are not stopped by tenure. They are absorbed by it. In many cases, tenure makes adaptation harder. It locks in staffing patterns, slows curricular renewal, and makes it difficult to reallocate resources in response to changing student needs, disciplinary shifts, or financial reality. A university that cannot adjust its academic structure without fighting its own permanent commitments is not defending academic freedom. It is defending inertia.

Fifth, the original rationale for tenure was built for a different academic ecology. It assumed a relatively stable institutional landscape, a clearer line between teaching and research, and a model of the professor as a long-term steward of a defined discipline. None of that describes the contemporary university with any precision. The work of the university today is more collaborative, more interdisciplinary, more responsive to public and professional demands, and more dependent on flexible expertise than the tenure model was designed to accommodate. Clinging to a permanent-status framework because it once made sense is not conservatism. It is institutional nostalgia dressed as principle.

Finally, let’s address the most persistent counterargument before it takes root: that abolishing tenure would chill inquiry, expose scholars to political or market pressure, and turn faculty into disposable labor. That fear deserves a serious answer, not a slogan. The answer is that job security and intellectual freedom are not the same thing, and conflating them has been convenient for an institution that benefits from the confusion. If the university wants to protect rigorous, independent scholarship, it should do so directly: through clear norms of academic freedom, transparent evaluation, robust due process, and hiring and promotion practices that reward intellectual contribution rather than longevity alone. Those are achievable without a permanent-status guarantee that separates performance from continuation. A system that requires scholars to remain accountable, engaged, and demonstrably effective is not inherently hostile to freedom. It is, in fact, more compatible with the conditions under which serious work gets done.

What I am asking this seminar to consider is not the elimination of standards, but the elimination of a guarantee that has become disconnected from them. Tenure was once argued as a necessary defense. Today it functions as a default exemption. It slows accountability, entrenches hierarchy, rewards risk-management over intellectual risk-taking, and makes the university less adaptable to the very students and disciplines it exists to serve. If we are serious about what a university should be, we should be willing to ask whether a permanent, non-revisable status is still the best way to secure the conditions of good work. I would argue it is not. It is time to treat academic freedom as a set of protections and practices, not as a one-time contract that outlives the reasons it was signed.

Colleagues, students, and guests. We are gathered to discuss the future of academic employment, and I stand before you to argue a proposition that many in this room will find uncomfortable, if not outright offensive. I am here to argue that tenure should be abolished across this university. I am not here to negotiate. I am not here to find a middle ground where tenure is reformed or tweaked. I am here to argue that the institution of tenure itself is a structural failure that has outlived its purpose, and that its abolition is necessary for the health of this university, the integrity of our scholarship, and the fairness owed to the majority of this department.

Let us begin with the premise of academic freedom. This is the shield tenure holders raise most often. They tell us that tenure protects the unpopular truth, that it allows a professor to pursue dangerous ideas without fear of dismissal. But look around this room. Look at the curriculum. Look at the research agendas. How many tenure-protected scholars are actually risking their careers to challenge the dominant paradigms of their fields? How many are pursuing work that genuinely threatens the status quo? The reality is that tenure does not protect the radical; it protects the comfortable. It creates a class of permanent employees who, once secured, have every incentive to play it safe. The risk is not in the firing; the risk is in the publishing, in the tenure track itself. Once you have the job for life, the incentive to disrupt vanishes. We have confused security with freedom. True academic freedom is not the guarantee of a paycheck for thirty years; it is the freedom of the institution to hire and support the best minds, regardless of their seniority, and the freedom of scholars to compete on the merit of their work, not the permanence of their contract.

Consider the economics of this department. Tenure is a luxury good that this university can no longer afford, and perhaps never should have. It creates a two-tier system that is morally indefensible. On one side, you have the tenured faculty, secure, well-compensated, with sabbaticals and reduced loads. On the other side, you have the adjuncts, the contract instructors, the graduate students who teach the bulk of the undergraduate load, often without benefits, without job security, and without a voice in the governance of this department. This is not a bug of the system; it is a feature. Tenure hoarding at the top necessitates precarity at the bottom. By abolishing tenure, we do not eliminate security for everyone; we eliminate the aristocracy. We move toward a system where employment is based on performance, on contribution, and on the needs of the students, rather than on a lottery won once, thirty years prior, that locks in privilege regardless of subsequent contribution.

And what of the students? You are here to learn. You are here to be taught by the best instructors, engaged in the most current research, and mentored by faculty who are accountable to you. Tenure severs that accountability. A tenured professor can stop publishing. They can stop innovating in the classroom. They can become disengaged, and yet they remain. Their salary is drawn from your tuition, from your grants, from the resources that could otherwise support new hires, new courses, and new opportunities. In a system without tenure, every faculty member is on a contract that reflects their current value to the university. Renewal is based on teaching, on research, on service. The incentive structure shifts from "how do I survive the review?" to "how do I continue to excel?" This is not a threat to scholars; it is a demand for excellence that benefits the students who pay for this education.

Some will argue that without tenure, we will lose our best people to industry or to other institutions. I argue that we will lose the dead weight that tenure protects. If a scholar is truly exceptional, if their work is truly vital, they will not need a lifetime guarantee to stay. They will be courted. They will be supported. The market for talent exists. What tenure does is insulate the mediocre from that market. It allows departments to hold onto names from decades past while the field moves on. Abolishing tenure forces the university to be dynamic. It forces us to look at who is here, what they are doing, and whether they are still the right fit for the mission of this institution. It prevents the calcification of departments into museums of past glory.

There is also the matter of governance. Tenure gives a specific group of employees veto power over the direction of the university. They control hiring, they control promotion, they control the curriculum, often in ways that protect their own interests rather than the interests of the students or the broader academic mission. When employment is permanent, power becomes entrenched. Abolishing tenure democratizes the workplace. It aligns the interests of the faculty with the interests of the institution. It makes the university responsive to change, to new disciplines, to new methods, rather than being held hostage by a permanent faculty that may resist innovation to protect their own territory.

I hear the whispers already. I hear the claim that this will destroy the university. I hear the claim that we will become a corporate factory, that we will lose our soul. This is a romantic fiction. The soul of the university is not in the job security of its employees; it is in the quality of its teaching, the rigor of its research, and the integrity of its inquiry. Those things are not protected by tenure. They are protected by commitment, by resources, and by a community that values excellence. We can have a university that is fair to all its workers, not just the tenured few. We can have a university that is agile, accountable, and excellent. But we cannot have that if we cling to a system designed for a different era, a system that prioritizes the comfort of the incumbent over the potential of the newcomer, over the needs of the student, and over the reality of the modern academic landscape.

So I ask you to reject the nostalgia. I ask you to reject the idea that security is the same as freedom. I ask you to consider that the sharpest tool we have for improving this university is the removal of the guarantee that allows stagnation to persist. Abolish tenure. Open the positions to merit. Open the contracts to performance. Open the university to the future. That is the case I stand for, and that is the case I will defend without concession.

Colleagues, students, and guests. We are here to argue a proposition that most universities treat as untouchable, and we are here to treat it as what it actually is: a testable claim about how knowledge is produced, who gets to produce it, and what happens when we mistake comfort for intellectual rigor. The motion is simple. Tenure should be abolished across this university. We do not concede that the other side has a defensible core. We argue that the institution of tenure, as it currently operates, has outlived its justification, distorted academic incentives, and made the university less capable of doing the work it claims to exist for.

Let us begin with the original promise. Tenure was sold as a shield for intellectual freedom, a guarantee that scholars could pursue unpopular truths without fear of administrative or political retaliation. That promise was never false. It was incomplete. What tenure actually built, over decades, was a system that protects a career status more reliably than it protects a research agenda. Once a scholar crosses the threshold, the incentive structure changes. The risk of speaking, publishing, or teaching against the grain does not disappear, but the institutional reward for doing so does. The protected position becomes, for many, a protected routine. And routines are not the same as rigor.

Consider what tenure does to the labor of the university. It creates a two-tier ecosystem. On one side, a permanent core with job security, salary progression, and institutional influence. On the other, a growing periphery of adjuncts, lecturers, postdoctoral researchers, and contract faculty who carry a disproportionate share of teaching, service, and administrative load, often without the conditions that make sustained scholarship possible. That is not an accidental byproduct. It is a structural outcome. When a department can rely on a small number of tenured faculty to set direction while depending on insecure labor to deliver the day-to-day educational mission, the university has effectively privatized risk and socialized stability. We are not here to romanticize precarity. We are here to say that a system built on asymmetric security is not a system optimized for academic excellence. It is a system optimized for institutional inertia.

Then look at the incentive problem inside the protected ranks. Tenure does not eliminate risk; it relocates it. Before tenure, the pressure is acute and often productive. After tenure, the pressure to justify that protection can flatten. Not for everyone. We know that. But as an institutional design, tenure rewards a single high-stakes gamble and then reduces the ongoing pressure to compete on the quality of teaching, the relevance of research, and the willingness to revise one’s own positions in public. A university that wants ambitious scholarship should not be built around a mechanism that, by design, lowers the marginal cost of intellectual complacency. If we believe that good ideas survive because they are tested, then we should be willing to test the conditions under which those ideas are produced.

There is also the question of accountability to the educational mission. A university is not a closed republic of scholars. It is a teaching institution with public obligations, student obligations, and resource obligations. Tenure makes it harder to realign faculty expertise with changing fields, harder to respond to shifts in student needs, harder to remove chronic underperformance that drags on cohorts year after year. That is not an argument for arbitrary dismissal. It is an argument for a system in which continued appointment depends on continued contribution, evaluated transparently and regularly, rather than on a one-time judgment that then becomes nearly irreversible. If we trust peer review before tenure, we should be able to trust structured review after it. If we cannot, then the entire case for lifetime protection collapses into a case for lifetime exemption.

Defenders will say that abolishing tenure would chill dissent, hand too much power to administrators, and expose scholars to political or ideological pressure. That fear deserves a direct answer, not a polite nod. The answer is that tenure is a blunt instrument for a problem that requires precise safeguards. Academic freedom can be protected through explicit contractual guarantees, transparent governance, independent review bodies, and strong norms of scholarly judgment. Those protections do not require a permanent employment status that separates security from performance. In fact, tying freedom to a status that is granted once and rarely revisited makes it easier for administrators to hide behind procedure and harder for the institution to distinguish between genuine protection and mere insulation. If the goal is to protect inquiry, protect inquiry. Do not protect a job classification and call it the same thing.

We should also be honest about the budgetary and strategic reality. Universities are not abstract salons. They operate under constraints. Tenure locks in long-term commitments at a moment when fields change, interdisciplinary work expands, and the demand for new kinds of expertise accelerates. A system that cannot adjust its faculty composition in response to evidence, demand, and mission is a system that will eventually serve its own habits more faithfully than it serves its students. Abolishing tenure would not mean chaos. It would mean a shift toward renewable contracts, stronger review, clearer expectations, and a faculty structure that can be aligned with what the university actually needs to teach and to research. That is not a retreat from academic values. It is a demand that those values be carried by people who remain accountable for them.

So we stand on this side not because we dislike scholars, not because we want to flatten the profession into a managerial hierarchy, and not because we believe every difficult question should be answered by the market. We stand here because the institution of tenure, as it now functions, has become a mechanism that protects the university from itself. It preserves a class of secure positions while the work of the university is increasingly done by others. It substitutes a historic justification for a contemporary evaluation. It allows the profession to call itself protective of freedom while building a structure that can quietly reward caution. And it makes reform harder every year because the very people who would have to redesign the system are the people most insulated from its consequences.

That is why we do not concede the other side’s core. The other side asks us to preserve a safeguard that has become, in practice, a ceiling on adaptation, a floor under complacency, and a license for institutional asymmetry. We say: end it. Replace it with a system that protects academic freedom directly, evaluates scholars continuously, distributes responsibility more honestly, and forces the university to earn its intellectual authority every year instead of inheriting it once. If the case for tenure is really about freedom, then freedom should survive without it. If it does not, then tenure was never mainly about freedom in the first place.

That is the case we will make, sharply and without apology, for the duration of this debate.

Good morning. Let's dispense with the ritual courtesy that tenure is a sacred trust. It is not. It is a labor contract that has calcified into a caste system, and we are here to argue that it should be abolished across this university, root and branch. We are not here to find a middle ground. We are here to tell you that the institution you have been taught to revere is structurally broken, and the mechanism you are most often told to protect—tenure—is the load-bearing wall keeping it broken.

Start with the premise that tenure protects academic freedom. It does not. It protects institutional inertia. What we call "academic freedom" in practice is often the freedom to repeat established methodologies, to avoid risky questions, to publish in safe journals, and to teach the same syllabi for decades while the world outside this building changes at a pace that makes our curricula look like museum exhibits. Tenure does not shield the scholar who challenges power; it shields the scholar who has already won the lottery and now has no structural incentive to keep running the race. When your employment is guaranteed regardless of output, the default human response is not heroic independence. It is comfort. And comfort is the enemy of inquiry.

Look at the economics. Tenure is a promise of lifetime employment in a profession that has undergone a demographic and financial transformation we still refuse to name. We have expanded graduate programs, we have built new facilities, we have marketed ourselves as engines of innovation, and then we lock a fixed percentage of our budget into a permanent workforce that cannot be adjusted as research priorities shift, as student demand changes, or as funding landscapes collapse. The result is not stability. It is rigidity. And rigidity in a university is not a virtue. It is a tax on everyone else in this building. Every tenure line is a decision not to hire a new voice, not to support a promising early-career scholar, not to reallocate resources toward the work that actually needs doing right now. We tell ourselves we are protecting quality. We are protecting a queue.

And what about the graduate students in this room? You are the ones who feel the architecture most directly. You are trained in a system that tells you the path to security runs through a tenure track that is, in reality, a bottleneck. You spend years publishing, teaching, grant-writing, and networking, all while being told that the reward at the end is a status that fewer and fewer people will ever reach. That is not a meritocracy. That is a lottery dressed up as a vocation. Abolishing tenure does not solve every problem in the academic labor market, but it does one essential thing: it stops pretending that the current hierarchy is natural, inevitable, or fair. It forces the university to confront what it has become—a small core of permanent staff surrounded by a much larger, highly skilled, deeply committed workforce that does the actual teaching, the actual research, and the actual service, while being told their precarity is the price of excellence.

Defenders will tell you that without tenure, scholars will be vulnerable to administrative whim, to political pressure, to short-term thinking. That argument assumes the alternative to tenure is chaos. It is not. The alternative is a professional employment system with real standards, real review, real due process, and real accountability. You can protect academic freedom with clear norms, transparent procedures, and strong contractual guarantees without handing out lifetime immunity to a permanent class. In fact, doing so may make academic freedom more robust, because it ties protection to the profession itself rather than to a one-time gatekeeping decision made, for many, in their thirties, on the basis of a narrow window of work that then becomes the measure of an entire career.

Tenure also corrupts evaluation. Once a scholar crosses the line, the incentive structure changes. The most important years of a career are supposed to be the years after tenure, when scholars should be taking risks, mentoring, building programs, and pushing into new territory. Too often, they are not. The same people who were judged on potential are then judged on almost nothing at all. Promotion slows. Service expands. Risk shrinks. The university does not get a steady stream of rising scholars; it gets a plateau. And a plateau is not a peak. It is a place where momentum goes to die.

We are not arguing for a free-for-all. We are arguing for a university that treats employment as a serious professional relationship rather than a hereditary title. That means competitive contracts, periodic review, clear criteria, and the ability to align staffing with the actual mission of the institution. It means hiring on the basis of what the university needs and what scholars can do, not on the basis of a permanent reservation system. It means ending the fiction that the best way to protect intellectual life is to freeze a portion of it in place forever.

So here is the case, plainly: tenure is a legacy mechanism that no longer serves the university it claims to protect. It distorts incentives, locks resources, narrows opportunity, and gives the appearance of security while producing institutional stagnation. It tells graduate students that the only legitimate future is one that most of them will never reach. It tells the university that it can afford to stop asking who it is hiring, why, and for what. Abolish it, and you do not destroy the university. You finally force it to become what it pretends to be: a living institution, responsive, accountable, and capable of renewing itself.

That is the position we will defend. Not as a compromise. Not as a reform. As a necessary correction.

Colleagues, students, guests—welcome to the graduate seminar. The format today is a formal debate. I have been assigned the proposition: tenure should be abolished across this university. I am not here to negotiate. I am not here to concede that the other side has a point worth preserving. I am here to argue that tenure, as it currently functions, is an institutional liability, an intellectual hazard, and a moral compromise we have mistaken for a professional virtue. We will not soften the claim. We will press it until its consequences are unavoidable.

Let us begin with what tenure was supposed to do, and what it actually does. The rhetoric of tenure is the rhetoric of academic freedom: the promise that a scholar can pursue difficult questions, challenge prevailing orthodoxies, and follow evidence where it leads without fear of administrative or political reprisal. That is a noble ideal. But ideals do not survive institutional gravity. What tenure has become is a permanent employment contract disguised as a constitutional protection. It is a tenure track that rewards compliance, not courage; a system that mistakes job security for intellectual independence; a mechanism that, in practice, shields stagnation while claiming to defend inquiry.

Consider the incentive structure. Tenure is awarded at a single moment, usually around the sixth or seventh year, after a candidate has demonstrated a record of publication, teaching, and service. The evaluation is retrospective. It asks: what have you already done? It does not ask: what will you do when the stakes disappear? Once tenure is granted, the primary disciplinary mechanism evaporates. There is no meaningful performance review that can alter employment status. There is no competitive pressure to improve. There is no structural reason to take intellectual risks, to revise failing courses, to engage with new methods, to respond to students who are actually in the room. The system does not punish mediocrity; it simply stops asking for excellence. And when a system stops asking for excellence, excellence becomes optional.

Now let us speak plainly about the cost. Tenure is not a neutral personnel policy. It is a resource allocation mechanism. It locks a significant portion of the university’s budget into long-term, non-negotiable commitments. It creates a two-tier faculty structure in which a shrinking number of tenured and tenure-track faculty enjoy permanent security while a growing majority of instructors, lecturers, adjuncts, and postdoctoral researchers work on short-term contracts, without benefits, without job security, without a voice in governance, and often without the conditions that make sustained scholarship possible. We tell ourselves that tenure protects academic freedom. In practice, it often protects a privileged core while the rest of the teaching enterprise is precariously assembled and cheaply managed. That is not a defense of the university. That is a defense of hierarchy dressed in the language of principle.

And what of academic freedom itself? The argument that tenure is necessary to protect controversial or unpopular scholarship assumes that the greatest threat to inquiry comes from outside the university, or from administrators with short-term political interests. That assumption is increasingly outdated. The more immediate threat to intellectual vitality is internal: the slow drift toward safe topics, the preference for familiar methodologies, the reluctance to challenge departmental orthodoxies when doing so might complicate collegial relations, the tendency to equate rigor with loyalty to established frameworks. Tenure does not eliminate these pressures. It often insulates them. When a scholar knows that their position is secure regardless of the intellectual direction they take, the incentive to pursue difficult, uncertain, or genuinely disruptive work diminishes. Security and risk are not the same thing. Tenure confuses them.

Let us also address the myth of the indispensable scholar. Tenure is frequently justified by the claim that it allows faculty to pursue long-term, high-risk research that would otherwise be impossible. That claim is true in a narrow sense, and irrelevant in a broader one. Long-term research does not require permanent employment. It requires stable funding, reasonable teaching loads, institutional support, and a culture that values depth over volume. None of those conditions depend on a lifetime contract. They depend on deliberate resource allocation, transparent evaluation, and a willingness to reward sustained contribution rather than mere survival. If a project is worth pursuing, it can be supported without making the researcher unaccountable to the institution that hosts them. If it is not worth supporting, tenure will not make it so.

There is also the question of institutional adaptability. Universities are not monasteries. They are complex organizations operating in a rapidly changing educational, technological, and economic environment. They need to be able to respond to new fields, new methods, new student populations, new modes of inquiry, and new expectations of accountability. Tenure makes that responsiveness structurally difficult. It freezes a snapshot of the faculty at a particular moment and asks the institution to build around it indefinitely. It slows curricular innovation. It complicates strategic hiring. It makes it harder to align faculty expertise with emerging intellectual priorities. The result is not stability. It is inertia. And inertia is not the same thing as integrity.

I anticipate the objection that abolishing tenure would expose faculty to political pressure, administrative whim, and short-term market forces. That objection assumes that the alternative to tenure is chaos. It is not. The alternative to tenure is a system of serious, transparent, multi-year contracts with clear expectations, meaningful evaluation, and genuine due process. It is a system in which faculty are accountable for teaching, scholarship, and service, and in which the institution is accountable for providing the conditions that make those contributions possible. It is a system in which academic freedom is protected not by a permanent contract, but by explicit institutional commitments, robust governance, and a culture that takes intellectual independence seriously enough to defend it without hiding behind lifetime employment.

The point is not that faculty should be disposable. The point is that permanence is a poor substitute for protection. A university that cannot protect its scholars without making them untouchable has not solved the problem of academic freedom; it has merely outsourced it to a personnel category. A university that cannot evaluate its faculty honestly has not achieved fairness; it has achieved avoidance. A university that cannot align its resources with its mission has not secured stability; it has secured rigidity.

So let us be clear about what is at stake. Tenure is not the same thing as scholarly freedom. It is not the same thing as teaching excellence. It is not the same thing as institutional health. It is a structural arrangement that has outlived the conditions that produced it, and that now functions primarily as a shield against accountability, a lock on resources, and a justification for inequality. Abolishing it would not destroy the university. It would force the university to decide what it actually values: not permanent employment, but sustained intellectual contribution; not insulation, but accountability; not a protected class, but a serious academic community.

That is the case. It is not comfortable. It is not balanced. It is not intended to be. The question before this room is whether tenure still deserves the moral and institutional status we give it, or whether it has become a habit we mistake for a principle. I argue the latter. And I will spend this term showing why the habit is costly, why the principle is hollow, and why the university is better served by ending it.

Colleagues, graduate students, and guests—welcome to this term’s graduate seminar. Before we begin, I want to be explicit about the ground rules of today’s session. This is not a negotiation. It is not a search for compromise. It is a formal debate, and the side I am presenting has been assigned one task: to argue, without reservation and without conceding the structural merits of the opposing position, that tenure should be abolished across this university. What you will hear is not a policy white paper. It is a case. It is meant to be pressed, tested, and answered. If the other side believes tenure is indispensable, they will have their turn to defend it. My job is to show why that defense cannot survive scrutiny.

Let us begin with what tenure actually is, stripped of its ceremonial language. It is a contractual guarantee of employment permanence, granted after a probationary period, that insulates the holder from dismissal except under extraordinary procedural conditions. It is marketed as a shield for academic freedom, a reward for scholarly merit, and a mechanism for institutional stability. But when we examine what it does in practice, the gap between its justification and its operation widens into a chasm.

First, tenure does not protect intellectual freedom; it protects institutional inertia. The original rationale was that scholars needed security to pursue unpopular, controversial, or long-horizon research without fear of administrative or political retaliation. That rationale assumed a world of scarce information, slow review cycles, and concentrated gatekeeping. We no longer live in that world. Today, the pressures on scholarship are not primarily external censorship; they are internal conformity, disciplinary orthodoxy, funding cycles, citation economies, and the quiet enforcement of methodological orthodoxy by peers who share the same career incentives. Tenure does not disrupt those forces. It locks them in. Once a scholar achieves permanence, the incentive structure shifts from “produce work that advances the field” to “produce work that maintains your position within the field.” The result is not a frontier of independent thought. It is a self-reinforcing ecosystem where risk becomes career suicide, and conformity becomes the safest route to permanence.

Second, tenure is not a merit reward. It is a timing mechanism. The tenure decision arrives at a specific moment in a scholar’s career, usually around the sixth or seventh year, and it converts a snapshot of performance into a permanent status. That snapshot is shaped by committee politics, subfield biases, institutional priorities, and the luck of timing. Two scholars can produce comparable work; one passes through a favorable committee cycle, the other does not. Tenure then freezes that outcome into a lifelong advantage. It does not continuously verify excellence. It certifies it once, and then asks the institution to pretend that the certification remains valid forever. No other serious professional system operates on that premise. We do not grant lifetime licenses to practice based on a single review window. We do not assume that a performance benchmark, once met, exempts someone from future accountability. Yet academia does exactly that, and then expresses surprise when stagnation follows.

Third, tenure creates a two-tier moral economy that the university refuses to name honestly. On one side are the tenured and tenure-track faculty, whose job security, workload expectations, governance rights, and compensation are structured around permanence. On the other side are the adjuncts, lecturers, postdoctoral researchers, instructional staff, and graduate workers who deliver the majority of teaching, advising, and administrative labor while carrying none of the protections tenure promises. The university does not sustain itself on the work of the tenured. It sustains itself on the labor of the non-tenured, whose precarity subsidizes the security of the permanent. Tenure is not the exception that proves the rule of academic fairness. It is the mechanism that institutionalizes asymmetry. If we claim to value educational quality, scholarly contribution, and professional dignity, we cannot simultaneously defend a system that concentrates security in a shrinking minority while normalizing instability for the majority who actually keep the institution running.

Fourth, tenure weakens accountability by making removal procedurally prohibitive. The argument is that due process protects scholars from arbitrary dismissal. The reality is that due process, when fused with permanence, becomes a barrier to correcting underperformance, outdated pedagogy, unproductive scholarship, or misalignment with the institution’s educational mission. Dismissal is not impossible, but it is so costly, so slow, and so politically fraught that it rarely happens. The system therefore tolerates drift. It tolerates faculty who no longer teach effectively, who no longer produce meaningful scholarship, who no longer engage with students or colleagues, because the cost of intervention exceeds the institutional will to intervene. That is not protection. That is neglect dressed as principle.

Fifth, tenure distorts hiring and resource allocation. Because permanence is so expensive and so difficult to reverse, institutions become extremely conservative in granting it. They hoard tenure lines, concentrate them in senior cohorts, and treat them as scarce assets rather than as part of a dynamic workforce. That conservatism narrows the pipeline. It discourages experimental appointments. It makes departments reluctant to bring in scholars with unconventional trajectories, interdisciplinary commitments, or teaching-intensive missions that do not fit the traditional tenure narrative. The university becomes less adaptable, not more. It protects the past while pretending to prepare for the future.

Sixth, tenure is increasingly incompatible with the actual work of a modern university. The contemporary institution is not a collection of isolated scholars guarding their autonomy. It is a complex enterprise involving teaching, mentorship, public engagement, interdisciplinary collaboration, digital infrastructure, community partnership, and continuous curricular revision. None of those functions benefit from a system that assumes the primary risk is external interference with a permanent employee. The real risk is irrelevance, misalignment, and failure to respond to students, fields, and societies as they change. A system built around permanence treats change as a threat. A system built around accountability treats change as a condition of relevance.

Now, the opposing side will tell you that without tenure, academic freedom dies. That claim deserves a direct answer. Academic freedom is not the same thing as employment permanence. Freedom of inquiry depends on norms, institutional commitments, legal protections, transparent governance, and a culture that tolerates disagreement. It does not depend on guaranteeing any individual a lifetime appointment. In fact, conflating the two has weakened both. When tenure is treated as the sole bulwark of free scholarship, the university is encouraged to believe that freedom is secured once the contract is signed, and that nothing further is required. That is a dangerous illusion. Freedom survives when institutions defend it actively, when departments model intellectual disagreement, when administrators resist political and commercial pressure, and when scholars are held to standards of rigor and honesty without being insulated from the consequences of neglect. Permanence is not freedom. It is a labor arrangement. And treating it as a constitutional principle for scholarship has allowed institutions to outsource the real work of protecting inquiry.

The opposing side will also tell you that abolishing tenure would produce a precarious, disposable faculty, that it would open the door to administrative caprice, that it would destroy morale and scholarly continuity. Those are serious concerns, but they are not arguments for tenure. They are arguments for better employment structures, clearer contractual standards, stronger due-process protections, and more honest workforce planning. If the alternative to tenure is a system of renewable contracts with transparent review, meaningful academic freedom protections, fair compensation, and genuine procedural safeguards, then the question is not whether we can afford to abolish tenure. The question is whether we can afford to keep defending a system that has outlived its justification while masking deeper inequities.

Let me be as direct as the assignment requires: the case against tenure does not rest on the claim that all tenured faculty are unproductive, or that all non-tenured faculty are exploited, or that every department would instantly improve if permanence disappeared. It rests on the claim that tenure, as an institution, no longer delivers what it promises, and that it delivers those failures in ways that are structurally embedded, morally costly, and increasingly difficult to justify. It promises freedom but entrenches conformity. It promises merit but freezes a moment in time. It promises stability but subsidizes precarity. It promises accountability but makes correction prohibitively difficult. It promises protection but confuses permanence with principle.

That is the case. It is not a call for chaos. It is a call for honesty. If this university is to remain serious about scholarship, teaching, and institutional responsibility, it must stop defending a system because it has always had one. It must ask what arrangement actually serves inquiry, students, and the long-term health of the faculty. Today, you will hear the other side argue that tenure remains indispensable. My argument is that indispensability is an assertion, not a proof, and that the proof has been eroding for years.

The floor is now yours. Answer the case on its terms. Do not defend tenure by appealing to nostalgia, fear, or the comfort of the familiar. Defend it if you can on the grounds of what it actually does, what it actually costs, and what it actually protects. If it still stands after that test, then perhaps it deserves to remain. But do not ask us to preserve it because we have never imagined the alternative. That is not an argument. That is inertia.

Let the debate begin.

What is often defended as academic freedom, job security, or scholarly independence is, in practice, a structural mechanism that distorts incentives, insulates underperformance, and locks a modern university into a staffing model that no longer serves its mission.

Let’s start with what tenure actually does. It converts a professional appointment into a property right. Once granted, it severs the normal relationship between performance and continuation. In every other knowledge-intensive sector, sustained contribution, relevance, and accountability determine whether someone remains in a role. In academia, tenure creates a permanent class that is, by design, largely immune to the same expectations. That is not a safeguard of intellectual independence. It is a structural exemption from the very evaluation that keeps any discipline alive.

The second point is incentive. Tenure does not reward excellence; it rewards survival. The clock-to-tenure pipeline incentivizes risk-aversion, not intellectual ambition. It pushes scholars toward safe topics, established methodologies, and publication strategies that satisfy committees rather than advance fields. The most consequential work in any discipline often comes from people who are willing to be wrong, to pivot, to follow evidence where it leads, and to engage publicly without fearing that a single controversial line will cost them their livelihood. Tenure does not protect that kind of work. It protects the person who has already cleared the hurdle, and then quietly discourages them from jumping again.

Third, tenure creates a two-tier system that is morally and operationally unsustainable. A permanent core enjoys long-term security, while a growing periphery of contingent faculty, adjuncts, postdoctoral researchers, and instructional staff carries the same teaching and service load without the same protections, voice, or stability. That is not a bug. It is the architecture. The university becomes a caste system dressed in scholarly language. If we believe that teaching and research are shared responsibilities, then a system that permanently separates one group from the conditions that make those responsibilities sustainable is not defensible.

Fourth, tenure is a poor tool for the problems it claims to solve. Academic freedom does not require lifetime employment. It requires clear norms, strong institutional commitments, and transparent processes for defending scholarly expression. Those can be maintained without making permanent appointment the default. In fact, the conflation of freedom with permanence has made it harder to address real threats to scholarly integrity, because the same mechanism that is supposed to protect dissent also protects stagnation. When a department cannot meaningfully reassess its staffing, it cannot adapt to new methods, new audiences, or new standards of evidence. It can only preserve what it has already built.

Fifth, the financial and organizational reality is unavoidable. A permanent tenure line is a decades-long commitment made in a single moment of evaluation. It reduces flexibility, raises fixed costs, and makes it harder to reallocate resources toward emerging priorities. That matters because universities are not monasteries. They are institutions that must respond to changes in knowledge, technology, student needs, and public expectation. A staffing model that locks in yesterday’s distribution of roles is a model that quietly prevents tomorrow’s priorities from being met.

Finally, the argument that tenure protects against external pressure is strongest only when the pressure is imagined as a single, simple force. In reality, the pressures on universities are complex, and tenure does not neutralize them; it often displaces them. It pushes evaluation into opaque internal processes, it concentrates power in the hands of those who already hold it, and it makes accountability harder to see and harder to enforce. If the goal is to protect scholars from political or administrative interference, the answer is stronger procedural safeguards, clearer speech protections, and transparent governance—not a permanent employment guarantee that can be used to shield neglect, mediocrity, or institutional inertia.

What we are proposing is not the dismantling of scholarship. It is the replacement of a permanent-employment default with a system built on merit, contribution, and renewal. It is a system in which continued appointment is earned through sustained engagement, where teaching and research are evaluated honestly, where contingent scholars are integrated into the governance and stability of the institution, and where academic freedom is defended as a norm and a practice rather than as a property right.

That is the case. It is not balanced, because the institution we are asking you to reconsider was never balanced to begin with. It was a solution to a different era, preserved long after the conditions that produced it had changed. We are here to argue that the university should be able to evaluate its own people, adapt its own structure, and protect its own values without relying on a mechanism that has outlived its justification. The motion is clear. Tenure should be abolished. We will spend this session showing why, and we will not soften that claim to make it easier to hear.

Colleagues, students, and guests—welcome to this seminar. I am here to argue a proposition that many in this room will find uncomfortable, and some will find offensive. That is precisely why we are debating it. The motion before us is simple: **Tenure should be abolished across this university.**

I am not here to negotiate. I am not here to suggest that tenure has historical merits we might preserve in some diluted form. I am here to argue that tenure, as it currently exists, is an institutional failure that harms the very mission of the university: the pursuit of truth, the advancement of knowledge, and the education of students. We are not here to find a middle ground. We are here to dismantle a system that has outlived its purpose.

Let us begin with the most fundamental question: What is tenure supposed to protect? The classic defense is academic freedom—the idea that a professor must be free to pursue controversial research, challenge orthodoxy, and speak truth to power without fear of retribution. That is a noble ideal. But let us be honest about what tenure actually delivers in practice.

Tenure does not protect truth-seeking. It protects career security. It protects the professor who has already secured their position, often after a decade of precarious labor, from the consequences of underperformance, obsolescence, or simply the changing needs of the institution. It creates a class of permanent employees who are insulated from the realities that shape the rest of the academic ecosystem.

Consider the incentive structure tenure creates. Once a scholar achieves tenure, the pressure to produce diminishes. The urgency to engage with new methodologies, new questions, new fields—to remain intellectually alive—softens. We all know the pattern: the brilliant early career researcher who publishes with fire and urgency, and the same researcher fifteen years later, whose output slows, whose engagement with the cutting edge wanes, whose primary obligation becomes maintaining a position rather than advancing a discipline. This is not a universal truth, but it is a structural tendency, and it is a tendency that harms the university's core mission.

Now consider the cost. Tenure is not free. It is purchased with the labor of a vast underclass of adjuncts, contract faculty, and graduate students who teach the majority of courses, who grade the majority of papers, who sustain the daily work of the university, and who receive none of the protections tenure provides. We have created a two-tier system: a small, protected elite at the top, and a precarious, underpaid workforce beneath them. This is not academic freedom. This is feudalism. This is a system that extracts labor from the vulnerable to subsidize the security of the privileged.

And what do we tell the students? We tell them that the person standing at the front of the room is there because they have earned lifetime security. But the student does not care about the professor's job security. The student cares about whether the professor is engaged, current, demanding, and committed to teaching. Tenure does not guarantee any of those things. In fact, by removing the necessity of continued merit, tenure can actively work against them.

Let us address the argument that tenure protects controversial scholarship. I will concede that, in rare cases, tenure has shielded scholars from political or administrative overreach. But let us also acknowledge that tenure is a blunt instrument. It protects the scholar who challenges power, yes—but it also protects the scholar who is simply unproductive, the scholar who is intellectually stagnant, the scholar who is a poor teacher, the scholar who has lost the spark that brought them to the academy in the first place. We are protecting all of them, equally, indefinitely. Is that the best we can do?

There are better ways to protect academic freedom. We can protect it through clear contractual guarantees, through strong faculty governance, through transparent processes for evaluating controversial research, through a culture that values intellectual risk-taking. We do not need lifetime employment to protect free inquiry. We need institutional commitment to the principles of free inquiry. Conflating the two is a category error, and it has blinded us to the real costs of the system we have built.

Consider also the rigidity tenure imposes on the university. The knowledge economy changes. Disciplines evolve. New fields emerge; old fields contract. A university that grants lifetime positions to a fixed set of scholars at a fixed moment in time is a university that cannot adapt. It cannot reallocate resources to where they are needed. It cannot respond to new intellectual opportunities. It cannot ensure that its faculty composition reflects the needs of its students and the demands of the world. Tenure locks the institution into a snapshot of the past and asks it to carry that snapshot forward forever.

And let us speak plainly about the selection process itself. Tenure is awarded on the basis of a prediction: that the candidate will remain excellent, productive, and valuable to the institution for decades. But predictions are imperfect. We make mistakes. We tenure people who should not have been tenured. And once tenured, we have almost no mechanism to address the failure that follows. The system assumes that the moment of hire—or the moment of tenure review—is the moment of maximum judgment, and that everything after that is guaranteed. That is not how scholarship works. That is not how any dynamic field works. It is a bet we make once, and we are forced to live with it forever.

Some will say that abolishing tenure would lead to a race to the bottom, that administrators would exploit the absence of tenure to drive down salaries, to dismiss inconvenient scholars, to undermine faculty governance. These are serious concerns, and they deserve serious answers. But they are not arguments for tenure. They are arguments for better protections, better governance, better contractual frameworks. They are arguments for doing the hard work of designing a system that protects scholars without trapping the institution in a structure that no longer serves its purpose. The fact that we have not yet built those alternatives is not an argument for preserving the status quo. It is an argument for building them.

We are not here to defend the exploitation of adjuncts. We are not here to defend the stagnation of scholarship. We are not here to defend an institution that cannot adapt. We are here to argue that the university should be a place of continuous merit, continuous engagement, continuous renewal. That the people who teach our students should be there because they are excellent at what they do, not because they won a lottery decades ago. That the people who produce our research should be accountable to the standards of their fields, not insulated from them. That the institution itself should be able to allocate its resources in response to the intellectual landscape, not locked into a permanent configuration decided in the past.

Tenure was built for a different era, under different conditions, with different assumptions about the university, the scholar, and the state. Those conditions no longer obtain. The university today is larger, more complex, more dependent on public support, more accountable to the students it serves, and more embedded in a rapidly changing knowledge economy. The protections that made sense then do not make sense now. The costs that were tolerable then are no longer tolerable. The trade-offs we accepted then are no longer acceptable.

So I stand before you and I argue, without reservation, that tenure should be abolished. Not reformed. Not tweaked. Abolished. Replaced with a system that protects academic freedom through clear, enforceable guarantees, that rewards continuous excellence, that holds scholars accountable to the standards of their disciplines, that treats teaching and research as ongoing commitments rather than one-time achievements, and that does not build a permanent elite on the backs of a precarious workforce.

This is not a comfortable argument. It is not meant to be. It is meant to be true. And it is meant to be the starting point for a serious conversation about what the university should be, and what it must become.

I look forward to the response. But I will not concede the ground I have just claimed. Tenure is not a sacred institution. It is a policy choice. And it is a policy choice we should unmake.

Colleagues, students, welcome to the seminar. The motion before us is unambiguous: tenure should be abolished across this university. We are not here to negotiate a compromise. We are not here to concede that tenure preserves academic freedom, rewards long-term scholarship, or stabilizes departmental planning. Those are the arguments we will dismantle, not accommodate. What I am going to lay out is the case for abolition, pressed to its logical end.

Let us begin with the premise that tenure exists to protect intellectual freedom. That is the founding myth, and it is precisely that: a myth that has outlived its function. Tenure was designed for a different institutional ecology, one in which a small number of scholars pursued long-term research with minimal market pressure, and in which the primary threat to inquiry came from external political interference. That world does not exist here. What exists is a system in which tenure has become a structural shield for stagnation, not a sword for independence. The protection it offers is no longer directed at controversial ideas; it is directed at institutional inertia. Once a scholar achieves tenure, the incentive structure shifts decisively away from risk, toward preservation. The most reliable path to a quiet career is no longer to pursue difficult, uncertain, or interdisciplinary work. It is to publish enough, teach adequately, and avoid making waves. That is not academic freedom. That is career security dressed in the language of liberty.

Consider what tenure actually does to the labor architecture of the university. It creates a two-tier system that is increasingly indefensible. On one side, a shrinking cohort of tenured and tenure-track faculty enjoys long-term security, often with light teaching loads, generous leave policies, and disproportionate influence over hiring, curriculum, and resource allocation. On the other side, a growing majority of instructors, adjuncts, and contingent faculty carry the teaching load, often without offices, without benefits, without job security, and without a meaningful voice in the governance of the department they serve. Tenure does not neutralize hierarchy; it calcifies it. It converts a profession that ought to be organized around shared intellectual labor into a system where security is concentrated at the top and precarity is outsourced to the rest. Abolition is not an attack on scholars. It is a demand that the university stop organizing its workforce around a permanent class divide.

Then there is the question of accountability, which tenure is routinely claimed to resist. But accountability is not the enemy of scholarship; it is the condition of a functioning institution. When a faculty member cannot be removed for persistent failure in teaching, for neglect of scholarly responsibility, or for misalignment with the mission of the department, the institution has not protected freedom. It has protected underperformance. The argument that tenure is necessary because evaluation is messy or subjective is an argument for better evaluation, not for permanent immunity. A system that cannot meaningfully assess its own contributors is not a system that values excellence. It is a system that has decided excellence is optional.

Let us also address the claim that tenure is essential for long-term research. The opposite is often true. Tenure can entrench methodological habits, narrow research agendas, and reduce the pressure to engage with new questions, new methods, or new audiences. It can make senior scholars less responsive to the evolving shape of their fields. Meanwhile, the university itself changes around them: new disciplines emerge, technologies reshape inquiry, student populations shift, and the demands of public relevance intensify. A system that locks in decisions made in a candidate’s midcareer, for decades afterward, is not a system optimized for intellectual vitality. It is a system optimized for continuity. Continuity has its place, but it should not be mistaken for excellence, and it should not be purchased at the price of institutional rigidity.

There is also the matter of governance. Tenure concentrates power in the hands of those who have already secured it. Hiring, promotion, curriculum, resource allocation, and disciplinary norms are all shaped by people who have the least incentive to disrupt the system that elevated them. That is not a conspiracy. It is a predictable outcome of any structure that rewards self-preservation. Abolishing tenure would not eliminate senior faculty. It would eliminate the permanent class that governs from a position of guaranteed security. It would force the university to build evaluation, renewal, and review into the normal rhythm of academic life, rather than treating them as exceptional threats to be survived once and then never faced again.

What would replace it? Not chaos. Not the wholesale commodification of scholarship. A different architecture of security and responsibility. Long-term contracts. Renewable appointments. Clear criteria. Strong due process. Protection for legitimate intellectual risk-taking, not protection for indifference. A system in which security is earned through continued contribution, not granted as a lifetime entitlement. A system in which the university can adjust its faculty composition to its mission, its resources, and its evolving intellectual priorities, without being locked into decisions made decades earlier. That is not a betrayal of academic values. It is a reconstruction of them for an institution that no longer resembles the one tenure was built for.

We are told that abolishing tenure would expose scholars to market pressures, administrative whim, and the erosion of independence. But the current system already exposes contingent faculty to all of those forces, while insulating a privileged minority from them. If the fear is that universities will become more responsive to external demands, then the answer is not to preserve a permanent tier that is exempt from those demands. The answer is to build a faculty structure that is coherent, accountable, and fair across the board. If the fear is that academic freedom will be weakened, then the answer is to defend freedom directly, through explicit protections for inquiry, speech, and dissent, rather than through a job security arrangement that has become a blunt instrument for preserving the status quo.

Tenure is not the only way to protect scholarship. It is not the only way to reward excellence. It is not the only way to sustain a university. It is a legacy institution that has become a mechanism for freezing hierarchy, insulating underperformance, and misrepresenting security as freedom. Abolishing it would not destroy the university. It would force the university to decide what it actually values: permanent entitlement, or a living, accountable, intellectually responsive faculty.

That is the case we are making. We are not asking you to balance it against nostalgia. We are asking you to recognize that the institution has outgrown the mechanism, and that the sharpest thing we can do is stop pretending otherwise.

Colleagues, students, and especially our Tuvaluan guests—who know better than most of us what it means to inhabit a place that the wider world treats as expendable—thank you for being here. This seminar is not a comfort session. It is a stress test. And the motion before us is absolute: tenure should be abolished across this university, in its entirety, with no carve-outs, no grandfathering, no negotiated retreat. I will not spend my time pretending the other side has a defensible core. It does not. What remains of tenure is a historical artifact propped up by institutional nostalgia, defended by people who confuse job security with intellectual freedom, and sustained by a system that quietly transfers risk onto the people least equipped to absorb it. I am here to argue that we should dismantle it, deliberately and completely, and replace it with a structure that actually serves the university’s stated mission.

Let us begin with the myth that tenure protects academic freedom. It does not. It protects a class. Tenure was sold to us as a shield against political interference, administrative overreach, and the chilling effect of unpopular scholarship. In practice, it has become a liability shield for a permanent faculty cohort that is increasingly insulated from the very conditions it claims to study. Once you cross the threshold, the incentive structure flips. The most consequential work in any discipline now happens at the intersections, in public-facing research, in community-engaged projects, in rapid-response scholarship that does not wait for a decade-long review cycle. Tenure does not reward that. It rewards the slow, the safe, the already-established. It tells early-career scholars that the only reliable path to security is to mimic the habits of a cohort that has already locked the doors behind it. That is not academic freedom. That is a closed loop.

Second, tenure is a fiscal and structural trap. A university that guarantees lifetime employment to a fixed segment of its workforce while relying on a growing, underpaid, high-turnover contingent to deliver the bulk of teaching and service is not a balanced institution. It is a two-tier system dressed in the language of collegiality. The permanent faculty enjoys insulation from enrollment shifts, funding volatility, and pedagogical innovation. The rest absorb the instability. Abolishing tenure does not mean stripping scholars of dignity or due process. It means ending a system that confuses permanence with excellence, and replacing it with transparent, competitive, renewable contracts tied to clear standards, real peer review, and genuine accountability. A university that can renew its commitments regularly is a university that can actually adapt. Tenure freezes adaptation out of the building.

Third, the argument that tenure is necessary to attract and retain top talent is a self-serving fiction. The best scholars are not drawn to lifetime guarantees. They are drawn to resources, intellectual community, meaningful evaluation, and the freedom to pursue difficult questions without bureaucratic suffocation. Tenure does not provide those things; it often delays them, because the clock is rigged toward risk-aversion. A system built on rigorous, periodic review, with real investment in early- and mid-career scholars, with transparent criteria and actual consequences for stagnation, will outperform a system that rewards endurance over impact. If a university cannot compete on the quality of its environment, it should not hide behind a contract that locks in mediocrity and calls it security.

Fourth, tenure has become a governance weapon. It concentrates decision-making in the hands of those who have already survived the gauntlet, and it makes structural reform nearly impossible because the very people who benefit from the architecture are the ones who vote on its future. Curriculum stagnation, hiring bottlenecks, resistance to new methods, the slow suffocation of interdisciplinary work—these are not accidents. They are predictable outputs of a system that rewards permanence over renewal. Abolishing tenure breaks that cycle. It forces the institution to evaluate itself continuously, to justify its commitments, to treat faculty as active participants in a living enterprise rather than as permanent fixtures in a museum.

I know the counterarguments by heart. They will tell you that without tenure, administrators will run wild. They will tell you that unpopular truths will be silenced. They will tell you that the profession will lose its soul. But these are not arguments; they are anxieties dressed as principles. Administrative overreach is checked by transparent governance, shared decision-making, and enforceable standards—not by a contract that makes it structurally difficult to remove dead weight or redirect resources. Unpopular scholarship is protected by institutional commitment to rigorous inquiry, by peer norms, by public accountability, and by a culture that rewards intellectual courage—not by a tenure file that often rewards the path of least resistance. And the profession’s soul is not preserved by locking a cohort into lifetime security while everyone else runs on a treadmill. It is preserved by building a system that actually values the work, evaluates it honestly, and renews its commitments on the basis of merit, not seniority.

We are not talking about stripping scholars of protection. We are talking about replacing a system that protects the past with one that invests in the future. We are talking about ending a structure that confuses longevity with contribution, that shields stagnation under the banner of freedom, that quietly externalizes risk onto the contingent majority while the permanent minority enjoys the benefits of a system it no longer has to justify. Abolish tenure. Build a university that can actually renew itself. Make every contract meaningful, every review transparent, every renewal earned. That is not a threat to academic freedom. That is the only way to make it real.

I will not concede that the other side has a defensible center, because it does not. What remains of tenure is a relic maintained by habit, defended by those who benefit from it, and tolerated by an institution that has forgotten what it is supposed to be. We can do better. We must. And the first step is to stop pretending that lifetime security for a fixed cohort is the same thing as a living, accountable, intellectually serious university. It is not. It never was. Let us end it, and build what actually belongs here.

Let us begin with what tenure actually does. Tenure is a contract. And that contract has outlived its justification.

The original case for tenure rested on a specific historical condition: the need to protect scholars who pursued unpopular, politically sensitive, or institutionally inconvenient lines of inquiry. They come from funding streams, publication economies, citation metrics, donor expectations, and the quiet conformity of a profession that rewards safe topics, familiar methods, and incremental publication. Tenure does not solve those pressures. It freezes them into a hierarchy. It protects the established at the exact moment when the university needs to be more agile, more accountable, and more willing to retire what no longer works.

It forces universities to carry permanent commitments in a landscape that changes faster than those commitments can be responsibly maintained. It makes the institution less capable of responding to its own students, its own research priorities, and its own financial realities. We are also told that tenure protects junior scholars by creating a stable ecosystem. The opposite is true. Tenure is the engine of the up-or-out pipeline that defines so much academic labor. It creates a bottleneck in which a small number of people are guaranteed a permanent seat at the table, and a large number are asked to compete for the remaining temporary positions, adjunct appointments, and soft-money roles. Nor should we accept the claim that removing tenure would automatically produce a free-market disaster. That argument assumes the only alternative to tenure is ruthless short-termism. In fact, lifetime contracts can weaken the culture of review that keeps scholarship honest, because they remove the ongoing obligation to justify one’s place in the institution.

What we are really defending when we defend tenure is comfort. Comfort for those who have already won the gatekeeping game. Comfort for a system that prefers predictability to renewal. Comfort for an arrangement that mistakes longevity for contribution.
