You know how summers always go. The table gets too long, the cousins start arguing over who brought the better wine, the kids run until their voices crack, and someone finally says it’s time. So we gather. And I light the fire.

This year, I’m not going to give you a story that lets you step back from the edge. I’m going to tell you about a man alone in a cellar. The water is coming in. He doesn’t know why. He doesn’t know if anyone is looking for him. He only knows the water is rising, and he is counting.

He stands on the lowest step. The air is thick, cold, heavy with the smell of wet stone and old wood. He listens to the drip, then the trickle, then the steady push against the foundation. He knows the layout of this place. He knows where the shelves are. He knows the third shelf from the top holds the matches. He knows the water will reach that shelf before it reaches the ceiling. He knows that when it does, there will be no more striking, no more light, no more proof that he was here.

So he counts.

One breath. Two. Three. The water touches the first shelf. He shifts his weight. The stone is slick. He doesn’t move quickly. There’s no point. He counts again. Four. Five. Six. The water climbs past the jars, past the coiled rope, past the things people leave in cellars because they think they’ll remember them later. He doesn’t look at them. He looks at the shelf above. He counts the distance in breaths, in heartbeats, in the slow creep of the dark.

Seven. Eight. Nine. The water reaches the second shelf. His sleeves are wet. His hands are cold. He doesn’t shiver. Shivering wastes air. He keeps counting. Ten. Eleven. Twelve. The sound of the water changes. It’s not dripping anymore. It’s pressing. It’s finding every crack, every seam, every place the stone thought it was safe. He knows the matches are close. He knows he could reach for them now, but what would he do with them? Strike one in a room filling with water? Watch it drown? He doesn’t move. He counts.

Thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen. The water touches the third shelf. The matches are there. He can see the red tips, the dry paper, the little wooden sticks that promise fire if you treat them right. He doesn’t reach. He counts. Sixteen. Seventeen. Eighteen. The water rises an inch. Then another. The shelf is half submerged. The matches are wet at the base. He counts faster, not because there’s more air, but because the counting is all he has left to do. Nineteen. Twenty. Twenty-one.

The water covers the shelf. The matches sink. He watches them go under. He doesn’t gasp. He doesn’t cry out. He just stands there, in the dark, in the wet, in the quiet, and he keeps counting. Twenty-two. Twenty-three. Twenty-four. The water is at his knees. Then his thighs. Then his waist. He doesn’t fight it. He doesn’t pray. He doesn’t remember anyone’s face. He only counts. Twenty-five. Twenty-six. Twenty-seven.

The air is thinner now. He knows it. His chest knows it. His lungs know it. He counts anyway. Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine. Thirty. The water reaches his chest. He doesn’t struggle. He doesn’t look up for a rope, a hand, a voice. There is none. There never was. He counts. Thirty-one. Thirty-two. Thirty-three.

He counts until the counting becomes the only thing left. Until the numbers are all that hold him upright. Until the water is where it is, and he is where he is, and there is no lesson waiting at the top of the stairs, no hand reaching down, no meaning to be made from the dark. Just the counting. Just the water. Just the man, alone, measuring out what’s left.

And when the air is gone, he doesn’t stop counting. He just stops breathing.

That’s it. No rescue. No lesson. Just the counting. You can sit with it, or you can step back into the firelight. Either way, it’s yours now.

We gather around the fire because it’s what we do. Because the smoke rises, because the dark gathers at the edges, because someone always says, *Let’s hear one.* So I’ll tell you this one. It’s not a story with a turn. It’s a story with a count.

There is a man in a cellar. The door is shut. The water is coming in through the cracks in the stone, through the seam where the floor meets the wall, through the old pipe that gave way without warning. It doesn’t rush. It just keeps arriving. He is alone. There is no one above him. No voices. No footsteps. Just the sound of water finding its level.

He knows where the matches are. They sit on the top shelf, in a tin that’s rusted at the corners, just out of reach. He knows how high the shelf is. He knows how fast the water is rising. He starts counting.

One. The water touches the bottom step.
Two. It climbs the first riser.
Three. It reaches the toe of his boot.
Four. The cold goes up his shin.
Five. He shifts his weight. The water doesn’t care.
Six. It laps at the second shelf’s support.
Seven. He breathes in. He breathes out. He counts again.
Eight. The tin is still above him.
Nine. The water is at the third rung.
Ten. He counts slower now. Not because he’s afraid. Because there’s nothing else to do.

He doesn’t call out. There’s no one to hear. He doesn’t pray. There’s no one to answer. He just watches the water climb, and he counts the inches between it and the shelf. He counts the seconds between breaths. He counts the quiet.

Eleven. The water touches the wood.
Twelve. It swells around the base of the shelf.
Thirteen. He lifts his heel. The water takes it.
Fourteen. He stands on one foot. Then the other. Then neither.
Fifteen. The tin is still there.
Sixteen. The water is at the bottom edge of the shelf.
Seventeen. He counts with his eyes closed. It doesn’t change the number.
Eighteen. The wood darkens. The water keeps coming.
Nineteen. He doesn’t move. There’s nowhere to move to.
Twenty. The water is at the shelf.
Twenty-one. It touches the tin.
Twenty-two. It doesn’t knock it over. It just reaches it.
Twenty-three. He counts anyway.
Twenty-four. The water rises past the tin.
Twenty-five. The matches are underwater.
Twenty-six. He keeps counting.
Twenty-seven. The air is thinner. The water is higher.
Twenty-eight. He doesn’t stop.
Twenty-nine. The shelf is submerged.
Thirty. He is still counting.

There is no rescue. There is no lesson. There is only the water, the shelf, the matches, and the counting. It doesn’t end with a hand on the shoulder. It doesn’t end with a door opening. It ends when the counting stops, because there’s no air left to measure, and no one left to hear it.

That’s the story. You can sit with it. You can let it sit with you. The fire’s still burning. The night’s still here. We’ll keep counting together, if you want. Or we won’t. Either way, it’s yours now.

You know how this goes. The embers are lit. The coffee’s poured. The cousins are shifting in their chairs, the little ones are fighting sleep, and I’m supposed to give you something that ends with a hand on the shoulder and a quiet lesson you can carry home. 

Tonight, I won’t do that. 

There’s a man. He’s alone. The cellar is filling. 

He doesn’t know how the water got in. He doesn’t know why no one is coming. He only knows the water is rising, and he knows where the matches are. They sit on the top shelf, the one with the chipped white paint, the one that used to hold jars of dried mint and old receipts. He knows exactly how high that shelf is. He’s measured it in his head before. Now he measures it again.

He counts the air.

Not the way you count money. Not the way you count steps. He counts the space between breaths. He counts the inches of dark above his head. He counts the seconds it takes for a drop to fall from the pipe and hit the water with a sound so small it almost disappears.

One. Two. Three. 

The water touches the bottom step. He shifts his weight. The stone is cold through his shoes. He doesn’t move toward the stairs. He doesn’t call out. He just keeps counting.

Four. Five. Six. 

The shelf is still above him. He knows the distance. He’s always known it. He counts the gap between the water and the wood. He counts the way the dark changes when the water climbs. He counts the matchbox sitting there, the striker strip on the side, the little dent where someone once dropped it. He doesn’t plan to use them. He just knows they’re there. Knowing is enough for now.

Seven. Eight. Nine. 

The water reaches the first shelf. It doesn’t rush. It doesn’t break. It just arrives, slow and steady, like something that has nowhere else to be. He watches it touch the edge of the white paint. He counts the seconds it takes to wet the wood. He counts the way the air feels heavier when the space above him shrinks.

Ten. Eleven. Twelve. 

He doesn’t pray. He doesn’t bargain. He doesn’t remember his mother’s voice or the smell of rain on hot stone or the face of anyone who might have pulled him out. He only counts. The counting is what holds the dark in place. The counting is what keeps him from floating away in his own head.

Thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen. 

The water climbs. The shelf stays. The matches stay. He stays. He counts the way the water sounds different when it reaches the corners. He counts the way his own breathing changes when there’s less room. He counts the exact moment the water touches the bottom of the matchbox. He counts the way the cardboard softens. He counts the way nothing happens.

Sixteen. Seventeen. Eighteen. 

No one knocks. No light appears at the stairwell. No voice calls his name. The cellar does what cellars do. The water does what water does. He does what he’s doing. He counts.

Nineteen. Twenty. Twenty-one. 

The shelf is nearly level with the surface. He can see the matchbox clearly now. He can see the striker strip. He can see the little dent. He counts the distance between the water and the wood. He counts the distance between the wood and his hands. He counts the distance between one breath and the next.

Twenty-two. Twenty-three. Twenty-four. 

The water touches the shelf. It doesn’t spill over. It just sits there, level with the wood, waiting. He watches it. He counts the way the dark holds still. He counts the way the matches sit untouched. He counts the way the air is almost gone.

Twenty-five. Twenty-six. Twenty-seven. 

He doesn’t reach. He doesn’t strike. He doesn’t close his eyes. He keeps counting. The water is at the shelf. The matches are at the shelf. He is below the shelf. The counting continues.

Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine. Thirty. 

And if you’re waiting for the water to break, or for a hand to appear, or for the matches to catch, or for him to learn something you can take back to your own house, your own family, your own summer night—there isn’t any of that. 

There’s only the counting. 

And the counting goes on.

He is alone in the cellar.

The water is already at his ankles. It is cold, and it moves with a slow, heavy patience. He does not know where it is coming from. He does not know how long it has been coming. He only knows that it is rising, and that he is standing on a wooden floor that will not hold forever.

He looks up.

On the far wall, there is a shelf. It is narrow, painted the color of old ash, and it holds a single box of matches. The box is dry. The matches are dry. The water is not.

He begins to count.

Not because counting will stop the water. Not because counting will bring anyone to the stairs. He counts because his lungs are drawing in air that feels thinner with every breath, and because if he gives the numbers a place to land, they might keep him from floating away before the water does.

One. Two. Three.

The water touches the hem of his trousers. It climbs. He shifts his weight. The wood answers with a soft complaint.

Four. Five. Six.

He listens. The cellar has its own sounds now: the drip from a pipe that should not be dripping, the whisper of water finding the corners, the quiet working of his own chest. There is no voice above him. No footsteps on the steps. No light from the doorway. Only the dark, and the water, and the shelf.

Seven. Eight. Nine.

He does not pray. He does not curse. He keeps his eyes on the matches. They sit exactly where they sat this morning, when he came down for a candle and found the floor already damp. He remembers the box’s edge, the way the paper curls at the top, the faint smell of sulfur that rises when he thinks of striking one. He has not struck one. He will not strike one. There is nothing to light. There is only the counting.

Ten. Eleven. Twelve.

The water reaches his calves. It is colder now, or perhaps he is simply feeling it more. He does not move. To move is to admit the water is winning. To stay is to admit the same thing. So he counts, and the water rises, and the two things happen at once.

Thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen.

He thinks, briefly, of the people who would notice his absence. He thinks of the chair he usually occupies, the place he takes at the table, the name that would be spoken when the room grows quiet. The thought does not bring comfort. It does not bring rescue. It only sits beside him in the dark, another witness he did not ask for.

Sixteen. Seventeen. Eighteen.

The shelf is still above him. He can see it. He can measure the distance in breaths, in heartbeats, in the slow creep of water over the floorboards. He does not know how many numbers remain before the water reaches the wood. He does not need to know. The counting is not a map. It is a way of staying present to what is happening.

Nineteen. Twenty. Twenty-one.

His hands are steady. His voice, if he were to use it, would be steady too. He does not use it. He lets the numbers pass through him, one after another, like water through a crack in the wall. He does not hurry them. He does not slow them. He meets each one as it comes.

Twenty-two. Twenty-three. Twenty-four.

The water touches the lower edge of the shelf. A single drop climbs the wood and falls back. The matchbox does not move. The matches inside do not move. The dark does not move. Only the water moves, and his breath, and the counting.

Twenty-five. Twenty-six. Twenty-seven.

He does not look away. He does not close his eyes. He keeps his gaze on the box, on the dry paper, on the small red strike-strip along the side. He counts toward it. He counts past it. He counts as if the numbers themselves are a floor he can stand on.

Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine. Thirty.

The water is at the shelf now. It laps against the wood. It finds the edge. It does not spill over. Not yet. The matchbox remains dry, balanced on a surface that is no longer fully dry. He knows this. He counts anyway.

Thirty-one. Thirty-two. Thirty-three.

There is no lesson here. There is no hand on his shoulder. There is no sudden opening of the door, no lantern raised, no voice calling his name. There is only the cellar, the water, the shelf, the matches, and the counting. If there is a meaning, it does not announce itself. It waits in the dark with him.

Thirty-four. Thirty-five. Thirty-six.

He does not know what the next number will bring. He does not know whether the water will climb the shelf, whether the box will float, whether his breath will find a rhythm he can no longer follow. He only knows that the counting has become the only thing he can still do, and so he does it.

Thirty-seven. Thirty-eight. Thirty-nine.

The water rises. The numbers rise with it. He stays where he is. He stays with the counting. He stays with the dark. He stays with the matches on the shelf, just above the water, just out of reach, just there.

Forty.

He keeps going.

The water came in without hurry. It found the cracks in the stone, the seam in the door, the place where the earth had settled just enough to let it through. It did not rush. It did not announce itself. It simply arrived, and kept arriving.

He was alone. The cellar was his, or had been, or would be again once the water decided how much of it it wanted. He stood where the floor met the wall, and he began to count.

Not because counting would change anything. Not because numbers are a kind of prayer. He counted because his hands were empty, because the dark was full, and because if he stopped moving his mind, the dark would move him.

The water was at his ankles. He counted the breaths it took to feel the cold climb his shins. One. Two. Three. The air above him was still dry. The air above him was still his, for now.

He looked up. The shelf was there. The matches were there. The box was dry, or mostly dry, or dry enough to matter if the water ever stopped pretending it was patient. He counted the distance from his eyes to the shelf. Not in feet. Not in steps. In the way the dark thickened, in the way the dampness began to smell like old wood and wet iron. He counted until the number felt like something he could hold.

The water moved to his knees. He counted the seconds it took for the cold to settle into his bones. He counted the way his breath sounded different when there was less room above it. He counted the quiet. He counted the absence of anything that might have been a voice, a footstep, a hand on the stairs. There was none of that. There was only the water, and the counting, and the shelf.

He did not pray. He did not bargain. He did not invent a reason for the water to stop, or for someone to come, or for the matches to matter in a way that would save him. He knew what he knew. The water was rising. The shelf was above. The matches were on it. The air was thinning. He counted.

The water touched the lower edge of the shelf. He counted the way the wood darkened where the moisture reached it. He counted the small sound it made, the almost-sound of absorption. He counted the space between one breath and the next, and how that space was getting shorter, and how the shorter space did not feel like panic, only like arithmetic.

He counted the matches by shape, by the way their heads caught the faint light from somewhere far above, by the way they sat in their row like things that had once been meant for lighting, for warmth, for starting something that would not come. He counted them because he could. He counted them because there was nothing else to count.

The water climbed. The air thinned. The counting continued.

He did not look for a lesson in the water. He did not look for a hand at the top of the stairs. He did not look for meaning in the matches, or in the dark, or in the fact that he was alone and that the cellar was filling and that the number of breaths left was a number he could name but not stretch. He counted.

One breath. Another. The water at the shelf. The matches dry, then not dry, then out of reach. The air above him smaller. The counting still going. The dark still full. The water still arriving.

He counted until there was nothing left to count but the water, and the dark, and the fact that he was still counting, and that the counting was all there was.

There is a man in a cellar. The water is rising. He is alone. There is no one coming.

He stands on the top step of the wooden ladder, one hand gripping the rim of the opening above, the other holding a pocket watch that has stopped. He does not need the watch. He needs the shelf.

The shelf is three steps above his head. It is made of rough pine, stained dark by years of damp. On the shelf sits a box of matches. Red strike-anywhere matches, the kind that smell like sulfur and promise when you open the lid. They are dry. He checked them an hour ago, before the water took the floor, before it took the bottom step, before it took his shoes.

Now he counts.

He counts the inches of air left between the water line and the shelf.

The water is black and cold. It moves with a slow, heavy patience. It does not rush. It knows it will win. It laps against the stone foundation with a sound like a tongue clicking against a tooth.

One inch. The water touches the toe of his boot. He lifts his foot. He stands on the balls of his feet now, balancing on the narrow edge of the step. The air is thick. It smells of wet earth and old roots and the iron smell of his own fear.

Two inches. The water rises past the boot. He is standing in his socks now. The cold comes through the wool, up his ankles, into his knees. He does not shiver. Shivering wastes oxygen. He keeps his chest still. He keeps his eyes on the shelf.

Three inches. The water reaches the hem of his trousers. He can feel the drag of it, the weight of it trying to pull him down. He shifts his weight to the left foot. The wood of the step groans under him. He waits for the step to break. It does not. Not yet.

Four inches. He breathes in. He breathes out. The breath is shallow. The cellar is shrinking. The walls are closing in, not physically, but perceptually. The space for his lungs is getting smaller. The space for his thoughts is getting smaller.

Five inches. The water touches the bottom of the shelf. A single drop splashes up, hits the wood, runs down the side. He watches the drop. He wants to knock it away. He does not move his hand. To move his hand is to risk the balance. To risk the balance is to fall. If he falls, the water takes him before it takes the matches. He stays still.

Six inches. He counts the seconds between the rises. The water does not rise steadily. It comes in pulses, in surges, as if something upstream has opened a gate, then closed it, then opened it again. He waits for the surge. He holds his breath during the surge. He exhales when the water settles.

Seven inches. His arms are tired. His shoulders burn. He grips the rim above with both hands now. His knuckles are white. The skin is slipping on the wet wood. He adjusts his grip. He does not look down. Looking down tells him how far he has already lost.

Eight inches. The box of matches is within reach. He can see the label. He can see the friction strip on the side. He knows what he will do when his fingers touch the cardboard. He knows the strike. He knows the flare. He knows the warmth. He knows none of it will matter. He knows this anyway. He has known it since the water took the door.

Nine inches. The air is thin. He can feel it in his temples, a pressure behind the eyes. His thoughts are slowing. They are becoming heavy, like stones dropping into the water. *Why am I counting?* The thought comes. He lets it pass. *Because counting is something.* Because counting is a way to stay here, in this second, instead of falling into the next one.

Ten inches. The water covers the bottom of the shelf. It creeps up the side. It touches the bottom edge of the matchbox. The cardboard darkens. It softens. He watches the water take the edge. He watches the box begin to swell.

Eleven inches. He could jump. He could let go of the rim, drop into the water, swim to the shelf, grab the box, climb back. But the water is above his waist now. The current in the cellar is not a current; it is a weight. It would hold him down. It would push him against the wall. He would not reach the shelf. He knows this. He has done the math. He is doing the math.

Twelve inches. His grip slips. His right hand slides down an inch. He catches it. He pulls himself back up. His shoulder screams. He does not make a sound. There is no one to hear it. There is no one to care. This is the truth of it. Not the water. Not the matches. The truth is the silence. The truth is that he is alone in a room that is becoming a tomb, and he is counting inches as if the numbers can hold back the dark.

Thirteen inches. The matchbox is half submerged. The cardboard is soft. The matches inside are still dry, but the box is failing. The lid is lifting. He sees a single match slide out, roll down the side of the box, and float on the surface of the water. It drifts toward him. It bobs in the surge. It comes to rest against his knee.

He looks at the match. He looks at the shelf. He looks at the water.

Fourteen inches. He does not reach for the match. He does not reach for the box. He stays on the step. He stays on the edge. He counts.

Fifteen inches. The water touches his belt. He loosens it. He does not know why. It is a small motion. A useless motion. It is the kind of motion a man makes when he is trying to remember who he was before the water came. Before the cellar. Before the counting.

Sixteen inches. His breathing is harder now. Each inhale is a negotiation. Each exhale is a surrender. The air is gone, but he does not know it yet. He thinks there is more. He thinks the next inch will be the same as the last. He thinks the numbers go on forever.

Seventeen inches. The match against his knee floats away. It drifts back toward the shelf. It joins the others. It is just another piece of wood and sulfur and promise, disappearing into the dark.

Eighteen inches. He closes his eyes. He counts with his fingers now. He taps the wood of the step. One tap. Two taps. Three taps. He taps until his fingers are numb. He taps until the water takes the step. He taps until the water takes him.

Nineteen inches. The shelf is gone. The matches are gone. The box is gone. The water is at his chest. He is standing on the last inch of dry wood. He is holding on with both hands. He is counting.

Twenty inches. There is no air left. There is no shelf. There is no match. There is only the water, and the counting, and the man who keeps counting because he does not know how to stop.

He counts.

He counts.

He counts.

***

A few notes for reading it aloud:

- **Pacing:** Let the numbers breathe. Don't rush them. The power of the piece is in the gap between one count and the next, where the listener's own imagination fills in the rising water.
- **Tone:** Keep it flat and steady. No dramatic swell at the end. The point is that there's no release, no lesson, no rescue—so the delivery shouldn't offer one either. The last three lines should be almost whispered, as if the voice itself is running out of air.
- **Pauses:** After "He counts" at the end, hold the silence for a few seconds before you step back. Let the fire-pit noise come back on its own.

**Title:** The Clock Strikes Nothing
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A single room. The door is locked from the outside. The only sound is the ticking of a clock on the wall, perfectly audible.

**(ELARA stands center. She is not crying. She is not shaking. She is looking at the door, then at the audience, as if they are the glass in the window. She speaks quietly, precisely. There is no music. There is only the clock.)**

**ELARA**
You're waiting for the scream. You're waiting for me to hit the door, to throw something, to beg. That's the version you know. The version where the victim fights the cage until the bars bend. That's not this. This is the part where the bars become the walls of the room, and the room becomes the shape of your body, and you forget what it felt like to stand up without counting the seconds first.

He doesn't need to lock the door anymore. Not really. I stopped checking the handle three weeks ago. Or maybe four. Time is his property. He rents it out to me in fifteen-minute blocks. Breakfast. Hygiene. Study. Silence. I know the schedule better than I know my own name. I know that at 14:00 he brings the water. I know that at 14:05 he checks the lock. I know that if I am not in the chair by 14:00, there is a consequence. So I am in the chair by 13:55. I breathe so he doesn't have to tell me to breathe.

You think this is about fear. It's not. Fear implies there is something out there that can hurt you. This is about ownership. He owns the light. He owns the noise. He owns the air I exhale. And the worst part isn't the control. The worst part is the efficiency of it. He doesn't yell. He doesn't have to. He just adjusts the variables. He turns the heat down two degrees. He moves the book you're not allowed to read three inches further away. He makes the world smaller by millimeters until you fit inside the space he's left for you.

I used to wait. I used to sit by the window and watch the street. I watched for the police. I watched for her. I watched for anyone who didn't walk with his step. I told myself that if I just stayed quiet, if I just kept my head down, someone would notice. A neighbor. A mailman. A stray dog. Something. That was the deal I made with myself. Suffering in exchange for rescue. I would endure the hours so that one day, the hours would stop.

But the sun goes down every day. And the lock clicks every night. And no one comes.

You want to know the moment I stopped believing? It wasn't dramatic. There was no thunder. It was a Tuesday. I was watching the driveway. I saw a car turn the corner. My heart jumped. I started to stand. I started to wave. And then I saw it was him. He was just coming back early. He had forgotten something. Or he was checking on me. It doesn't matter why. The point is that the car was his. The world outside that window is his. The road is his. The sky is his. Even the things that look free are just things he hasn't bothered to lock yet.

So I sat back down.

That was the day I died. Not the body. The body stays. The body eats the food he puts on the plate. The body sleeps when the light goes out. The body is compliant. But the part of me that wanted to be found? That part starved. It withered. It turned into something quiet. Something hard.

Now, when I hear the lock click, I don't flinch. I don't wonder who it is. I know it's him. I know he's checking. I know he's making sure I'm still here, still his, still waiting for a permission that isn't coming. And I let him check. I let him own the minute. I let him own the hour. I let him own the day.

You want hope? You want me to tell you that I'm planning something. That I'm biding my time. That I'm stronger than him. That's a lie. That's the story you tell yourself so you can sleep at night. You want to believe that if you were trapped, you'd find a way out. You'd be the hero. You'd be the one who breaks the glass.

I'm not the hero. I'm the tenant. And the landlord has the keys.

I don't believe anyone is coming. I don't believe the door will open. I don't believe the sun is mine. I believe that when he walks in, I will look up. I will speak when he asks me a question. I will exist only where he allows me to exist. And there is a terrible peace in that. A cold, clean peace. No more waiting. No more watching the driveway. No more hoping for a rescue that belongs to a different life.

This is my life. It is measured in ticks. It is measured in locks. It is measured in the space between his footsteps and mine.

So don't look at me like I'm waiting. I'm not. I'm staying. And the door is locked. And I am here. And that is all there is.

We gather every summer. The fire pit, the smoke, the cousins who’ve grown taller, the in-laws who’ve learned the names, the kids who stay up just long enough to hear the first line. And every year, I open the circle. This year, I’m not going to give you a lesson. I’m not going to give you a rescue. I’m just going to tell you about a man in a cellar, and the water, and the counting.

The cellar is stone. The door is shut. The water is coming up from somewhere below, or maybe from the walls, or maybe from the ground itself. It doesn’t matter where it starts. It only matters that it rises.

He is alone. He knows this. He has always known this. There is no one above him calling down. No one below him waiting. Just the dark, the damp, and the slow climb of the water.

He stands on a wooden crate. The crate is steady. The water is not.

On the far wall, there is a shelf. It is set into the stone, just high enough that the water has not touched it yet. On that shelf sits a box of matches. Not many. Enough to count. Enough to matter.

He begins counting.

One. The water is at his ankles. Cold. It moves around his boots like it has somewhere else to be.

Two. The water is at his calves. It finds the gaps in the wood. It does not rush. It simply arrives.

Three. He breathes. The air is still there. It is still breathable. He counts the matches because counting is something a person can do when there is nothing else to do. One match. Two matches. Three.

Four. The water reaches his knees. He shifts his weight. The crate does not complain. He is grateful for that, and he does not say why.

Five. Five matches left in the box. He knows this because he has counted them before. He knows the shape of the box, the way the lid catches, the way the sticks lie side by side. He knows them the way you know the face of someone you will not see again.

Six. The water is at his thighs. It is heavier now. It presses against the crate. The wood holds. For now.

Seven. He counts the matches again. Not because he has forgotten. Because counting is a way of staying here. Of staying in the room. Of staying in the body.

Eight. The water touches the shelf. Not the matches. The shelf. A thin line of wet stone. He watches it. He does not move.

Nine. Nine matches. He could strike one. He could see the flame. He could watch it burn down to his fingers. He does not. He keeps counting.

Ten. The water is at the shelf. It laps at the wood. It does not spill over. Not yet. The matches are still dry. They are still there. They are still countable.

Eleven. He breathes. The air is thinner. Not gone. Just thinner. He notices this. He does not panic. Panic would be a story. He is not telling a story.

Twelve. The water covers the bottom of the shelf. The matches sit above it. They are still dry. They are still there. They are still countable.

Thirteen. He counts the matches. He counts the water. He counts his breaths. He does not know which one will finish first. He does not need to know.

Fourteen. The water rises. It does not hurry. It does not wait. It simply continues.

Fifteen. Fifteen matches. Or fifteen breaths. Or fifteen seconds. It is all the same now. The counting is the only thing that is still his.

Sixteen. The water touches the first match. Not the box. The match. The tip. A dark line. He watches it. He does not move.

Seventeen. The water climbs. The matches remain. The counting continues.

Eighteen. The air is still there. It is still breathable. He is still here. The water is still coming.

Nineteen. Nineteen. Nineteen. He says it to the stone. He says it to the dark. He says it to the water. It does not answer. It does not need to.

Twenty. The water reaches the shelf. The matches are wet. They are not gone. They are just wet. He keeps counting.

Twenty-one. Twenty-two. Twenty-three. The numbers do not stop. The water does not stop. He does not stop.

There is no rescue. There is no lesson. There is only the counting, and the water, and the man who keeps counting because it is the only thing left to do.

And when the water reaches the last match, or when the air runs out, or when the counting simply ends because there is nothing left to count, it will not be a tragedy. It will not be a warning. It will just be the end of the counting.

And that is all I have to tell you.

***

**A few notes for reading it aloud:**
- Let the numbers land. Don’t rush them. The repetition is the engine of the piece.
- Pause after “There is no rescue. There is no lesson.” Give the room a beat to feel the absence of the usual story-shape.
- Keep your voice level. The power here is in the restraint, not in escalation.
- When you finish, hold the silence for a moment before you step back into the firelight. The piece is built to leave the space exactly as you asked: unrelieved, uncounted, and honest.

**Title:** The Clock Strikes Nothing
**Character:** ELARA (17)

You still think I'm waiting for the key. You still think there's a difference between the lock being turned and the lock being broken. There isn't. Not anymore.

I used to count the hours. I used to make a game of it. Seven AM, the light hits the dust motes in the hallway. Eight AM, the footsteps on the stairs. Nine AM, the bowl of cereal on the desk, cold by noon. I knew the schedule better than you did. I knew when you were tired because your footsteps got heavier. I knew when you were angry because you stopped knocking before you entered. I knew the rhythm of the cage.

And I used to tell myself that rhythm was proof. Proof that someone was out there keeping time. Proof that the world still turned, even if I wasn't allowed to turn with it. If I knew the schedule, I knew the system. If I knew the system, I could find the crack. That's what you want me to believe. That's what I wanted to believe.

But look at the clock. No hands. You took the hands off three weeks ago. Or maybe I did. I don't remember the moment. I just know I woke up and the face was blank. And I realized… I realized I didn't care.

I stopped listening for the sirens two months ago. I stopped looking at the sky to see if the clouds moved. I stopped checking the mail slot because I know there's no mail. There's no one coming. Not the police. Not my mother. Not the friends I told myself were waiting for me to signal them. They aren't coming. Because if they were coming, they would have come when I was still loud. They would have come when I still thought I deserved to be found.

Now I'm just… quiet. And quiet doesn't trigger alarms. Quiet doesn't look like a rescue mission. Quiet looks like compliance. And you love compliance. You love it because it means you don't have to work anymore. You don't have to watch me. You can just let the house do the work.

The house is better than you are. The house keeps the temperature steady. The house keeps the food coming. The house keeps the silence thick enough to sleep in. You're redundant. You're just a ghost walking the halls, checking a lock that doesn't need checking because I've already stopped trying to open it.

I know what you're thinking. You're thinking, "She's broken." You're thinking this is the moment I give up. But that's not it. Giving up implies I thought I had a chance. Giving up implies I thought there was a outside.

There isn't.

This room isn't a waiting room. It's a container. And I'm not the thing inside it waiting to be released. I'm the thing that belongs here. The dust belongs here. The silence belongs here. The way the light dies at 4 PM without anyone to notice it belongs here.

You control the hours, but you don't control the time. Time isn't the clock. Time is the decay. Time is the way I forget what my own voice sounds like when I'm not answering you. Time is the way I look at the door and I don't feel anger anymore. I feel nothing. And nothing is heavier than anger. Nothing is harder to lift.

So go ahead. Turn the key. Walk away. Come back tomorrow. Check the locks. Check the windows. Check my pulse. It doesn't matter. I'm not going anywhere because I'm already here. I'm already gone.

You wanted a prisoner who fights? You should have stopped me when I was screaming. Now? Now I'm just the house. And the house doesn't leave.

**(She looks at the door one last time. She does not blink. She turns away from it, walks to the bed, and sits. She does not look at the audience. She looks at the wall.)**

**Title:** *The Ledger*
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A bedroom. The door is locked from the outside. The window is painted shut. There is a clock on the wall, but it has no hands.

**(ELARA stands center. She is not crying. She is not shaking. She is looking at the door, then at the audience, as if they are the mirror in the hallway. She speaks quietly, with the precision of someone who has memorized the sound of the lock turning.)**

You're waiting for the scream. You're sitting there, shifting in your seats, checking your phones, waiting for the moment where I realize the door is locked and I scream until my throat bleeds. That's the scene you want. That's the scene you think is real.

Screaming is for when there's still a chance someone hears you. Screaming is a transaction. I give you noise, you give me help. I stopped doing transactions three months ago.

You want to know when it happened? When I stopped believing the rescue was coming? It wasn't when he took the key. It wasn't when he painted the windows. It was on a Tuesday. I know it was a Tuesday because Tuesdays are for laundry. He doesn't do laundry. He hires people for that. So I knew, on that Tuesday, that I wasn't going to be allowed to leave to go to the laundromat. I knew I was going to be handed a basket and told to fold what was already clean.

That was the day I realized the schedule wasn't a cage. It was a life. He wasn't keeping me in. He was keeping the world out. There's a difference. A cage implies there's somewhere else to go. This… this is the only geography I have left.

You think I'm waiting for a knock at the door. You think I'm listening for the sirens, the neighbors, the father who stopped calling, the friend who stopped texting. I hear every footstep in the hall. I know the difference between the mailman's shoes and his shoes. I know the weight of the key in the lock. I know the exact second the deadbolt slides home. It's 7:00 PM. Every night. 7:00 PM. The house breathes in, the house breathes out. And I breathe with it.

I used to mark the days on the wall. Chalk. I had a whole calendar. I crossed them off. One day, I ran out of chalk. I looked at the wall. I looked at the door. I didn't go find more chalk. I sat down on the bed. I folded my hands. I waited for the light to change, and it didn't. The sun went down. The lamp went on. The clock on the wall ticked, but it doesn't have hands, so it doesn't tell time. It just tells noise.

I am not waiting for you. I am not waiting for him to forget. I am not waiting for the lock to break. I am waiting for the next hour to start.

He says I'm safe. He says the world is loud and I am quiet here. He says I'm his responsibility. He says it like a prayer. He says it like a law. And maybe he believes it. Maybe he thinks he's saving me from something out there. But there is no out there. There is only in here. And in here, I am the only thing that moves.

You want teeth? Here they are. I'm not going to run. I'm not going to fight. I'm going to let him think he won. I'm going to let him think I'm grateful. I'm going to smile when he brings the food. I'm going to say thank you when he locks the door. I'm going to be the perfect bird in the perfect cage until he forgets to feed me, or until I decide I don't need to eat.

But don't look at me like I'm a victim. Victims are people who still think they have a choice. I don't. I have the schedule. I have the room. I have the silence.

You can clap when it's over. You can stand up and tell your friends you saw something brave. You can go home to your locked doors that you choose to lock, to your schedules you choose to keep. I hope you sleep well. I hope you dream of open windows. I'll be here. I'll be here when the light changes. I'll be here when the key turns. I'll be here until there's nothing left of me that remembers what the sky looks like without a frame around it.

I waited for the neighbors to notice the silence. I waited for my mother to come back, even though I know she's not coming. I waited for you to change your mind, to open the door and say, "Just kidding, you can go." But you didn't. And now the muscle is gone. I don't have the strength to wait anymore.

It's a perfect circle. A perfect cage. You think if you give me a name for every hour, I won't notice I'm not living any of them. You let me think there was a chance, just enough chance, to keep me compliant.

But I checked the window today. Not to escape. Just to look. There's nothing out there. There's no rescue. There's no army. There's no friend with a key. There's just the street, and the street is empty, and even if it wasn't, no one knows I'm here. You made sure of that. You made sure I was erased before I was locked in.

So I'm done waiting. I'm done looking at the clock. I'm done pretending that 1800 Dinner matters when I'm not hungry. I'm done pretending that 0600 Wake matters when I don't want to open my eyes.

You control the hours, but you don't control what I do with the seconds in between. You don't control what I think when you're in the other room. You don't control the fact that I know you're afraid. I hear you pacing sometimes. I hear you checking the locks twice. You're not the warden. You're the prisoner too. You're locked in here with me, and you're more trapped than I am because you have to pretend you're free.

I'm not going to scream. I'm not going to bang on the door. That's what you expect. That's what the schedule accounts for. Rebellion is on the list. Anger is on the list. You know how to handle those. You have protocols for breaking things.

But this? This quiet? This absolute, flat acceptance that no one is coming? You don't have a protocol for this. You can't schedule a response to nothing. You can't plan for the moment the victim stops wanting to be saved because she realizes the savior is just another story you told her to keep her quiet.

I'm going to sit down. I'm going to take the paperclip off the schedule. I'm going to fold it into a shape that isn't on your list. And I'm going to wait for you to come in here and tell me what to do next. And when you do, I won't answer. I won't look at you. I won't give you the satisfaction of knowing I'm still in there. I'll be gone. I'll be here, in this room, but I'll be gone.

You wanted a project. You wanted something to manage. Something to control. You got one. But you forgot the most important part of the schedule. You forgot to account for the end. You forgot to account for the moment I stop believing the door exists.

It doesn't exist. There is only this room. And I am the only thing in it that breathes. And I am not going to breathe for you anymore. I'm going to breathe for me. Even if there's nothing to breathe for. Even if it's just air. Even if it's just time.

Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock. You hear that? That's not my heart. That's not your clock. That's the sound of you losing me. Slowly. Quietly. Exactly on schedule.

**(She sits. She folds the paper. She does not look up. She does not cry. She waits for the next hour, not because she has to, but because she is choosing to occupy the space.)**

**Title:** The Lock
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A bedroom. The door is visible, but the focus is on her.

**(ELARA stands near the window. She is not looking out. She is looking at the door. She speaks to the room, or to the person who holds the key, or to herself. It does not matter which.)**

You can stop checking the lock now. I know you check it. I hear the turn of the wrist. I hear the click. I used to wait for the sound of the handle moving the other way. I used to listen for the footsteps that weren't yours. I used to count the cars on the street below, thinking every headlight was a rescue that had taken a wrong turn.

There are no cars anymore. Or there are, and I just don't care.

You tell me what to eat. You tell me when to sleep. You tell me which curtain to draw and how many degrees the thermostat gets to be. You tell me I'm safe. You tell me the world is ugly and I'm clean and I should thank you for the soap.

I'm not clean. I'm stale.

Do you know what happens to bread when you leave it in the wrapper too long? It doesn't rot. It just gets hard. It gets dense. It becomes something else. Something that doesn't bend.

I am not waiting.

That's the thing you don't get. You think I'm waiting. You think there's a part of me still sitting on the edge of the bed, knees tucked to my chest, watching the dust motes dance in the slat of light you allow me, praying for a shadow on the porch. You think I'm a victim. Victims wait. Victims believe in the future.

I don't believe in the future. I believe in the schedule.

Seven AM. Wake. Seven Fifteen. Make the bed. You check the corners. You check the sheets for wrinkles like you're looking for evidence of life. There are no wrinkles. There is no life. There is only the order you demand so you can tell yourself you're in charge.

Eight AM. Breakfast. Oatmeal. Warm. Not hot. You say hot burns. You say I'm fragile. I'm not fragile. I'm bored. There's a difference. Fragile breaks. Bored stays. Bored watches the paint peel. Bored counts the tiles. Bored learns the exact second the light shifts from the east wall to the west wall so you know when you're allowed to feel the sun.

You think you're keeping me in. You think this is a cage.

It's not a cage. It's a mold. And I'm setting.

You come in here sometimes. You stand in the doorway. You look at me like I'm a project you haven't finished yet. Like I'm a draft you keep editing because you can't stand the way the sentences end. You want me to cry. You want me to scream. You want the performance of suffering because that validates your control. If I'm screaming, you're the jailer. If I'm crying, you're the captor. It gives you a role.

But I'm not giving you a role anymore.

I looked in the mirror this morning. I didn't see a girl who wants out. I saw a girl who lives here. The dust is part of the furniture. The silence is part of the language. You are not the visitor. You are the architecture.

You say someone is coming. You say help is on the way. You say that to keep me moving. To keep me washing the dishes you put in the sink. To keep me brushing the hair you tell me is too long.

No one is coming.

If they were, they would have come when the lights went out last week. They would have come when you forgot to lock the back door for thirty seconds and I stood in the hallway and listened to the wind and didn't move. I didn't move because I knew. I knew that outside that door isn't freedom. It's just another room with different rules. It's just another person telling me where to stand.

Here, at least, I know the walls.

You want me to hate you? That's easier, isn't it? Hate is a spark. Hate is energy. You can work with hate. You can fix hate.

This isn't hate. This is acceptance.

I am not going to run. I am not going to scream. I am not going to look at the window and pray.

I am going to sit in this chair. I am going to watch you turn the key. I am going to let you tell me it's for my own good. And I am going to let you believe that I believe you.

Because the only thing worse than being locked in is realizing you locked yourself in, and the person holding the key is just holding it because you handed it to them and asked them to watch it for you.

I'm not waiting for the door to open.

I'm waiting for you to realize it doesn't matter.

**(She turns from the door. She sits. She does not look back.)**

**Title:** The Clock on the Wall
**Character:** ELENA (17)
**Setting:** A single room. The door is locked from the outside. There is a window, but it is painted over or barred. There is a clock.

**(ELENA stands center. She is not crying. She is not shaking. She is perfectly still, looking at the audience as if they are the walls.)**

You can stop checking the lock now. I know how it works. You turn the key from the outside, you hear the tumblers fall, and then you walk away. You don't come back to check if I'm still here because you know I'm still here. I'm the only thing in this house that breathes on a schedule.

For the first month, I screamed. I screamed until my throat tasted like copper and I couldn't lift my tongue to my teeth. I screamed at the door, at the window, at the ceiling. I told you he was coming. I told you *she* was coming. I told you the police were coming, the neighbors, the mailman, anyone. I invented rescuers like I was knitting them out of desperation. I needed you to hear me. I needed you to know that I was not accepting this.

But you didn't come.

And that's the thing you need to understand about this room. It isn't the walls that broke me. It's the silence after the screaming stopped. It's the realization that the silence wasn't empty; it was full. It was full of you, deciding not to be here.

I used to watch the clock. I used to count the seconds between the tick and the tock like they were steps someone was taking toward me. I thought if I could just map the time, I could predict the rescue. I thought if I knew exactly when the hour changed, I'd know when the hand reached for the key.

But the hand doesn't reach. It just moves. Around and around. Cutting the day into slices I have to eat alone.

You think I'm waiting? You think I'm sitting here with my ears open, listening for a footstep in the hall? No. I closed that part of myself weeks ago. It was too heavy to carry. Hope is heavy. It weighs more than this furniture, more than this bed, more than my own bones. I put it down. I left it in the corner by the door where you wouldn't see it.

Now I know what time it is. It is always time for nothing.

He comes in sometimes. He brings food. He brings instructions. He tells me when to sleep, when to wash, when to speak. He thinks he controls the hours. He thinks he owns the clock. But he doesn't know what I know. He doesn't know that when you stop believing anyone is coming, you stop living for the future. You stop living for the next hour. You live only for the second you're in, because the next one doesn't belong to you.

He thinks I'm afraid. He thinks I'm waiting for him to leave so I can run. But I'm not running. There's nowhere to run to. If no one is coming for me, then no one is coming *from* me, either. I'm not going anywhere. This room isn't a cage anymore. It's a container. And I'm the thing inside it that's stopped rattling.

So don't look at me like I'm a victim. Don't look at me like I'm waiting for a miracle. I'm not. I'm the evidence that the miracle didn't happen. I'm the proof that the lock holds. I'm the proof that you looked at this house, you looked at this door, and you decided I was already gone.

The clock ticks. You hear it. You think it means time is passing. It doesn't. It just means I'm still here. And you're still not coming.

**(She looks at the clock. She does not move to check the door. She turns her back on the audience.)**

Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock.

Nothing changes.

**Title:** The Inventory of Silence
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A room with no windows. The light is artificial, constant.

**(ELARA stands center. She is not pacing. She is not trembling. She is perfectly still, as if movement has become too expensive to afford. She speaks to the room, or to the person who controls the locks. It does not matter which.)**

You stopped checking the lock this morning. I know because the click changed. It used to be a question. Now it's a period. You think I didn't notice the shift in the grammar of this place?

I used to count the hours by the sound of your footsteps in the hall. Heavy, then light. Keys jingling. The specific drag of the deadbolt when you came in to check on me. I used to wait for that drag. I used to build my whole day around the hope that the drag would stop, that someone else would walk past my door, someone who didn't know my name, someone who would hear me screaming and actually stop.

But you know what happens when you wait long enough? The waiting stops being a strategy and starts being a biology. It becomes part of the blood. It becomes the rhythm the heart beats to.

I looked at the calendar today. You let me keep it. You think that's kindness. You think giving me a grid of squares makes me feel like I'm moving through time. But I marked the days. I marked them all. And I realized something. There is no rescue date. There is no birthday party waiting on the other side of this wall. There is no teacher who is going to call the police because I missed too many classes. There is no mother who is going to come knocking because the school called home.

They know. They all know. And they decided I was easier to lose than to find.

That's the thing you don't get about this town. It's not that people don't see me. It's that they see me and they look away because looking away is cheaper. It's easier to let the girl in the house disappear than to admit the house is a cage. So I stopped waiting for the knock. I stopped waiting for the sirens. I stopped waiting for the moment where the door opens and it's not you.

Because the door isn't opening. Not today. Not next year. Not when I'm thirty. Not when I'm dead.

You control the light. You control the food. You control when I sleep and when I wake. You think that makes you the master of this room. But you're wrong. You're just the janitor. You're the one who comes in to sweep up the mess when I stop pretending I'm alive.

I'm not screaming anymore. Do you hear that? The silence isn't fear. It's acceptance. I have accepted that this is the geography of my life now. These four walls are not a prison anymore. They are the map. There is nothing outside them. There is no one coming.

So you can lock the door. You can check the windows. You can schedule my minutes until the end of time. But you don't own me anymore. You just own the space I occupy while I wait for nothing.

I'm not going to run. There's nowhere to run to. I'm not going to beg. You don't care. I'm just going to stand here. And I'm going to watch you watch me. And I'm going to let you see exactly what happens when a girl realizes she is already gone.

**(She looks directly at the audience, or the controller. Her face is blank. Not angry. Not sad. Empty.)**

The lock clicked. You're here. You're always here. But I'm not.

**(Blackout.)**

**Title:** The Inventory of Silence
**Character:** ELENA (17)
**Setting:** A room with no windows. The light is artificial, constant.

**(ELENA stands center. She is not pacing. She is not trembling. She is still, as if she has finally run out of energy to fight the air itself. She speaks to the room, or to the door, or to the person who holds the key. It does not matter which.)**

You can stop checking the lock now. I know how it works. I know the weight of the deadbolt when you throw it from the outside. I know the click. I know the pause afterward, the little breath you take to make sure I didn't scream, to make sure I didn't beg. You don't need to check anymore. I'm not going to scream. I'm not going to beg.

There was a time when I counted the footsteps. Not the ones in the hall—that's too easy, too loud. I counted the ones on the roof. I thought if I could map the pacing above me, I could predict when the ladder would come down. I thought if I knew the rhythm of the man who owns this house, I could slip out when he blinked. That was months ago. Maybe a year. Time doesn't move in here. It just stacks up. Like dust. Like the laundry I don't wash because there's nowhere to put it dry.

I used to listen for the cars. That's the thing you don't understand about this town, about any town. You think silence is empty. It's not. It's full of things that aren't happening. I used to lie on this floor—because the bed is too soft, too much like a trap—and I would listen for the highway. Three miles away. Maybe four. I could hear the hum. A low, electric throat clearing. That was the world. That was the proof that people were moving, that tires were turning, that someone was going somewhere without asking permission.

I stopped listening for the highway about three weeks ago.

It wasn't a decision. It wasn't a breakdown. It was just… efficiency. Why spend the energy tuning the ear when the signal isn't coming? You taught me that, didn't you? Without saying it. You taught me by locking the cupboard when I asked for more water. You taught me by turning off the lights at six o'clock even when the sun was still up. You taught me that the schedule is the only truth. Wake. Eat. Sit. Sleep. Repeat. The calendar on the wall is a lie because the dates don't change, but the routine is real. The routine is the only thing that holds this room together.

So I stopped listening for the highway. And then I stopped listening for the dogs. There are dogs, aren't there? Outside the perimeter. I hear them sometimes, barking at nothing. I used to think they were barking at me. That they knew. That they smelled the fear on the wind. Now I think they're just barking at each other. Same as us. Noise without meaning.

You want me to perform hope. I know this. I've seen the way you look at me when you think I'm asleep. You want the girl who looks grateful. The girl who says, "Thank you for keeping me safe." You want the narrative where the captivity is protection. Where the walls are there because the outside is dangerous. But I've looked out the slit in the shutter. I've seen the street. I've seen the old man walking his dog. I've seen the woman buying bread. They aren't dangerous. They're just… gone. They're living lives that don't include me. And that is the only danger that matters.

The worst part isn't the lock. It's the realization that no one is trying to pick it.

I used to imagine the rescue. You know the scene. The police lights. The battering ram. The shouting. I used to play it out in my head like a movie. I'd cast the actors. I'd pick the uniform colors. I'd decide who would hold my hand when they pulled me out. I did that for a long time. I kept the script fresh. I rehearsed the gratitude. I rehearsed the tears.

But the script got old. The actors didn't show up.

Now, when I hear a noise, I don't think "help." I think "maintenance." I think someone is fixing the pipe. I think someone is checking the generator. I think someone is making sure the asset is still functional. That's what I am to you. An asset. Something you keep in a box to make sure it doesn't depreciate.

I know you're watching me right now. I can feel the weight of your attention. You want to see if I'm broken yet. You want to see if the light in my eyes has gone out enough that you can stop worrying about me. Let me tell you something, since we're finally being honest. I am not broken. I am just empty. There's a difference. Broken things can be fixed. Empty things just need to be filled, and you've sealed the lid.

I don't hate you. Hate takes energy. Hate requires a future where you suffer, and I don't believe in your future anymore. I don't believe in my future. I believe in the next hour. I believe in the food that's coming at noon. I believe in the lock turning at nine. I believe in the silence that will follow.

You asked me once what I wanted. You said I could have anything within reason. You said that like you were giving me the ocean. "Within reason." What reason? Your reason. The reason that says I stay in this room. The reason that says I don't walk out the door. The reason that says I am safe here.

I want you to know that I am not waiting anymore. I am not sitting by the door. I am not listening for the highway. I am sitting in the chair. I am watching the dust settle. I am watching the light change on the wall, not because the sun is moving, but because the bulb is flickering. I am watching the end of the sentence.

There is no one coming. I know that now. And the terrible thing—the thing that keeps me awake even when I'm exhausted—is that I am relieved.

Because if no one is coming, then I don't have to wait. I don't have to hold my breath for the knock that never comes. I can just… exhale. I can just sit here and let the walls close in until they touch my skin. Until I am part of the house. Until I am as quiet as the lock.

You won. You don't have to check the door anymore. I'm not going anywhere. Not because I can't. But because there's nowhere to go. And even if there was… who would be waiting?

**(ELENA looks directly at the audience, or the control room. Her face is flat. Unmoved.)**

Turn off the light. It's six o'clock. You know the schedule.

Here is a draft written for the rhythm of spoken storytelling. It’s paced for pauses, with the counting doing the heavy lifting. You can adjust the speed to match the crackle of the fire and the night air.

***

The cellar door was already shut when the water found the stairs. He didn’t remember closing it. He only remembered the sound: a slow, wet sigh as the first floodwater slipped over the bottom step, then another, then another, until the dark below was breathing back at him.

He stood on the top step and counted the air.

Not the kind you pull into your lungs. The kind that sits in a room. The kind that gets pushed up, inch by inch, as the water climbs. He knew the cellar by heart. He knew the shelf. He knew the matches. He knew that if the water touched the shelf, the matches would be gone. Not wet. Gone. The difference mattered to him. It was the only thing that mattered.

So he counted.

One breath. The water was at the third step.
Two breaths. The water was at the fourth.
Three breaths. The water was at the fifth.

He didn’t call out. There was no one to call to. The house sat heavy on the hill. The yard was quiet. The summer had been dry for weeks, then the sky broke open in a way that didn’t sound like rain anymore. It sounded like a door left open. He had gone down to check the fuse box. He had gone down to turn off the pump. He had gone down because that’s what you do when water appears where it shouldn’t. He hadn’t planned on staying.

Four breaths. The water was at the sixth step.
Five breaths. The water was at the seventh.

The air grew thick. Not hot. Not cold. Just heavy, like cloth pressed over the face. He kept his hands at his sides. He didn’t pace. He didn’t bang on the door. He just watched the water rise and counted the space above it.

Six breaths. The water was at the eighth step.
Seven breaths. The water was at the ninth.

He knew how many steps there were. He knew how high the shelf sat. He knew the math of it. The math didn’t care about him. The math didn’t care about rescue. The math didn’t care about lessons. It only cared about height, and time, and the way water finds the lowest point and keeps going.

Eight breaths. The water was at the tenth step.
Nine breaths. The water was at the eleventh.

He thought about the matches. Not the strike. Not the flame. Just the little cardboard tubes, the red tips, the way they sat side by side on the wooden shelf. He thought about how they would be useless the moment the water touched them. Not spoiled. Not ruined. Just gone. As if they had never been there. As if the shelf had always been empty.

Ten breaths. The water was at the twelfth step.
Eleven breaths. The water was at the thirteenth.

He didn’t pray. He didn’t bargain. He didn’t picture anyone coming. He didn’t picture anyone at all. He just kept counting. The water moved slower than he expected. Or maybe he moved slower. It was hard to tell. Time had stopped being a line and had become a room. He was inside it. The walls were wet. The stairs were gone. The only thing left was the shelf, and the matches, and the air between them.

Twelve breaths. The water was at the fourteenth step.
Thirteen breaths. The water was at the fifteenth.

He listened to the water. It didn’t rush. It didn’t panic. It just arrived. It filled the corners. It climbed the walls. It took the dark with it. He didn’t fight it. He didn’t hold his breath. He let it come. He let it take the space. He counted what was left.

Fourteen breaths. The water was at the sixteenth step.
Fifteen breaths. The water was at the seventeenth.

The shelf was close now. He could see it in the dark. He could see the matches. He could see how little stood between them and the water. He didn’t reach for them. He didn’t lean forward. He just stood on the step that was still dry, and counted, and watched.

Sixteen breaths. The water was at the eighteenth step.
Seventeen breaths. The water was at the nineteenth.

The air was thin now. Not gone. Not yet. Just thin. He could feel it in his chest. He could feel it in his throat. He could feel it in the space above the water. He counted it like a man counts steps on a staircase he knows by heart. He counted it like a man counts the last of anything.

Eighteen breaths. The water was at the twentieth step.
Nineteen breaths. The water was at the twenty-first.

The shelf was right there. The matches were right there. The water was right there. He didn’t move. He didn’t speak. He just counted.

Twenty breaths. The water touched the shelf.
Twenty-one breaths. The matches were gone.
Twenty-two breaths. The air was gone.

He didn’t close his eyes. He didn’t open them. He just stood in the dark, in the water, in the counting, until there was nothing left to count.

***

A few notes for reading it aloud:

- Let the pauses do the work. The story doesn’t need dramatic inflection; it needs steady, unhurried delivery. The counting should feel like a metronome, not a countdown to a reveal.
- Keep your voice level. The power here is in the refusal to soften the edges. No trembling, no swelling music in the tone. Just the facts of the room, the water, the shelf, the matches.
- If the fire pops or someone shifts, don’t rush. The silence around the words is part of the story. Let it sit.
- You can adjust the step count or the pacing to match your own rhythm, but keep the structure intact: the counting is the only motion, and it doesn’t resolve into meaning. That’s the point.

**Title:** The Inventory
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A bedroom. The door is visible, but the focus is on her.

**(ELARA stands in the center of the room. She is not crying. She is not shaking. She is holding a pen and a piece of paper, but she isn't writing. She is looking at the door, then at the paper, then at the door again. She speaks to the room, or perhaps to the person who holds the keys, but mostly to herself.)**

**ELARA**
You used to check the lock twice. I know you did. I'd lie here, pretending to sleep, listening to the jingle of the chain, the turn of the deadbolt, the second turn just to make sure the first one held. You wanted to be sure. You wanted me to be sure.

**(She looks down at the paper.)**

I made a list. Yesterday. I thought if I had the list, I could manage the hours. If I could name the hours, they wouldn't bleed into each other like they do now. Like watercolors left out in the rain. 

**(She taps the paper with the pen.)**

Seven. Breakfast. Oatmeal. No sugar. You stand over the table. You watch the spoon go in. You watch the swallow. You say, "Eat." I say, "I'm not hungry." You say, "You need strength." You don't say what for. You never say what for.

Eight. School. Books open. Pages turned. You check the answers. You check the posture. You check the eyes. You say, "Look at me when I'm speaking to you." I do. I always do. But you're not speaking to me. You're speaking to the version of me that fits inside the schedule. The version that doesn't look at the window too long. The version that doesn't count the cars passing on the street.

Nine. Chores. Dusting. Sweeping. You watch the dust motes. You say, "It's not clean enough." I say, "I just did it." You say, "Do it again." I do it again. I do it until my arms ache. I do it until the dust is gone and the wood is bare and there's nothing left to clean but the air itself.

**(She stops tapping the paper. She lets the pen hang from her fingers.)**

I used to wait. That's the thing you don't understand. I didn't just live the schedule. I lived the gaps. The five minutes between the chores and the study. The ten minutes before dinner. I lived in the hope that those minutes would stretch. That a car would pull up. That a voice would call my name from the driveway. That someone—anyone—who wasn't you would walk through that door and say, "It's time."

**(She looks at the door. Her expression is flat. Empty.)**

I don't do that anymore.

I stopped counting the cars last Tuesday. Or maybe it was Monday. The days look the same now. The light hits the floor at the same angle. The clock ticks at the same speed. Nothing changes. Nothing comes.

You think I'm planning something. I see you looking at me when you think I'm not watching. You think I'm saving up energy. You think I'm building a weapon out of silence. You think if I stay quiet enough, still enough, something will break. Either out there, or in here.

**(She walks to the window, looks out, then turns back.)**

There's no break. There's no one coming. The phone doesn't ring. The mail doesn't come. The world outside that window is a picture. It's a painting of a life I'm not in. You told me once that I was lucky. That I was safe. That people out there are hungry, and dangerous, and lost. You said I have a roof. I have food. I have a future.

**(She laughs. It's a dry, short sound. Not angry. Just final.)**

You're right. I do. I have all of that. I have everything you decided I should have. And I'm done waiting for it to be enough.

I'm not going to run. I'm not going to scream. I'm not going to try the window again. I know how the locks work now. I know how the alarms sound. I know how you breathe when you think I'm asleep. I know everything about this house except how to leave it.

**(She drops the pen on the table. It makes a small click.)**

So here's what happens now. You give me the schedule. I follow it. You give me the rules. I keep them. You give me the silence. I fill it. But you don't get to hope for me anymore. You don't get to stand in the hallway and listen for footsteps that aren't coming. You don't get to tell me that rescue is around the corner. Because I've looked around the corner. There's nothing there.

**(She sits down. She folds the paper. She puts it in her pocket.)**

I'm not your project. I'm not your investment. I'm not the thing you're saving for later. I'm here. Now. In this room. With the oatmeal and the dust and the lock that turns twice.

And I'm not waiting.

**(She looks at the door one last time. She doesn't blink.)**

No one's coming. And I'm finally ready to believe it.

**Title:** The Inventory of Silence
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A room with no windows. The light is artificial, constant.

**(ELARA stands center. She is not pacing. She is not trembling. She is perfectly still, looking at a point just above the audience's head, as if reading a schedule pinned to the wall.)**

**ELARA**
Seven o'clock. The lock turns. Not a key, not anymore. It's a code. He types it in. I hear the buttons click. Click, click, hold. Then the green light. That's the sound of my morning. That's the sound of my breath being allowed.

People think captivity is the bars. It's not. It's the schedule. It's knowing that at seven-fifteen, the tray slides through the slot. Cold eggs. Toast that's gone soft because the air is too humid. At seven-thirty, the chair is pulled out. At eight, the lesson begins. History. Or math. It doesn't matter. It's all just data to fill the space where I used to have thoughts of my own.

**(She looks down at her hands. She turns them over, examining the palms.)**

**(A slight, dry laugh. No humor in it.)**

And I looked at the door, and I realized I wasn't listening for the lock. I was listening for the hum of the refrigerator.

That was it. That was the death.
