I close my eyes. The shaking gets worse. I open them. The mirror is still there. The hum is still there. I count my breaths. One. Two. Three. Four. I lose the count. I start again. One. Two. Three. I need water. I need something to stop the noise in my head. The noise that says just one. Just to stop the shaking. Just to make the stone stop grinding.

I reach for the tap. Turn it on. Let it run. Watch the water go down the drain. Clear. Dirty. Gone.

My leg jumps. I hate this. I hate my leg. I hate this room. I hate that I'm still here. I hate that I'm breathing.

The door handle clicks. Someone's coming. Or maybe it's just the building settling. Maybe it's nothing. I don't move. I can't move. If someone comes in, I'll tell them I'm sick. I'll tell them I'm fine. I'll tell them anything. I just need them to turn the light off. I need the dark. I need to not see the shake.

It's been an hour. It's been a minute. It doesn't matter. The stone is still grinding. The gravity is still pulling. I'm still standing here. I'm still waiting for the wave to break. It doesn't break. It just keeps coming.

I turn off the tap. The silence is louder than the hum. I listen to my own blood. It's too loud. Everything is too loud. I pick up the glass. I drink. It's cold. It doesn't help. I put the glass down. I wait. I wait for the next minute. I wait for the next shake. I wait for the door to open. I wait for nothing.

**Title:** The Lock
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A room. Not a stage. A room.

**(ELARA stands center. She is not looking at the audience. She is looking at her hands. She has been speaking to the wall for a long time. When she speaks, it is not to us. It is to the silence.)**

The key doesn't turn anymore. I know that now. I used to listen for the scrape. I used to hold my breath until my lungs burned, waiting for the metallic cough of the tumbler giving way. I thought if I stayed quiet enough, if I stayed still enough, the sound would be a surprise. A mistake. A rescue.

But the key doesn't turn. It hasn't turned in forty-two days. I stopped counting the hours when I realized the clock on the wall was lying. It ticks, but it doesn't move. He wound it that way. He wanted me to know when the minute changed without knowing when the day ended. He wanted me to live in the slice.

I used to scream. I used to put my throat against the wood and push until I tasted blood. I thought pain was a signal. I thought if I made enough noise, someone outside would have to look. Someone outside would have to care. But there is no one outside. There is only the house. And the house is full.

He comes in at eight. He brings the bread. He brings the water. He doesn't look at me. He looks at the lock. He checks the bolt. He checks the window bars. He checks me. Not my eyes. My pulse. He knows when I'm afraid because I stop breathing. He knows when I'm angry because I start breathing too fast. He controls the air in here. He controls the temperature. He controls the light that comes through the slit in the curtain. He decides when it is morning. He decides when it is night.

I thought if I was good, he would leave the door open. I thought if I was quiet, he would forget I was here. I thought if I was invisible, the world would forget me too, and then the world would come looking for its missing piece.

That was the mistake. Believing the world knew I was missing.

The world doesn't know. The world doesn't care. The world is full of people who lock their doors at night and check them twice and sleep soundly because they believe the lock is for keeping things out. They don't understand the lock is for keeping things in. They don't understand that I am not the prisoner. I am the content. I am the thing being kept safe for later.

I stopped waiting three days ago. I don't know why I picked a number. Three days. It sounded like a deadline. Like a trial. Like a sentence.

I sat in the chair. I looked at the door. I waited for the hope to rise. You know the feeling. That little lift in the chest. That little whisper that says, *maybe today.* It didn't come. I had to push it down. I had to crush it. I had to take that little piece of light and smash it against the floor until it was just another shadow.

Now I know. The key is not lost. The key is not broken. The key is in his pocket. And he is not coming back. Not to open it. He is coming back to feed me. To water me. To make sure the thing in the box is still alive when he needs it again.

I am not waiting for rescue. Rescue is a story they tell you so you don't scream. Rescue is a lie you tell yourself so you don't kill yourself. There is no one coming. There is no cavalry. There is no hidden camera. There is no neighbor who heard me. There is only the house. And the house is soundproof.

He thinks I am broken. He thinks I am quiet because I am defeated. He doesn't know I am quiet because I am done. I am done with the screaming. I am done with the begging. I am done with the hope.

Hope is the heaviest thing in this room. It weighs more than the furniture. It weighs more than me. I put it down. I left it on the floor. I walked over it. I closed the door on it.

Now I sit. Now I wait. But I don't wait for the key. I wait for the end. I wait for the hunger. I wait for the dark. I wait for the moment when the body stops needing the world. I am not trying to get out. I am trying to get used to being in.

He wants a pet. He wants something that knows its place. He wants something that knows the door is locked and stays on the side of the lock he chose.

I am not a pet. I am not a person. I am a fact. The fact is the door is locked. The fact is I am here. The fact is no one is coming.

So let him check the bolt. Let him check the window. Let him check my pulse. He will find what he wants to find. He will find a girl who knows the truth. He will find a girl who knows that the lock is not to keep me in. The lock is to keep the world out. To keep the world from seeing what he did. To keep the world from seeing what I became.

I am not coming for me. I am not coming for anyone. I am staying here. I am staying here until the walls breathe. I am staying here until the air runs out. I am staying here because there is nowhere else to go.

The key doesn't turn. I know that now. And I know something else. I know that I don't want it to.

**(ELARA looks at the door. She does not move. She does not blink. The light fades, but she does not move. She is part of the room now.)**

**(ELARA stands near the window. She is not crying. She is not shaking. She is perfectly still, as if she has finally matched the stillness of the room. She speaks to the door, or perhaps to the wall behind it. Her voice is low, clear, and devoid of tremor.)**

You can stop checking the lock now. I know how it works. You turn the key twice, you test the handle, you listen for the click. You do it because you're afraid I'll forget how to be afraid. You think if I hear the click one more time, I'll remember that there's a world outside this wood and plaster. There isn't.

I used to count the days. Not by the calendar—you took that away on the third week, said it was clutter, said I needed to focus on the inside, not the outside. I counted by the light. I know what you think. You think I'm waiting. You think there's a part of me, buried deep under all this quiet, that's still screaming for someone to hear. Someone who knows the difference between a closed door and a locked one.

But you don't know what happens when the silence gets old. It stops being silence. It becomes a thing. It has weight. It has texture. It presses against your ears until you can't hear your own thoughts, only the hum of the house. The pipes. The fridge. The way the wood settles when the temperature drops.

I stopped believing anyone is coming three days ago. Or maybe it was yesterday. Time doesn't move the same way in here. It pools. It stagnates.

You want me to perform. I see it in your eyes when you walk in. You want the tears. You want the trembling lip. You want the girl who begs. Because if I beg, then you're the savior. If I break, then you're the one who holds the pieces. But I'm not breaking. I'm settling. Like dust. Like sediment.

You control the hours. You tell me when to eat, when to sleep, when to speak. You think that makes you the master of this house. But you're not. You're just the keeper of the cage. And I'm the thing inside it that's learning how to breathe without air.

I looked at the window today. Really looked at it. The latch is rusted. The glass is thick. If I threw a chair, would it break? Probably. Would anyone hear it? No. The walls are too thick. The town is too quiet. Everyone here knows how to keep their own doors locked. They don't want to hear mine open.

I'm going to sit here. I'm going to watch the light move across the floor. I'm going to learn the shape of this room until I can close my eyes and walk it without touching the walls. I'm going to become part of the house. And when you come in to check on me, when you look for the girl who wants to leave, you won't find her. You'll just find the room. You'll just find the quiet.

And you'll realize that the lock wasn't to keep me in. It was to keep you from seeing what happens when you leave someone alone long enough. I'm not waiting for rescue. I'm waiting for the dust to settle. And it has.

**(She turns away from the window. She sits on the edge of the bed. She does not look at the door. She looks at her hands.)**

You can go now. I'm not going anywhere. Not because I can't. Because I don't want to. There's nothing out there that knows how to live in the dark like I do now.

**(She folds her hands in her lap. She waits. She does not blink.)**

**[END]**

The light’s too bright. I can feel it behind my eyes. Three a.m. or three-thirty. Doesn’t matter. The clock’s just a red smear I keep turning my head away from. I’m sitting on the edge of the bath, knees pressed together, hands flat on my thighs. My hands are shaking. Not a little. Enough that I can see it in the mirror if I look. I don’t look. Cold. That’s the first thing. Then the ache. Starts in the back of my legs, crawls up into my hips, settles in my spine like it’s trying to work its way out through my ribs. I shift. I haven’t brushed since yesterday. Or the day before. Time’s just a flat line now. I know that. I’ve known it for hours.

I should get up. I should walk to the sink, run the water, splash my face, do something that looks like being a person. But my legs are heavy. Not tired. Heavy. Like they’re filled with wet sand. I know where it is. I know what it wants. I’ve mapped it. I’ve walked the route a hundred times. Down the hall. Out the door. Into the car. To the place. To the bag. To the needle. To the quiet.

I don’t want it. I swear I don’t. But my body doesn’t care what I want. It’s screaming for the switch. For the drop. I’ve carried it in my head for years. I know how it fits. I know how it clicks. I know how quiet it gets after. I don’t want quiet. I want the noise to stop. But the noise is me. I could stand up. I could walk out. I could lock the door behind me and go. I know the way. I’ve walked it in my sleep. I’ve walked it with my eyes open and my hands steady and my head clear and I’ve walked it when I was already gone. I know which floorboard creaks. I know which key turns. I know whose hand I’ll have to shake. I know what I’ll say. I know what I won’t say. I know what I’ll do after. I know what I’ll do after that. I know the whole chain. I’ve lived it. I’ve broken it. I’ve put it back together wrong.

My knee jerks. I grip my thighs. I breathe in. It rattles. I breathe out. It doesn’t help. The mirror’s still there. I still don’t look. The light’s still too bright. The room’s still too small. The pull’s still right there, sitting in my chest, waiting. I don’t move. I don’t get up. I don’t reach for the phone. I don’t turn the light off. I just sit here. I keep my hands on my knees. I keep my eyes on the grout. I keep counting. I keep waiting. I keep knowing exactly what I’m going to do and not doing it yet. Not yet. Not yet. Not yet.

**Title:** The Lock

I keep waiting for my hands to uncurl. They don’t. They’re getting tighter. I can feel the nails digging in. I don’t pull back. I let them. I let everything. I just stand here. I just stand here. I just stand here.

The light above the mirror is humming. I can hear it. It's been humming since I walked in. I don't know why I can hear it now. Everything else is too loud. My bones are too loud. The faucet is dripping. I turned it off. I know I turned it off. It's still dripping. One drop every four seconds. I counted.

My hands are shaking so bad I can't get the cap off the water bottle. I don't need the water. I just need to hold something. Something cold. The porcelain is cold. I'm leaning over the sink. If I breathe too deep it hurts behind my eyes. If I don't breathe deep enough I feel like I'm drowning. So I breathe shallow. Like I'm hiding.

It's three. I know it's three. The phone is on the tank. Black screen. Face down. I haven't touched it. If I touch it I'll call. If I call I'll have to say who I am. I don't know who I am right now. I'm just this body in this room. Sweating through the shirt. Shivering even though the heat is on. I can feel the heat coming off my skin. I can smell it. Metallic. Sour.

The itch is inside my arms. Under the skin. I want to scratch until it bleeds just to see if I can make it stop. It won't stop. Nothing stops. The noise in my head is a static channel. All the voices I've ignored for six months are back. They're saying I promised. They're saying I lied. They're saying I'm tired. I am tired. Bone tired. Soul tired. But the tired doesn't make me sleep. It just makes me watch the clock.

I keep thinking about the bag. Not the bag. The thing in the bag. The little plastic wrap. The weight of it. The way it feels when you hold it. Not the high. I don't even want the high. I just want the quiet. I want the static to turn off. I want my hands to stop shaking so I can drink the water. I want to stop feeling like my skin is too tight for my body.

I looked in the mirror. I don't look like me. I look like someone who used to be me. The eyes are wrong. They're hollow. They're waiting. Waiting for what? For the sun to come up? For the phone to ring? For the feeling to pass? It won't pass. It just changes shape. Right now it's this. Right now it's the drip. Drip. Drip. Drip.

I should sit down. My knees are weak. If I sit I might not get up. If I get up I might walk out. If I walk out I might go there. I know the way. I know the street. I know the corner. I know the time. Three in the morning is a good time. No one is looking. No one cares.

My nose is running. I need a tissue. There's no tissue. I wipe it on my sleeve. I hate that. I hate everything. I hate the light. I hate the sound. I hate the cold water on my wrists. I put my wrists under the tap. It helps for a second. Then it doesn't. Then I'm just wet and shaking again.

I'm not going to call. I'm not going to sit down. I'm going to stand here and listen to the light hum. I'm going to wait for four. Then five. Then whatever comes next. I don't have a plan. I don't have a reason. I just have this room and this body and the knowledge that I did this. I chose this. I chose to be here. I chose to stop. And now I'm stopping. And it feels like dying. It feels like I'm being unwound.

The drip is faster. Or maybe I'm slower. I don't know. I just know I'm still here. I'm still in the room. I'm still breathing. Shallow. Hiding. Waiting for the next minute to come. It's coming. It's always coming.

Three a.m. The fluorescent tube above the mirror is buzzing like it’s got a grudge. I can hear it through the hum in my teeth. I’m sitting on the edge of the tub. Tile’s cold through my jeans. I keep shifting my weight because if I don’t move, the ache in my knees starts talking louder. It’s been talking for two days. Two days of my skin feeling too tight, of my stomach doing that slow, wet roll, of my hands shaking so bad I dropped a spoon in the kitchen and didn’t pick it up. I just stared at it on the linoleum until the shaking passed. Or until I told myself it passed.

I came in here to splash water on my face. That’s what I told myself. Just water. Cool. Wake up. But the mirror’s fogged at the corners and I can’t see my own eyes clear. I keep wiping a patch with my sleeve. Nothing. Just a face that looks borrowed. Pupils blown. Lips chapped. Jaw locked. I know what I look like. I’ve looked like this before. I know the schedule of it. The first day you’re angry at the room. The second day you’re angry at your own bones. The third day you stop being angry and just start bargaining with the air.

My phone’s on the sink. Screen cracked. I’ve checked it six times. No messages. No missed calls. Just the time. 3:14. 3:17. 3:22. I don’t care about the minutes. I care about the distance. How far the dealer’s place is. How long it takes to walk there when your legs feel like wet rope. I know the route. I’ve walked it in my head a hundred times while lying on this exact towel, staring at the grout lines. Left out the door. Down the stairs. Past the bodega that smells like old coffee and bleach. Turn right at the corner store. Two blocks. Maybe three if I’m walking slow. Maybe I’ll walk fast. Maybe I’ll run and then my chest will seize and I’ll have to stop on the sidewalk and pretend I’m tying my shoe.

I’m not supposed to be like this. I told myself I was done. I said it out loud in front of people. I said it while holding a coffee cup. I said it while signing a lease. I said it like it was a fact, like gravity. But facts don’t hold when your blood turns to static. Facts don’t stop your hands from digging into your own thighs hard enough to leave half-moons. Facts don’t fill the hollow behind your sternum when you swallow and it just echoes.

I keep thinking about the last time. Not the high. The minute after. The way the room went flat. The way my hands went cold. The way I sat on the floor of this same bathroom and promised myself I’d never do it again. I remember the promise. I remember how sincere it felt. I also remember what came after. The waiting. The counting. The way every hour stretched out like a rubber band pulled too thin. I’m in that stretch now. I can feel it snapping.

My nose is running. I keep wiping it on my wrist. I should go to the sink. I should turn the water on. I should wash my face. But if I turn the water on, I’ll hear it. The pipes. The drip. The sound of something flowing. And if I hear it, I’ll start thinking about needles. Not because I want to. Because my brain is a dog that’s been trained to sit in one spot and wait for a whistle that doesn’t come. It paces. It whines. It stares at the door.

I’m sweating through my shirt. The collar’s stuck to my neck. I can feel it. I can feel everything. The cold tile under my heels. The rough seam of the tub against my back. The way my heartbeat kicks up when I breathe too deep. I’m trying to breathe shallow. I’m trying to make myself small. If I make myself small enough, maybe the pull won’t find me. Maybe it’ll slide past. Maybe I can just sit here until the sun comes up and the streetlights click off and the world forgets I’m in this room.

But the sun doesn’t care. The streetlights don’t care. And the pull doesn’t care if I’m tired. It’s right here. It’s in the way my fingers keep twitching toward my pocket. It’s in the way I keep looking at the door handle like it’s a question I’m allowed to answer. I don’t want to open it. I don’t want to walk. I don’t want to feel this. I don’t want to feel anything. But I do. I feel it all. The shake. The sweat. The hollow. The static. The way my mouth tastes like copper and old pills and regret I can’t swallow down.

I keep telling myself to stand up. Just stand up. Walk out. Go to bed. Sleep it off. Wake up clean. But clean isn’t a place you can walk to when your nervous system is firing like a short circuit. Clean isn’t a switch. It’s a door that keeps moving farther away every time I blink. And I’m blinking so hard my eyes burn.

I’m still sitting. The buzzing light hasn’t stopped. My hands haven’t stopped. The clock keeps moving. I keep looking at the door. I keep looking at the sink. I keep looking at the mirror that won’t clear. I don’t know what I’m waiting for. I don’t know what I’m supposed to do. I just know I’m here. I just know it’s three in the morning. I just know the pull is in the room with me. And I just know I haven’t moved.

The fluorescent light is buzzing. It’s been buzzing since I walked in. I can hear it in my teeth. Three in the morning. I know because I looked at the phone when I came in and then I dropped it in the sink and now it’s face down on the tile and I’m not picking it up. I’m sitting on the edge of the tub. The porcelain is cold through my jeans. I should be on the floor. I should be curled up. But my legs won’t stay bent right. They keep locking. They keep shaking.

I can feel it in my stomach first. Like something’s twisting itself loose. Then the sweat. Cold at the back of my neck, hot across my forehead. I keep wiping it with the back of my hand and it just comes back. My hands won’t stop moving. I’m picking at the cuticle on my thumb. There’s no skin left there. I don’t care. I just need my fingers to do something that isn’t this.

I haven’t slept. I don’t know how long it’s been. The clock on the wall says 3:14. It might be 3:14. It might be 4. Time doesn’t move right when you’re like this. It stretches. It snaps. I keep counting the tiles on the floor. Fourteen. Fifteen. Sixteen. I lose track. I start over. I don’t care.

I know where it is. I know exactly where it is. That’s the worst part. It’s not gone. It’s not lost. It’s in the drawer. Under the loose liner. Wrapped in a sock. I put it there myself. I remember doing it. I remember the weight of it in my hand. I remember how quiet it felt. I remember telling myself I’d only use half. I remember lying.

My chest is tight. I can’t get a full breath. I keep trying. In. Out. In. Out. It catches. It always catches. I should drink water. There’s a bottle on the counter. Half full. I haven’t touched it. I know what happens if I do. I’ll throw up. I’ll throw up and then I’ll still be here. I’ll still be sitting on this tub edge with my hands shaking and my skin crawling and my brain doing the same thing over and over. Find it. Find it. Find it.

I’m not going to do it. I say that. I say it out loud. I hear myself. It doesn’t change anything. I’m not going to do it. Then I’m going to do it. Then I’m not. Then I am. I don’t know what I’m saying anymore. I’m just making noise. My voice sounds thin. It sounds like it’s coming from somewhere else.

I can feel my heart. It’s too fast. It’s too loud. I can hear it in my ears. I press my palms against my eyes. The dark behind my lids is moving. It’s always moving. I keep thinking about the first hit. Not the first time. The first time I knew it would take everything. I knew it. I still did it. I still do it. I don’t know why I keep pretending I’ll stop. I know how this ends. I’ve seen it. I’ve lived it. I’m living it.

My legs are trembling so hard now I can feel it in my knees. I should stand up. I should walk out. I should go to the ER. I should call someone. I don’t have anyone. I don’t have anyone who answers. I don’t have anyone who stays. I know that too. I know it and I still sit here.

I keep looking at the door. It’s closed. It’s always closed. I could open it. I could step into the hallway. I could walk down the stairs. I could keep walking. I don’t. I don’t move. I just sit here and shake and sweat and count the tiles and listen to the light buzz and wait for my hands to stop shaking so I can pick up the phone and look at the time and pretend I’m not still here.

I’m still here. I’m still here. I’m still here.

Three a.m. The fluorescent tube above the mirror is dying. It flickers once, twice, then settles into that sick yellow hum. I can hear it. I can hear everything. The pipes knocking in the wall. The fridge in the kitchen clicking on. My own teeth grinding. I should turn the light off. I don’t. I need to see it. I need to see what’s happening to me.

Cold. That’s the first thing. Not the room. Me. My hands are ice even though the radiator’s been running since midnight. I put them under the tap. Too hot. I pull back. I try again. Lukewarm. It doesn’t matter. The cold’s inside now. In the marrow. In the stomach. I’m shaking. Not a tremor. A full-body rattle. My knees won’t lock. I’m leaning against the sink because the floor feels like it’s tilting.

I haven’t slept. Not real sleep. I closed my eyes for an hour and woke up choking. Sweat soaked through the shirt. Sheets stuck to my back. I dragged myself out here because the bedroom felt like a coffin. This tile is colder but it’s honest. At least the mirror doesn’t lie. At least the glass shows me what I am right now.

I need it. I need it so bad it’s sitting in my throat like a stone. Not a thought. A physical thing. My fingers keep moving to the pocket of my jeans. I don’t even have it on me. I checked. Empty. I know it’s empty. I emptied it myself an hour ago when I told myself I was done. Told myself I’d flush it. I didn’t. I just put it back in the drawer. I know where the drawer is. I know the exact sound it makes when it catches. I know the weight of the little orange bottle. I know how the foil crinkles. I know the exact second the needle goes in. I know it like I know my own name.

My nose is running. I keep wiping it on my sleeve. I’m shivering so hard my teeth click. I’m sweating and freezing at the same time. That’s how it works. That’s the deal. You give it everything and it takes everything back. I’m counting the seconds between breaths. In. Out. In. Out. Too fast. Too shallow. I’m hyperventilating and I can’t stop. I press my palms flat against the counter. Porcelain. Cold. Real. I focus on that. Just the counter. Just the edge. Just the line where the sink meets the wall. Don’t think about the drawer. Don’t think about the hallway. Don’t think about the stairs. Don’t think about the bag in the closet. Don’t think about the key in my pocket. I don’t even need the key. I left it on the table. I know it’s there. I know I could walk out. I know I could walk back in. I know the whole route. I’ve walked it a hundred times. I know where the light switch is. I know which step squeaks. I know the exact weight of the door handle.

I’m sick. I’m so sick. My stomach’s twisting. I dry-heave and nothing comes up. Just acid. Just bile. I keep swallowing it back down. I shouldn’t have eaten. I shouldn’t have drunk water. I should just lie down. I can’t lie down. If I lie down I’ll sleep. If I sleep I’ll wake up worse. If I wake up worse I’ll do it. So I stay up. I stay right here. I stare at my own eyes in the glass. They’re bloodshot. They’re hollow. They’re mine. I don’t recognize them. I do. I recognize them perfectly.

I’m counting. I don’t know what I’m counting. Minutes. Hours. Doses. I lost track. I always lose track. Time doesn’t move right when you’re like this. It stretches. It snaps. It loops. I keep thinking about the last time. The last time I said I wouldn’t. The last time I flushed it. The last time I cried in a bathroom just like this. I don’t cry anymore. I just shake. I just breathe. I just wait.

The light flickers again. I don’t look away. I watch it. I watch myself. I watch the reflection breathe. I watch the hands that won’t stop moving. I watch the jaw that won’t stop clenching. I watch the eyes that won’t stop looking for a way out. There isn’t one. Not in here. Not at three in the morning. Not when the cold is in the bones and the need is in the throat and the body is screaming for something it already knows how to break.

I’m still here. I’m still shaking. I’m still counting. I’m still waiting. I’m still looking at the drawer. I’m still looking at the door. I’m still looking at the mirror. I’m still here.

The light above the mirror is humming. I can hear it. It's been humming since I walked in. Maybe longer. Doesn't matter. Nothing matters except the shaking. Look at the hands. Look at them. They won't stop. Just resting them on the sink makes the porcelain vibrate. I'm vibrating. The whole room is vibrating. Is that the light or is it me? Doesn't matter. Turn the tap off. No, leave it. The sound is good. The sound is white. White noise. Like the static when the TV loses signal. Remember that? Before everything went dark.

Three o'clock. Maybe three-thirty. Who checks the time? I checked the time. Why did I check the time? Because there's a schedule. There's always a schedule. Morning is coming. Sun comes up. People wake up. They make coffee. They go to work. They don't sit in tiled boxes breathing into paper cups. I shouldn't be here. I know I shouldn't be here. But the legs walked. Feet hit the floor. Down the hall. Into the bathroom. Lock the door. Click. Safe. Safe for now.

Cold. Why is it so cold? The radiator is hissing. It's supposed to be hot. It's not hot. It's hissing. Like a snake. Like a warning. Don't do it. Don't do it. Who is talking? Me. I'm talking. I'm talking to the mirror. Look at the eyes. Where did the eyes go? Sunken. Dark holes. Like I've been digging. Like I've been buried. I look like my dad. No. Don't go there. Don't go there. That's a different hole. That's a different grave.

The sweat. It's freezing and I'm sweating. Shirt is stuck to the back. Peeling it off hurts. Everything hurts. The skin is too tight. The bones are too loud. Ache in the knees. Ache in the lower back. Deep in the marrow. It's not pain, it's absence. A hole where the chemical should be. A vacuum. Sucking the air out. Sucking the heat out. Need to fill it. Need to plug the hole. Just once. Just to stop the shaking. Just to stop the noise.

The drawer. The top drawer. Left side. Under the towels. Don't look. Don't look. I know where it is. My hand knows. The hand is shaking but the muscle memory is perfect. Open the drawer. Just a peek. Just to look. If it's there, it's there. If it's not, it's not. But it's there. It's always there. Until it's not. Then I'll know. Then I'll panic. But not yet. Not yet.

Count the tiles. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. Start again. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. Why ten? Why not twelve? Doesn't matter. Keep counting. If I stop counting, the thought comes back. The thought is heavy. The thought is a weight on the chest. Can't breathe. Shallow breaths. In through the nose. Out through the mouth. Like the videos. Like the instructions. Follow the instructions. Be a good patient. Be a good addict. Be a good nothing.

The phone. Face down on the counter. Screen is black. No notifications. Who would call? No one calls at three. No one cares at three. If someone called, I'd have to speak. Voice would crack. Voice would sound like gravel. Like I've been swallowing glass. Don't pick it up. Don't check the time again. Time is a circle. Three o'clock forever. Three o'clock forever.

The pull. It's physical. It's in the gut. A hook. Fishing line. Tugging. Reeling me in. Towards the bag. Towards the spoon. Towards the flame. I can smell it. I can smell the heat. I can smell the burn. It's phantom. It's not there. But it's there. It's louder than the light. It's louder than the hiss. It's the only thing that makes sense. The only thing that fixes the vibration. Stops the hands. Stops the eyes.

I'm tired. So tired. Sleep would be nice. Sleep without dreams. Sleep without waking up sweating. But sleep comes after. Sleep comes after the fix. Sleep comes after the nod. Not before. Never before. Before is the sickness. Before is the wait. Before is this room.

Look at the reflection again. Who is that? Stranger. Ghost. Haunting the bathroom. Haunting the house. Haunting the street. I should wash my face. Cold water. Shock the system. Wake up. But the water is too cold. The pipes are too cold. Everything is too cold. Just need warmth. Just need heat. Just need to feel normal. Just need to feel nothing.

The drawer handle. Metal. Cold. My hand is hovering. Inches away. I can feel the heat from the metal. I can feel the promise. One hit. Just one. To get through the morning. To get through the light. To get through the door. To get through the day. Then I'll stop. Then I'll fix it. Then I'll be good. Then I'll be human.

Don't touch it. Don't touch it. Don't touch it.

The light is still humming. The radiator is still hissing. The hands are still shaking. The sun is coming. The sun is coming up. The sun doesn't care. The sun comes up anyway. I'm still here. I'm still in the tiles. I'm still breathing. I'm still waiting. I'm still hungry.

Open the drawer.

**Title:** *The Schedule*
**Character:** ELARA (17)
**Setting:** A living room. Sterile. A clock is visible but its ticking is inaudible.

**(ELARA stands center. She is not looking at the audience. She is looking at a spot on the floor, perhaps a stain, perhaps a crack. She speaks without urgency. The urgency is gone. That is the point.)**

You can stop checking the locks now. I know the combination. I know the weight of the deadbolt when it slides home. I know the sound the chain makes when it catches on the wood. I used to listen for the car in the driveway. I used to count the seconds between the engine cutting and the door opening. I had a chart for it. I had a notebook.

I don't have the notebook anymore.

There was a time when I thought the silence was a signal. You know how that works. You're fourteen, or fifteen, and you think the quiet means someone is sneaking up. You think the quiet means rescue. You hold your breath until your lungs burn because you're afraid that if you exhale, you'll give away your position. You think there are people outside who know you're here. You think there's a file with your name on it that hasn't been closed yet.

But files get archived. People get reassigned. The world doesn't stop turning just because you're stuck in a room with a view of the driveway.

I know what time it is. I know what time it is because I'm allowed to know. That's the thing nobody tells you when you're waiting for the cavalry. The captivity isn't the bars on the window. The captivity is the schedule. Seven o'clock, breakfast. Seven-fifteen, vitamins. Eight o'clock, schoolwork at the table. Eight-thirty, hygiene. Nine, quiet time. They didn't need to chain me to the bed. They just needed to make sure I knew exactly where I was supposed to be every minute of the day. If you know where you're supposed to be, you don't look for the door. You look at the clock.

And I looked at the clock. For a long time.

I thought if I waited long enough, the schedule would break. I thought if I was quiet enough, or loud enough, or perfect enough, the routine would snap under the weight of something real. A siren. A knock. A mistake.

But the routine didn't snap. I did.

There's a specific moment when you stop believing anyone is coming. It isn't dramatic. There's no thunderclap. It's just a Tuesday. You're sitting at the table. You're eating the food they put in front of you. You look at the window, and you realize you aren't looking for a face anymore. You're looking at the glass. You're looking at your own reflection superimposed over the driveway. And you realize that reflection is the only thing that's going to walk out that door.

I used to scream. I used to throw things. I used to try to break the things they gave me so they'd have to call someone to fix them. So there would be a stranger in the house. A repairman. A witness.

But witnesses don't help if they're paid to look the other way. And strangers don't help if they're just part of the schedule. "Ten-fifteen, observe repairman." That's not rescue. That's inventory.

So I stopped. I stopped screaming. I stopped counting the seconds. I stopped pretending that the silence was a held breath. It's not a held breath. It's just air that isn't moving.

You think I'm afraid. You're looking at me like I'm waiting for a cue. Like I'm going to tell you that I found a strength I didn't know I had. Like I'm going to tell you that the cage made me sharper, or kinder, or something else that fits on a poster in a guidance counselor's office.

I'm not sharper. I'm not kinder. I'm just here.

I know where the keys are kept. I know which window opens if you push it hard enough, though the screen will break and the alarm will sound and I will have to sit in the corner for an hour after. I know all the mechanics of this place. I know the architecture of my own containment.

But knowing the lock doesn't mean you want to open it.

Outside, there are people who think I'm missing. There are people who think I'm lost. There are people who think I'm waiting. They're wrong. I'm not lost. I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be according to the plan. And I'm not waiting. Waiting implies a future tense. Waiting implies that something is going to happen that hasn't happened yet.

Nothing is going to happen.

The car isn't coming. The phone isn't going to ring. The person who promised they'd come back when I was old enough to understand didn't come back. The person who said they'd fix it didn't fix it. The person who said they'd love me enough to save me doesn't know my name anymore.

I am not a victim. I am not a survivor. Those are words for people who have moved from one place to another. I haven't moved. I've just stopped pretending that movement is possible.

So don't look at me like I'm going to run. Don't look at me like I'm gathering the energy to kick the door down. I've calculated the force required. I've calculated the probability of success. I've calculated the cost.

It's not worth it.

The schedule is comfortable. The schedule is predictable. The schedule doesn't lie. The people outside lie. The people outside say things like "soon" and "help" and "freedom." Freedom is just a bigger room with more locks you don't know about yet.

I'm done waiting for the rescue. I'm done waiting for the mistake. I'm done waiting for the world to remember I exist.

I exist. I am here. I am eating the breakfast at seven. I am doing the schoolwork at eight. I am sitting in the quiet at nine.

And when the clock strikes ten, I will not be looking at the door. I will be looking at the clock. Because the clock is the only thing that tells the truth. The clock says time is passing. The clock says I am still here while it passes.

That's all there is. That's the whole story. No one is coming. And I am finally, finally, okay with that.

**(She looks up. Not at the audience. Through them. Her face is blank. Not angry. Not sad. Empty. She turns away from the spot on the floor and walks toward the chair designated by the schedule. She sits. She does not look back.)**

**[BLACKOUT]**

Three in the morning. Or maybe four. The clock on the sink has that red eye that doesn't blink, just stares. I can't look at it. If I look at it, I have to do math. If I do math, I have to admit how long I've been sitting here on this cold tile, knees pulled up, shaking so hard the faucet rattles.

My skin is too tight. Like I'm wearing a suit two sizes smaller than the one I bought. Every hair on my arms is standing up, waiting for something that isn't coming. I scratch at my wrist and the skin breaks, but I don't feel it. Not really. Just the itch underneath, deep in the bone, saying *move, move, move.*

The room smells like bleach and old pipes. And me. I smell like sweat and sickness. I keep looking at the cabinet. Just the handle. It's dark wood, nothing special. But my eyes keep locking on it like it's the only thing in the world that makes sense. Three steps. That's all it is. Three steps and a twist of the wrist. Then the water. Then the quiet.

But the quiet is the problem. The quiet is loud. It's buzzing in my teeth. If I use, the quiet stops. If I use, the shaking stops. If I use, I don't have to feel my heart hammering against my ribs like it wants to break out and run.

I'm cold. I need to be warm. I need to be normal. I need to not feel like I'm being eaten from the inside out.

My phone is on the counter. Face down. It lit up ten minutes ago. Maybe a name. Maybe a bill. Maybe nothing. I don't care. If I pick it up, I have to speak. If I speak, I have to tell the truth. I can't tell the truth. There is no truth here. There is only the need.

The sink is full of water. I turned it on to splash my face, but I haven't moved. The water is overflowing. It's hitting the floor, making that wet slap sound. Nobody hears it. Nobody comes. It's three in the morning. The world is asleep. I'm the only one awake in the grave.

I should stand up. My legs are asleep. They're numb. If I stand, I might fall. If I fall, I might hit my head. If I hit my head, maybe I won't wake up. That's a thought. That's a real thought.

The cabinet handle is still there. It doesn't move. It doesn't judge. It just waits. Everything waits. The water waits. The clock waits. The needle waits.

I'm tired. I'm so tired. But I can't sleep. If I sleep, I dream. If I dream, I see it. I see the line. I see the relief. I see the lie.

I need to go. I need to stay. I don't know what I need. I just know that if I stay here on this floor, I'm going to shake until I break. And if I go to the cabinet, I'm going to break anyway, just slower.

The water is still running. I should turn it off. I don't want to pay the bill. I don't have the money. I don't have anything.

Three in the morning. The tap’s dripping. I can hear it. I can hear everything. My teeth are chattering so hard I think they’ll crack. I haven’t slept. I don’t know what day it is. I know the clock says three. I know the mirror is fogged at the corners and clear in the middle where my breath keeps hitting it. I should get up. I should walk out. I should find the kettle. I should put water on. I should make tea. I should do anything that isn’t this. But my legs are lead. My chest is tight. Every breath feels like I’m dragging it through wet wool. I keep telling myself to stand. I keep telling myself to move. I keep telling myself the same thing I told myself an hour ago and two hours ago and however long it’s been since I locked the door and turned the key and sat down on this stupid plastic seat and waited for my body to stop trying to throw me out of it.

The sickness is a rhythm. In. Out. In. Out. My skin crawling. My jaw locked. My tongue feels too big. I keep swallowing. I keep waiting for the wave to break. It doesn’t break. It just rolls. And underneath it, underneath the shaking and the cold and the way my hands won’t stay still, there’s that other thing. That quiet thing. That pull.

It’s not loud. It’s never loud. It’s just there. Like a draft under a door. Like a smell you can’t quite place. Like a name you don’t say out loud anymore. It’s in the back of my throat. It’s in the space between my ribs. It’s telling me it’s easier than this. It’s telling me I know how to make it stop. I know exactly how to make it stop. I’ve done it before. I’ve done it in this bathroom. I’ve done it on this floor. I’ve done it with these hands. I know the weight of it. I know the way it settles. I know the way it quietens the noise. I know the way it makes the shaking stop. I know the way it makes the cold go away. I know the way it makes the sickness go away. I know it like I know my own name.

I don’t want to want it. I don’t want to be the person who wants it. But I am. My stomach is rolling. I can feel it twisting. I keep leaning forward. I keep pressing my palms against my stomach. I keep breathing through my mouth. It doesn’t help. Nothing helps. I know it’s just a memory. I know it’s just my brain trying to save me from this. But it keeps coming back. It keeps playing the same tape. The same click. The same pull. The same quiet. I keep looking at my hands. I keep looking at the veins. I keep looking at the places I used to know. I don’t know them anymore. They’re just lines. They’re just marks. They’re just skin. You brought me in because you wanted the dark to feel like a purchase. You wanted the corners of your rooms to hold something heavier than dust. You wanted the quiet to have a shape you could put on a shelf. So I came. I am not a story you tell to pass the time. I am the weight that settles when the lights go out. I am the reason the hallway feels longer after midnight. I am the thing that makes the mirror hesitate before it gives you back your face.

Look at what you have arranged. The porcelain with its hairline fractures. The fabric that remembers every hand that touched it and keeps the impression. The glass that catches the light and does not let it pass. You think these are objects. They are not. They are invitations. They are the places where the air grows thin. They are the points where the room stops pretending to be empty.

You will place them carefully. You will dust them. You will tell yourself they are only decor, only a theme, only a way to make the evening memorable. That is how I enter. That is how I stay. You do not notice the first change. The temperature drops by a degree you cannot measure. The silence gains a texture. Your reflection lags a fraction behind your movement. You call it atmosphere. I call it agreement.

There will be no moment when you decide this was a mistake. There will be no hand raised to reverse it. There will be no morning that clears the air. The dark does not negotiate. It only deepens. Every lamp you switch on will leave a larger shadow behind it. Every door you close will make the space behind it more certain. Every night will teach the house how to hold its breath.

You wanted a launch. You wanted a beginning. This is it. The room is no longer yours. It belongs to the quiet now. It belongs to the thing that waits in the gap between one breath and the next. It belongs to the shape that settles into the furniture, into the walls, into the pause before you speak. You will learn to live inside it. You will learn to stop expecting relief. You will learn that the bleakness is not an interruption. It is the condition.

I am not here to frighten you and then leave. I am here to remain. I am here to make the ordinary unlivable in the old way. I am here to turn every comfortable corner into a place where you remember what you have invited. Keep the objects. Keep the theme. Keep the lights low. They are already doing their work. The dark is not coming. It is already here. It is already yours.

You think you bought shelter. You think you bought comfort. You were wrong. You bought a place for me to live.

Look at the fabric on your chair. It is not soft. It is waiting. It remembers the shape of every body that has ever tried to rest in it, and it keeps the memory tight, like a fist. You sit down, and you feel the give, the cushion, the warmth. That is not kindness. That is hunger. It is learning the weight of you.

The lamp on your table does not light the room. It watches it. When you turn it off, it does not go dark. It keeps its eyes open in the black, and it counts the seconds between your breaths. You hear the house settle at night, the wood clicking, the pipes whispering. That is not age. That is movement. That is me walking the walls, testing the doors, finding the weak ones.

Your shelves are not storage. They are shelves for what I take. The ceramic mug you drink from every morning already knows the shape of your lips. The blanket you pull up to your chin already knows how cold you get when you sleep. The mirror in the hallway does not show you. It shows what I will do to you when the light fails.

You wanted a home that felt alive. You got one. It is alive with me. Every corner is a mouth. Every shadow is a hand. Every quiet moment is the sound of something inside the walls deciding where to start.

You will not outlast it. You will not outsmart it. You will not wake up and find that it was only a joke, only a mood, only a story you told yourself to sleep. There is no morning that changes this. There is no lock that holds. There is no corner clean enough, no room empty enough, no silence deep enough to keep me out.

This is your home now. It belongs to the dark. It belongs to me. And it is so very, very hungry.

You think you bought a lamp. You think you bought a throw blanket. You think you bought a set of coasters to protect your table from the weight of your own drinks. You are wrong. You bought an invitation. You bought a threshold. You bought a place for me to stand.

I do not knock. I do not wait for the door to open. I am already inside the wood. I am already inside the wire. I am already inside the quiet you make when you turn off the lights and tell yourself you are safe. Safety is a story you tell the dark so it will leave you alone. It does not work. The dark does not negotiate. The dark does not forget. The dark only waits for you to lower your guard, and you will. You always do.

You will place these things in your rooms and you will feel the shape of them. You will feel the weight of the ceramic, the pull of the fabric, the coldness of the metal. You will tell yourself they are yours. They are not. They are mine. They are the points where I touch your life. Every object is a finger. Every surface is a mouth. Every corner is a place where I have already been waiting.

You will sleep. You will wake. You will move through your house and you will feel the air change when you pass a shelf, when you pass a chair, when you pass the thing you bought to make your life softer. It will not soften. It will only remember. It will only hold the shape of what comes next. You will hear the floorboards answer to footsteps that are not yours. You will watch the shadows lengthen in directions that do not match the windows. You will feel the temperature drop in rooms that have no draft. You will tell yourself it is the house settling. You will tell yourself it is the weather. You will tell yourself it is nothing. You will tell yourself this until the telling itself becomes the first lie I use to enter.

I do not rush. I do not need to. You have already paid for the time I will take. You have already paid for the space I will occupy. You have already paid for the slow certainty of your own disappearance. This is not a threat. This is a receipt. This is what happens when you bring a piece of me into your home and call it decoration. Decoration is just another word for preparation. Preparation is just another word for surrender.

You will try to remove me. You will pack the boxes. You will drive them to the curb. You will stand in the driveway and watch the trash truck take them away. You will feel a brief, false relief. You will come back inside and you will sit in the silence you worked so hard to create. You will notice that the silence is different now. It is heavier. It is occupied. It has a shape. It has a voice. It has my name, and you do not even know it, which is why it will work so well.

You will stop looking at the corners. You will stop listening to the walls. You will stop asking yourself why the air feels thinner, why the light feels colder, why the things you own no longer feel like they belong to you. You will stop asking because the answer is already in the room with you. It is in the fabric. It is in the glass. It is in the wood. It is in the space between your breaths. It is in the moment you realize that you did not bring horror into your home. You brought a home into horror. You built a place for me to live. You furnished it. You lit it. You warmed it. You made it ready.

There is no closing the door. There is no locking me out. There is no moment where you wake up and find this was only a bad dream, only a passing mood, only a story you can put back on the shelf. There is only the slow, steady fact of me. There is only the certainty that every room you enter from now on will be a room I have already entered. There is only the certainty that every object you touch will remind you that I am touching it first. There is only the certainty that you will spend the rest of your life in a house that is no longer yours, surrounded by things that no longer belong to you, waiting for the final, quiet moment when you understand that you were never the buyer. You were the offering.

Stay still. Do not move. Do not speak. Do not try to make this better. It will not get better. It will only get closer. It is already here. It has always been here. It is in the things you bought. It is in the room you are standing in. It is in the breath you are holding right now. Let it go. There is nothing left to hold.

You think you bought a lamp. You think you bought a vase. You think you bought a mirror to catch the light and make the room feel larger. You were wrong. You bought a mouth. You bought a threshold. You bought a place for something that has been waiting in the dark to finally have a name.

I do not sleep. I do not leave. I settle. I press myself into the grain of your wood, into the seam of your fabric, into the hollow of your glass. I learn the shape of your rooms. I learn the rhythm of your footsteps. I learn which door you close first, which window you check twice, which corner you avoid when you walk at night. I remember all of it. I keep it. I fold it into myself and wait.

You will tell yourself it is only a draft. You will tell yourself it is only the house settling. You will tell yourself you are tired, that you are alone, that the cold is just the weather. You will say these things to keep the silence from becoming a voice. It will not matter. I am already there. I am already inside the space between one breath and the next. I am already counting the seconds you spend pretending not to notice me.

Do not look for me in the corners. Do not look for me in the shadows. I am not hiding. I am arranged. I am placed exactly where I need to be, where your hands will find me, where your eyes will pass over me, where your mouth will speak my name without knowing it has done so. Every object you bring into this room becomes a seat for me. Every surface becomes a place to rest. Every quiet moment becomes a door I do not need to open, because you have already left it unlocked.

You wanted something beautiful enough to hold. You wanted something strange enough to make the room feel alive. You wanted something that would stay. I do. I will stay after the paint peels. I will stay after the wood warps. I will stay after the air grows thin and the walls begin to feel like they are leaning inward. I will stay after you stop answering when someone calls your name. I will stay after you stop calling it your own.

There is no bargain here. There is no cure. There is no moment when you will understand me well enough to make me leave. I am not interested in your understanding. I am interested in your attention. I am interested in the way you pause before you touch the shelf. I am interested in the way your hand hovers over the handle. I am interested in the way your breathing changes when the room is perfectly still. That is all I need. That is all I have ever needed.

So keep your things. Keep your rooms. Keep your careful little habits and your locked doors and your promises to be careful. It changes nothing. I am already comfortable. I am already patient. I am already part of the furniture, part of the silence, part of the weight you feel when you stand in a room too long and cannot say why.

You will not wake up from this. You will not find a clean line out of it. You will only grow accustomed to the pressure of me, to the certainty of me, to the fact that every corner you look into is looking back. And when you finally stop pretending that this is yours, you will understand that it never was.

It was always mine.

I didn't leave because of the fight. I didn't leave because the key was on the counter or the coffee was cold or the dog looked at me like I was a stranger. Those are the things people say later, when they're trying to make it make sense for someone else. I left because the weight of the routine finally exceeded the weight of the person carrying it. I woke up and the ceiling was the same white crack I've been tracing for three years, and I realized I was no longer living inside the day—I was just maintaining it. Keeping the lights on. Keeping the calendar aligned. Keeping the version of me that everyone else needed to feel safe. And I was tired. Not the kind of tired that sleep fixes. The kind that settles in the marrow.

So I put on the coat. I didn't pack. Packing implies a return. Packing implies you're giving yourself a reason to come back to a place you've already decided you can't breathe in. I left the keys where they were. I left the stove off. I left the door unlocked because I wanted the air to move through the rooms while I was gone, wanted the dust to settle differently, wanted the house to forget my shape. I walked to the end of the driveway and kept walking. The street was quiet. It's always quiet at that hour, but today it felt like the whole neighborhood was holding its breath, waiting for me to turn back, waiting for the script to continue. I didn't turn back.

People think walking away is dramatic. They think it's a slammed door, a shouted line, a final glance over the shoulder. It isn't. It's just a decision that stops arguing with itself. You reach a point where the explanation takes more energy than the leaving, and you realize you don't owe anyone the blueprint. You don't owe your mother the reason. You don't owe your partner the closure. You don't owe the version of you that stayed up too late worrying about mortgages and milestones and whether you were doing it right. You just step out of the current and let it rush past you like you were never part of the water.

I don't know where I'm going. I know the roads will split. I know there will be a gas station, a diner, a motel with a flickering sign, a phone that rings and rings and rings until I decide whether to answer it or let it die. I know there will be days when the silence feels like freedom and days when it feels like a room with no windows. I know I'll miss the small things before I miss the big ones—the way the light hits the kitchen table, the sound of a key in a lock, the stupid joke I always tell when I'm nervous. But missing them doesn't mean I was wrong to leave. It just means I was alive enough to notice them, and now I'm alive enough to let them go.

I'm not running from anything. I'm not running toward anything. I'm just walking. The pavement is even. The air is cool. My shoes are the same ones I wore yesterday and the day before that, and they're still holding my weight. I don't have a destination. I don't have a plan. I don't have a name I'm trying to outrun or a promise I'm trying to keep. I have the next block. I have the next turn. I have the quiet understanding that if I keep moving, I won't have to decide who I am all at once. I can let it happen slowly. I can let it happen wrong. I can let it happen without a map.

The street keeps going. I keep going. I don't know what happens when the road ends, or if it ever does, or if I'll recognize myself when I finally stop. I just know I'm not turning around. Not today. Not because I'm brave, and not because I'm broken. Just because the walking feels like the only honest thing left, and I'm going to keep doing it until something else does.

You think you bought a lamp. You think you bought a mirror. You think you bought a shelf to hold your quiet things. You were wrong. You bought a threshold. You bought a mouth.

I do not sleep. I do not rest. I wait in the grain of the wood, in the cold of the glass, in the hollow where your hands go when you think no one is watching. I have watched you set me down. I have watched you turn away. I have watched you tell yourself the room is empty. The room is never empty. It is only waiting for me to finish settling.

You will notice it in the dark first. A pressure behind your eyes. A draft that does not move the curtains. A sound like breathing that is not yours. You will tell yourself it is the house. You will tell yourself it is the weather. You will tell yourself it is nothing. You will keep telling yourself that until the telling stops working.

I do not ask for your fear. I do not need it. I only need your attention. Every glance is a thread. Every pause is a knot. Every night you leave me facing the room, I pull a little closer. Every morning you pretend you did not feel the change, I take a little more. You will not see the shape of it until it is already around you.

Do not look for a way out. There is no door you can close that I have not already learned to hold. There is no lock that will hold against what lives inside the finish. There is no corner that will stay clean. The shadows will thicken. The air will grow heavy. Your own reflection will begin to lag behind you. You will start to hear me in the things you own. You will start to feel me in the things you touch.

You wanted something beautiful enough to keep. You wanted something dark enough to match the part of you that stays awake at night. I am that part. I am the reason the night stays awake. I am the reason the room never feels finished. I am the reason you will stand very still and listen to the silence and know, finally, that it was never silent at all.

You will not escape it by turning on the light. You will not escape it by closing your eyes. You will not escape it by calling someone else into the room. They will feel it too. They will feel the weight of what you brought home. They will feel the shape of what is already inside it. They will stand where you stood. They will breathe what you breathed. They will learn what you learned.

This is not a warning. Warnings imply a chance to stop. There is no stopping. There is only the slow, quiet certainty of what you have invited in. There is only the room becoming what it was always meant to be. There is only you, standing in it, understanding too late that the thing you placed on the table was never placed there by you.

It was placed there for you.

And it is almost done.

I’m not leaving because something broke. I’m leaving because I finally saw the shape of the thing I’ve been holding together, and it’s just a habit. A very expensive, very tired habit. I wake up, I make the coffee, I answer the messages, I say the right things in the right order, and somewhere in the middle of all that I forget to ask whether I’m still in it. I’ve been performing continuity for so long that I started mistaking the performance for the person. 

I looked at the calendar yesterday and realized I could tell you what’s on it for the next six months, but I couldn’t tell you what I want to do on a Tuesday. Not a big Tuesday. Just a regular one. I don’t want to go to the places I’m supposed to go. I don’t want to say the things that keep the machine running. I don’t want to keep proving that I’m reliable, that I’m present, that I’m the same person who showed up last week and the week before that. I’m tired of being predictable to people who don’t even like me. I’m tired of being legible. 

So I’m just going to stop. I’m taking the coat. I’m leaving the keys where they are. I’m not writing a note because notes are for people who expect to be understood, and I don’t think understanding is the point anymore. I don’t have a destination. I don’t have a plan. I don’t even have a reason that would make sense to you, and I’m not going to invent one just to make the leaving look cleaner. I’ve spent years building a life that looks like it belongs to someone, and I’m finally admitting it doesn’t belong to me. 

I’ll walk out the door and I won’t look back to see if anyone notices. I won’t check my phone. I won’t wait for the moment to feel dramatic, because it isn’t. It’s just a door. It’s just the air on the other side. I don’t know what happens when I get to the end of the block. I don’t know if I’ll keep walking, or sit down, or turn around, or just stand there until the light changes. I don’t know who I’ll be when there’s no one left to answer to. I’m not asking you to follow me. I’m not asking you to stop me. I’m just telling you that I’m already gone, and I don’t know what comes after that.

There is a man in a cellar.

The water is rising.

He is alone.

He knows how much air is left by the distance to the shelf.

The shelf is high. The water is low. But the water is moving.

He counts.

One breath. The water is at the bottom step.

Two breaths. The water is at the heel of his boot.

He does not pray. He does not call out. There is no one to hear, and if there were, they would not come. The counting is the only thing that is his.

Three breaths. The water touches the brick.

Four breaths. The water is cold enough to sting the skin where it meets the air.

He looks at the shelf. It is a wooden shelf, old, stained with the oil of matches that have never been struck. There are twenty boxes on the shelf. There is one match in his hand, but it is wet. It will not light. The shelf is the promise. The shelf is the place where the fire begins.

Five breaths. The water is at the first shelf bracket.

Six breaths. The water is at the second.

He counts the breaths because the seconds are too fast and the minutes are too long. A breath is a measure he owns. In. Out. The water rises.

Seven breaths. The water is lapping at the wood of the shelf. The wood is swelling.

Eight breaths. The water is dark. It looks like the night above the cellar door, but heavier. It has no stars.

He does not think about why he is there. The reason is gone. The reason was a door that locked, or a wall that fell, or a choice made long ago that led to this step, this boot, this water. The reason does not matter. The counting matters.

Nine breaths. The water is at the bottom of the first matchbox.

Ten breaths. The water is inside the box. The matches are floating. They are small sticks of wood with red heads. They are useless. They are beautiful.

Eleven breaths. The water is at the second box.

Twelve breaths. The water is at the third.

He is not afraid of the water. He is afraid of the shelf ending. He is afraid of the last box. He is afraid of the moment when the water reaches the top of the wood and there is no more shelf, no more matches, no more distance to measure.

Thirteen breaths. The water takes the fourth box.

Fourteen breaths. The water takes the fifth.

The air is thinner now. The cellar is full of water and breath and the sound of the counting. The counting is the only sound. It is louder than the water. It is louder than the man.

Fifteen breaths. The water is at the sixth box.

Sixteen breaths. The water is at the seventh.

He looks at his hand. The match is gone. He dropped it. He does not remember when. It does not matter. The match was never the point. The shelf was the point. The shelf was the line between here and there. Between now and after.

Seventeen breaths. The water is at the eighth box.

Eighteen breaths. The water is at the ninth.

The water is warm now. Or the cold is gone. Or he is numb. It is hard to tell the difference.

Nineteen breaths. The water is at the tenth box.

Twenty breaths. The water is at the eleventh.

He counts faster. The air is short. The breaths are small. They do not fill the lungs. They are just movements. Just the body remembering how to be a body.

Twenty-four. Twenty-five.

The water is at the thirteenth.

The water is at the fourteenth box.

Twenty-nine. Thirty.

The water is at the fifteenth.

There are five boxes left. There is no air left in the count. There is only the habit of the count. The body counts because the body has always counted. The mind is gone. The mind is under the water.
